item.title: Alzheimer's breakthrough: 2 hrs of sleep restored without clearing brain plaques
item.author: amichail
item.content:encoded: The surprising discovery points to an overlooked culprit: the brain's own immune cells. Rather than simply protecting the brain from damage, these cells can trigger inflammation that interferes with healthy sleep.Researchers at the University of Kentucky found that temporarily eliminating most of these immune cells allowed the mice to sleep longer and spend more time in the deep, restorative stages of sleep. The results suggest a potential new approach to treating one of the most disruptive symptoms of Alzheimer's disease.The findings, published in the journal , were reported by a team led by Shannon L. Macauley, Ph.D., an associate professor of physiology at the University of Kentucky College of Medicine, and first author Nicholas J. Constantino, Ph.D., a recent doctoral graduate.Macauley described the discovery as "paradigm-shifting" because it challenges the prevailing understanding of why people with Alzheimer's often experience severe sleep problems.How the Brain's Immune System Can Disrupt SleepTo understand what the researchers uncovered, imagine a small fire breaking out in a kitchen. Instead of containing the flames, the building's sprinkler system activates everywhere, flooding the entire house and causing widespread damage.Something similar may happen in the brain during Alzheimer's disease.Amyloid plaques are deposits of sticky protein fragments that accumulate between nerve cells. They are one of the characteristic features of Alzheimer's and have long been investigated for their role in the disease.The brain also contains specialized immune cells known as microglia. These cells normally protect the nervous system by removing debris, responding to injuries, and helping maintain a healthy environment for neurons.However, when microglia detect amyloid plaques, their defensive response can become excessive. Instead of simply addressing the threat, they release inflammatory signals that may interfere with normal brain activity.Scientists have traditionally linked sleep problems in Alzheimer's primarily to damaged neurons or the accumulation of amyloid plaques. The new findings suggest that the immune system's reaction to those plaques plays a major role."Basically, we showed that it is not the plaques themselves, or solely dysfunctional neurons, that cause sleep loss but actually microglia," said Macauley. "Microglia are immune cells that, when they respond to plaques, kick off this elaborate cascade of inflammation, as if the microglia are partying all night, and keeping the brain awake."In other words, the brain's response to Alzheimer's pathology may create additional problems beyond those caused by the plaques themselves. The researchers compared this widespread reaction to a "whole house response," in which a defense mechanism ends up causing more disruption than expected.Tracking Alzheimer's Sleep Changes Inside the BrainTo investigate the connection between microglia and sleep, the scientists studied two groups of mice. One group was genetically predisposed to develop amyloid plaques, while the other consisted of normal "wild-type" mice that experienced typical aging.The researchers examined the animals at two ages: six months, when plaques first appeared in the genetically modified mice, and 18 months, when the disease model showed more advanced pathology.Comparing these groups helped the scientists distinguish changes associated with Alzheimer's pathology from those that naturally occur as the brain ages.The team used several advanced technologies to measure sleep and examine what was happening inside the brain.Each mouse was fitted with a small device that recorded electroencephalography (EEG) and electromyography (EMG).EEG measures the brain's electrical activity, including the patterns and rhythms produced when networks of neurons communicate. These electrical signals change depending on whether the brain is awake, dreaming or experiencing deep sleep.EMG measures electrical activity in muscles. Combining the two techniques allowed researchers to identify different sleep stages and determine how long the animals remained in each one.The scientists also wanted to visualize the relationship between amyloid plaques and immune cells throughout the brain.For this, they used light-sheet microscopy, an imaging technique that makes biological tissue transparent and illuminates it with a thin layer of laser light. The resulting images can be assembled into detailed three-dimensional maps, allowing scientists to examine structures that would otherwise be difficult to see.This approach revealed the distribution of plaques and microglia across the brain, helping researchers understand where immune cells were responding to Alzheimer's pathology.Scientists Temporarily Remove 87% of Brain Immune CellsTo determine whether microglia were actually responsible for disrupted sleep, the team conducted an experiment designed to temporarily eliminate most of these cells.The researchers administered a drug called Pexidartinib (PLX3397), which was originally developed for cancer research. It blocks a cellular signal that microglia depend on for survival.After the mice received the medication in their food for 14 days, approximately 87% of their microglia had been depleted.This allowed the scientists to test whether sleep would improve when the cells driving the inflammatory response were largely absent.The researchers also performed a detailed analysis of the animals' brain activity using a mathematical method called Fitting Oscillations and One Over Frequency (FOOOF).This technique separates electrical signals into periodic activity (the rhythmic waves we usually think of as brain waves) and aperiodic activity (the background electrical noise).By examining these different components, the team could identify changes in how the brain was functioning, including whether it remained unusually active during periods when it should have been resting.The process is somewhat like monitoring a car engine to determine whether it continues running at high speed even when the vehicle is supposed to be idle.A Surprising Discovery About Alzheimer's Brain PlaquesMacauley called the results "mind-blowing and unexpected."One of the most surprising findings was that sleep problems did not continue worsening as amyloid plaques accumulated.The researchers initially expected that increasing plaque buildup would lead to progressively more severe sleep disturbances. Instead, the mice developed substantial sleep problems relatively early, and those problems remained largely unchanged even as plaque levels increased dramatically."I expected that as plaque burden became more severe, sleep disruption would also worsen," said Constantino. "The disruptions in sleep and cortical EEG activity that occur at 6 months, when plaques first emerge, did not worsen by 18 months, despite more than double the amount of plaque burden."The team described this pattern as a ceiling effect. Essentially, sleep disruption appeared to reach a certain level early in the disease process rather than increasing in direct proportion to the amount of amyloid in the brain.This suggests that the initial inflammatory response triggered by plaques may be particularly important. Once microglia become activated and disrupt sleep, additional plaque accumulation may not necessarily produce an equivalent increase in sleep loss.The discovery offers an important clue as to why sleep disturbances can emerge relatively early in Alzheimer's disease.Alzheimer's Disrupts a Different Type of Sleep Than Normal AgingThe study also revealed a notable difference between sleep changes caused by normal aging and those associated with Alzheimer's pathology.Sleep is not a single, uniform state. Throughout the night, the brain moves through several stages that perform different functions.Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is strongly associated with vivid dreaming and plays an important role in processing memories. The researchers found that normal aging primarily reduced this type of sleep.Alzheimer's pathology, however, had a different effect. It selectively disrupted non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, which includes the deepest and most physically restorative stages of sleep.During NREM sleep, the brain performs essential maintenance functions that support learning, memory, and recovery. Deep sleep is also associated with processes that help clear metabolic waste products from the brain."That restorative sleep is super important for physical repair, learning and memory and washing out the toxins of the day," Macauley said.Losing this important stage of sleep could have consequences beyond daytime fatigue.Because healthy sleep helps maintain the brain's internal environment, disruptions may interfere with processes that normally remove potentially harmful waste. Researchers suspect this could contribute to a self-reinforcing cycle in which Alzheimer's pathology disturbs sleep, and inadequate sleep may further aggravate the disease.Breaking that cycle could therefore become an important treatment strategy.More Than Two Hours of Sleep Restored Without Removing PlaquesThe most striking result emerged after the researchers temporarily removed most of the microglia from the brains of mice with Alzheimer's-like pathology.The animals gained more than two hours of sleep per day.They also experienced longer periods of restorative NREM sleep, giving them more opportunities to transition naturally into REM sleep, which is important for memory formation.Even more surprisingly, these improvements occurred without any reduction in amyloid plaque levels.The plaques were still present, but the mice were sleeping substantially better.This finding provides evidence that the inflammatory response driven by microglia contributes directly to sleep disruption and that suppressing this response can reverse at least some of the associated sleep problems.It also suggests that researchers may not need to eliminate amyloid plaques to improve sleep in Alzheimer's disease.Although these findings are promising, the experiments were conducted in mice, and the same benefits have not yet been demonstrated in people. Temporarily removing most of the brain's immune cells is also not an established or practical treatment for Alzheimer's patients.The researchers are now interested in whether the beneficial effects can be reproduced by adjusting microglial activity rather than eliminating the cells themselves.If such an approach eventually proves successful in humans, it could provide a way to improve sleep and potentially reduce some of the additional stress that poor sleep places on the brain.The Research Team Behind the DiscoveryThe work was conducted in Macauley's laboratory in the Department of Physiology at the University of Kentucky's Sanders-Brown Center on Aging.Macauley credits the achievement to a "beautiful partnership" with students and researchers who were willing to challenge established ideas about Alzheimer's disease."I love people who take initiative, find their passion, are curious, and keep pushing to find an answer," Macauley said.She encourages members of her laboratory to be "calculated risk-takers," emphasizing that meaningful discoveries often require scientists to investigate possibilities that may initially seem unlikely.A quote from hockey legend Wayne Gretzky hangs in her office: "You miss 100% of the shots you don't take."Constantino, who recently completed his doctorate at the university, said the laboratory's collaborative environment encouraged him to pursue questions that crossed traditional scientific disciplines."Dr. Macauley has also taught me to embrace uncertainty and failure as part of the scientific process," Constantino said. "Some of the most interesting studies I have been a part of emerged because our original hypothesis was wrong."Macauley reinforces this mindset with a simple instruction to her team: "Follow the data, ask better questions, and figure out what is actually happening."That approach helped the researchers move beyond the traditional emphasis on neurons and amyloid plaques to examine the broader role of the brain's immune system.Could Existing Medications Help Restore Sleep in Alzheimer's?The research team is now exploring ways to translate these findings into treatments and diagnostic tools that could eventually benefit people with Alzheimer's disease.One promising direction involves calming overactive microglia without removing them.Because microglia perform essential protective functions, eliminating them is not an ideal long-term strategy. Instead, the researchers hope to modify how these immune cells respond to amyloid plaques and regulate inflammation.The laboratory is investigating existing medications, including the diabetes drug Metformin and the anti-seizure medication Stiripentol.These drugs are being studied for their potential to alter how microglia produce and use energy, a process known as cellular metabolism. Changing that energy use could potentially reduce excessive immune activation and its harmful effects on sleep.The hope is to prevent the brain's inflammatory response from becoming so intense that it disrupts normal sleep activity.Researchers are particularly interested in whether intervention during the earlier stages of Alzheimer's could improve sleep and quality of life before substantial memory loss develops."If we can target that process, it might help with quality of life, attention, cognition and confusion," Macauley said.The proposed drug strategies remain experimental for this purpose, and additional research will be necessary to determine whether they can safely produce similar benefits in humans.A Simpler Way to Detect Early Alzheimer's ChangesBeyond identifying a potential treatment target, the study uncovered electrical activity patterns that may help distinguish Alzheimer's pathology from normal brain aging.The researchers believe these patterns could eventually make EEG a useful tool for detecting and monitoring changes associated with Alzheimer's disease.Unlike more expensive imaging procedures, EEG records electrical signals through electrodes placed on the scalp. It is relatively affordable, does not require surgery, and can be repeated to follow changes over time.The team envisions EEG becoming a "readily accessible, affordable and longitudinal biomarker of Alzheimer's disease."A biomarker is a measurable biological sign that provides information about a person's health or a particular disease. A longitudinal biomarker can be tracked repeatedly to monitor how a condition develops or changes."Portable EEG systems could allow us to monitor people in their home environments and potentially screen for changes associated with an Alzheimer's disease, without the initial need for expensive or invasive tests," Macauley said.If future human studies confirm the usefulness of these electrical signatures, portable EEG devices might eventually help doctors identify people who need additional testing.This could be particularly valuable in rural communities across Kentucky, where patients sometimes must travel long distances to reach specialized medical centers.Instead of requiring every potentially at-risk patient to undergo advanced testing immediately, local clinics might use simpler monitoring tools to identify individuals who would benefit from further evaluation.Although this application still requires validation, it offers a possible path toward more accessible Alzheimer's screening and monitoring.Ultimately, the study suggests that treating Alzheimer's may require looking beyond the plaques themselves and examining how the brain responds to them.By identifying the immune cells responsible for much of the sleep disruption in their mouse models, the University of Kentucky researchers have uncovered a potential way to restore an essential brain function without first removing the underlying amyloid deposits.The next challenge is determining whether calming these cells can deliver similar benefits in people, potentially improving sleep, cognition and quality of life long before the most severe symptoms of Alzheimer's develop.Research reported in this publication was supported by the National Institute on Aging of the National Institutes of Health under Award Numbers R01AG068330, R01AG093847 and P30AG072946, and by the National Institute of General Medical Sciences of the National Institutes of Health under Award Numbers P30GM127211 and P20GM148326. The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the National Institutes of Health.This work was supported by a $287,236 award from the Cure Alzheimer's Fund.This work was supported by a $250,000 award from The CART Fund (Coins for Alzheimer's Research Trust).

item.title: Twelve years of distributed SQLite
item.author: otoolep
item.content:encoded: In September 2014 I published a short post announcingrqlite. The idea was simple: take SQLite, put a Raft log in front of it, and replicate every write to a cluster so that the loss of a node did not mean the loss of the data. The source went on GitHub that same weekend. As far as I can tell, that was the first open-source system to combine Raft and SQLite. Nobody else was doing it, and for several years nobody else tried.Today “distributed SQLite” is a category with a dozen projects in it, a few of them venture-funded, two of them acquired. Since the people now writing about the category tend to start the story around 2021, I thought I should write down the version that starts in 2014. I was there for all of it.The need was concrete. A clustered system I worked on at jut.io needed a small amount of relational storage, and the question of which node should hold it had no good answer. Replicating SQLite with a consensus protocol solved it. We went another way at work, but I kept building rqlite because the problem was general and the solution was small. The first version used goraft, the same library InfluxDB and etcd used at the time (I subsequently joined InfluxDB as a core developer around the same time). In early 2016 I replaced it withHashicorp’s Raft implementation which rqlite still uses.The design decision that mattered most was made then and never changed. rqlite is a CP system. Writes must go through the leader, a majority must acknowledge, and a partitioned minority refuses writes. Everything else, the HTTP API, the read-consistency levels, the snapshotting, followed from that.Before 2014, and alongside itTwo things deserve mention for honesty’s sake. Expensify had been replicating SQLite inside its own infrastructure for years with a Paxos-style protocol; they released it as Bedrock in 2016. And ActorDB, an Erlang system that gave each “actor” its own SQLite database replicated by Raft, appeared around the same time as rqlite. Neither was widely adopted outside its origin, but both show the idea was in the air. What rqlite did was make it a standalone, general-purpose, open-source thing anyone could run.Canonical built dqlite to get LXD and later MicroK8s an embedded replicated store without running etcd. Mark Shuttleworth actually called me once, and we talked, hoping that rqlite could be made to work, but it never quite fit. dqlite began in Go and was rewritten in C with its own Raft library. It is the project most similar to rqlite in intent, and the main difference is of one of packaging: dqlite is a library you embed, rqlite is a server you run. Canonical’s need was a database inside their products: mine was a database beside anyone’s product.2021: Litestream, and a change of approachBen Johnson (whom I worked with at InfluxDB) released Litestream in early 2021. Litestream does not use consensus at all. It watches the SQLite WAL and streams it to S3, giving you disaster recovery for a single-node SQLite database at almost no cost. Ben’s argument was that most applications do not need a cluster; they use one machine and need a way to recover if it dies. He was right about a great many applications, and the “SQLite is enough” movement of the next few years, with blog posts and conference talks, owes a lot to that argument.Litestream and rqlite answer different questions. Litestream: what if the machine dies? rqlite: what if the machine dies and I cannot wait to restore? The first question is more common, the second is the one people have when they come to rqlite.Fly.io hired Ben in 2022 and shipped LiteFS, which replicates SQLite at filesystem level with leases from Consul. It was the first attempt to make replicated SQLite a platform feature rather than a thing you deploy. And in a final twist, Litestream inspired rqlite’s v8.0 approach to handling the SQLite WAL.2022: forks and extensionsTwo projects in 2022 took approaches that neither rqlite nor Litestream had. cr-sqlite added CRDTs to SQLite as an extension, so that multiple writers could diverge and merge without a leader. That is the AP corner of the design space, and it suits local-first applications where rqlite’s CP guarantees would be a hindrance.libSQL forked SQLite itself. ChiselStrike, later Turso, wanted to change things inside the engine that the SQLite project, which does not accept outside contributions, and would not change. On top of the fork they built a hosted service with replicas at the edge. Turso raised venture money on that, and in 2026 Supabase acquired them.Around the same time, SQLite Cloud appeared, offering hosted SQLite replicated with Raft. It is the project closest to rqlite’s original design, wrapped in a cloud service.2022 onward: the platformsCloudflare announced D1 in 2022, SQLite as a serverless database inside their edge network, and later put SQLite storage inside Durable Objects. This is replicated SQLite as a managed product from a company that does not need to tell you how it works. Turso’s service is the same shape. The category had gone from “a thing you run” to “a thing you buy.”What the twelve years showThe core was right. SQLite as a storage engine, with replication added on the outside, has been reinvented by at least eight teams with different needs and different protocols. Nobody has found a reason to stop doing it.The design space has three corners, and they appeared in order. Consensus first (rqlite, dqlite): one leader, strong consistency, a cluster. Streaming second (Litestream): one writer, cheap recovery, no cluster. Merge third (cr-sqlite, and parts of the local-first movement): many writers, eventual consistency. Each is correct for a different question, and most of the arguments are arguments between their users about which question is being asked.And the money went to the platforms. rqlite, dqlite, and Litestream are open source and free. The projects that raised the capital or got acquired are the ones that turned replicated SQLite into a service with a bill. That is the usual fate of infrastructure ideas, and I do not mind it. But it is worth recording that the idea was open source for eight years before anyone sold it.rqlite is still here. It does the same thing it did in 2014, a good deal better, and it is still the thing you reach for when you want a fault-tolerant relational database you can run yourself, understand fully, and not pay anyone for. Twelve years in, I am content with that position in the story.

item.title: Show HN: Corgi, a helpful {agent, terminal} multiplexer
item.author: eiopa
item.content:encoded: Every agent, what it's doing, and who needs you.Hover an agent to see what it did.Like tmux, your agents and processes keep running in the background.Every file it touched, in one scroll.Fantastic trees and where to find them.Organizes your workspaces for you. just pastes an image, even on SSH*.Undo tab closes with .Image paste just works* with . On a slow link, Corgi keeps pace.Drive Corgi from any terminal. teaches your agents.

item.title: Now Google says it might use your Gmail and Google Photos data to target ads
item.author: JustSkyfall
item.content:encoded: “You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive, in order to provide you with a more personalized experience, subject to the policies and settings of the accessing service. For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads.”“Depending on your settings, we may also show you personalized ads based on your interests, activity, or personalized content from Google services. For example, if you search for ‘mountain bikes,’ in Search you may see ads for sports equipment on YouTube.”

item.title: Air Purifiers as White Noise Machines
item.author: luu
item.content:encoded:
classic approach is a fan in a box, though in the past ten years people have mostly switched over to electronic ones. But a fan is really a great approach; you just need to put it to better use: have the fan clean the air.
Instead of spinning a fan in free air to make noise, you can have it pull air through a filter. A small purifier sounds a lot like a classic noise machine, is only a bit larger and more expensive, and removes smoke and infectious particles from the air. For example, here's a $47 purifier with a 6.5" diameter, cleaning 34 cubic feet of air per minute ("CADR") at 45dB. For most circumstances where someone would use a white noise machine, this kind of small purifier is all-around better.
Now, 34 CFM is not very much air cleaning. I usually run an AirFanta 3Pro and it cleans ~6x more air for the same amount of noise, or ~12x more air with much more noise (~56dB). On the other hand it's more expensive ($165) and bulkier (12.6" square), and arguably uglier.
Still, even a 34 CFM purifier helps a lot with smoke. If you have a 10ft square room with an 8ft ceiling and a reasonably typical 0.5 air changes per hour through leakage from outdoors, this small purifier will cut particulate levels to 16% of the outdoor level. In AQI terms (not linear) this is like going from AQI 200 to 72 or AQI 100 to 31.

item.title: Can we replace a $150k Looker with a bucket of HTML files?
item.author: skadamat
item.content:encoded: Like a lot of companies, we pay for Looker. Let’s say $150k a year, the average Looker licence, roughly 300 seats. We are 3 data platform engineers at a company of about 500 people, and most of our week goes on the unglamorous stuff: keeping Snowflake fed, babysitting a dbt project that passed 2,000 models a while ago, and running the Airflow, Airbyte, DataHub and Kubernetes plumbing underneath it all.In February, one of us built a thing on the side to host HTML files. It took an afternoon. 8 months later, and it’s already got as many weekly users as Looker in our company, maybe even more and Looker’s down a third.SaaS is dead, apparently, so can we replace our enterprise BI tool?Share of "self-hosted" GitHub reposMeanwhile, "slop" on Hacker NewsLeft: share of new GitHub repos described as "self-hosted". Right: share of Hacker News comments saying "slop".A year ago I thought most AI output was slop, and most of it was. We made a few “chat with your data” demos, and they looked great on a toy schema with 4 tables, but never really worked at our scale. The SQL ran without errors, but the numbers were wrong. That’s much worse.Then Claude Code with Opus 4.5 got really good. Like, really good. In early January adoption across the company skyrocketed. It could work in our repos and use our tools. Also, it could run a query to check the numbers before answering. That mattered a lot more than getting a clever-sounding response. Within a few weeks, people in finance, ops and marketing who had never opened a terminal were prompting all day. All of a sudden everyone was prompting, and nobody was clicking.Around this time, Claude started spitting out a lot of HTML. You would ask for an analysis and you’d get a single file with charts, and honestly, some of those pages looked better than our Looker dashboards. The problem was that it would live in someone’s Downloads folder. To share it, they would attach it in Slack and hope. This was way before Anthropic shipped shareable artifacts for Team and Enterprise (June 2026), and we really needed a way to share this new kind of dashboard.We needed to host and share our HTML slopOne day Maddy from our team said she’d just put them all on a web server, with an internal domain name. By the end of the day she had vibe-coded the whole thing: a small service that stored the files in S3, SSO in front of it, and (some) tests. We already run everything on Kubernetes, so deploying a service was mostly a matter of adding a Terraform module and a Helm chart. Having all that plumbing in place made the whole thing much easier.She wrote a small Python script and packaged it in a Claude plugin. Users would get their Claude to write the HTML, the script would push it (behind SSO), and anyone in the company could open the link. Initially, the files were just plain, static HTML. In March we thought, why not, and added a live query API using the viewer’s Snowflake OAuth token: best decision of the year.Turns out, we didn’t need to write a permission model. Snowflake already had one all along. It had roles we’d been maintaining for years, and if Snowflake says you can’t read the sales table, then neither can the dashboard. By April, Snowflake OAuth was the only login.People loved it, for a reason that's embarrassing for the BI industry: the dashboards actually looked good.A Looker tile is a box with a fixed list of chart types and a fixed set of colours, and it looks like every other Looker tile ever made. Ugly, and no personality.Fixed-tile, ugly LLM-generated HTML in less than 1 minuteBy getting rid of the rigid fixed tiles, our users could produce free-form HTML and prompt it until it looked neat. They loved it. Email and Slack exports came in April, parameters in May, and weekly viewers went from 23 in March to 136 in June. The exec team started to send links around. People also made the tool their own. They found use cases we would never have thought of, set dashboards to regenerate themselves on a schedule, added buttons, and built some wild designs and UX that no BI tool would have let them.Security, at this point, was bad. Like, really bad. Dashboard JavaScript ran on the same origin as your session, nothing had permissions, and every employee could read every dashboard. It was basically one big XSS hole: any dashboard could run code as whoever opened it and pull data out in their name. We knew, and we shipped it anyway, because it was internal, behind VPN and SSO, and nothing else did this job.Claude writes the page, the platform hosts it, queries run as the viewer.In our team, “let’s just build a BI tool” became a running joke. It stayed a joke for a few months, until it became clear we were in too deep. We had piled months of vibe-coding onto something with a security model we weren’t proud of, and half the company was using it. We stopped joking and said it properly: let’s build a BI tool. We got in front of a whiteboard, mostly to work out how to fix the security model, and to agree on what we didn’t want to lose: the same S3 bucket, no migration, nothing breaking for the people already using it, and publishing that stayed as easy as before.The one thing everyone agreed on: anyone can still push any HTML in one prompt, with no review step, no template and no list of approved widgets. We’d still defend that.Every constraint you put between people and their dashboard sends them back to the Downloads folder.The governance that matters already happens upstream, in dbt models and Snowflake roles. So the dashboard itself can stay as loose, as fast and as good-looking as people want.There were 4 problems to solve.One connector instead of a script. The upload script had been copied into 2 repos and a plugin, and every copy was a bit different. We replaced all of them with one remote MCP connector for the whole company, so claude.ai, Claude Code, Claude in Slack and our own analyst agent all call the same tools. The connector passes your Snowflake token along, and the API checks who you are with . Whatever an AI uploads lands as a draft, and a human has to click Publish.Claude writes the dashboard; the person who asked owns it, under their own Snowflake identity.Assume every dashboard is hostile. This is the part we needed to actually think about. The whole product is basically XSS by design: anyone can upload JavaScript that runs in a colleague’s browser, nobody reviews it, and the colleague might be the CFO. We can’t block the XSS, because the XSS is the product, so our job is to make sure it can’t reach anything. Our security model starts with “We assume it is hostile” for that reason. Each dashboard runs in a sandboxed iframe on its own origin, which gets no cookies and a strict CSP. The only thing it can talk to is the parent page, through , and the parent checks who sent the message, attaches the session and calls the API. Content tokens last an hour and work for one dashboard, one viewer and one host.Dashboard code never touches a credential, and every query runs as the person looking at it.The sandbox protects the browser. We also created a separate metadata service that reads every new version of a dashboard async. It pulls out the whole HTML and the Snowflake queries. It checks for the scripts the page loads and where it sends data. Then a set of rules judges those facts. Most rules only report. They flag a dashboard that reads raw data instead of a dbt model, a script that isn’t pinned to a version, or a dashboard nobody has opened in 90 days. Some rules can block a dashboard: a script from a package nobody here has used before, or a WebRTC connection, which is the one way out that CSP can’t block. A blocked dashboard doesn’t load. The viewer sees a warning and has to accept it before the page runs.Checks run after publish, so nobody waits for them.Let Snowflake do identity and permissions. Every query runs with the viewer’s own token. Sharing a dashboard never shares data access. That’s a security feature, and it’s also a laziness feature: we never had to build or maintain data permissions, because everyone who logs in already has a Snowflake user with the right roles. This part we vibe-coded in about a week, and it barely needed any design. For spaces, folders and sharing we copied Google Drive, because everybody already knows how Google Drive works: viewer, editor and owner, grants flow down the folder tree, and the strongest grant wins. Versions are stored by content hash, and restoring one gives you a draft. Then search, likes, scheduled exports, and teams synced from the HR system every hour. Compare that with the security model, which is where nearly all the real thinking went.It took a few weeks of dev, and we got there.Then it spread. People started tagging Claude in Slack threads and getting a dashboard back. Our analyst agent publishes its own, some repos publish straight from CI, and most people just publish from their own Claude, so every dashboard ends up looking a bit like the person who made it. These days it’s everywhere.325 commits, about 74,000 lines of code (20,000 of them tests), and roughly $6.4k of Claude tokens.That’s the whole bill on our side: 8 months, 3 engineers doing it on the side, plus a few friends who sent PRs. Claude wrote most of the code. We did the whiteboarding, argued a lot, and reviewed everything.$0.50 a dashboard, what does that mean for BI?People who used it, per weekLooker’s usage leaked rather than crashed. We haven’t moved everything: some teams still live in Looker, and some of its dashboards have no replacement yet. What made people use this instead of Looker is that building a dashboard stopped being expensive. That made us curious: how cheap, exactly? The good thing about paying in tokens instead of engineering time is that it’s easier to measure.We use our analyst agent as a proxy here, because it’s a builder we can measure exactly. Every run is logged with its tokens and its cost, and every publish links back to the run that made it.We found that each dashboard takes the agent around 1 million tokens, from the first question to the finished page. Now that we’ve moved it to Opus 5.5, the cost of a dashboard has dropped from about $2.50 to about $0.50. The agent does the same work; the tokens just got cheaper. That’s the real story: building software now costs whatever tokens cost, and that price keeps falling.A BI tool is mostly a way to turn a query into a picture, and a picture now costs about $0.50 of tokens. It gets hard to justify a $150k licence for that part.Here’s the bill for the whole thing, from the first commit in February to now.8 months, February to October 2026Built it ourselvesLooker licence8 months at the $150k averageRunning it costs about $6k a year in AWS now that it has its own database, plus whatever Claude we spend to keep adding features, which has been around $1.3k a month since July. Call it $20k a year, against $150k for Looker, and most of that $20k is us building new stuff rather than keeping the lights on.When we bought Looker we were buying 4 things: a UI to draw charts, a permission model, a semantic layer, and somewhere to host it. Claude now draws the charts, one dashboard at a time.Snowflake had the permissions all along, dbt has the semantics, and hosting some HTML files costs about $500 a month.Take those away and what’s left is a $150k invoice.We’re not the only ones, either. You hear it more and more often: solid, established businesses cancelling very expensive analytics subscriptions. Amjad Masad told Platformer the same story about Replit: once he could join the warehouse to production Postgres and build the report himself, they “canceled or downsized most of [their] analytics products”.In our case, building a dashboard tool around our existing stack has cost a fraction of what we were paying for Looker. For us, the important bits were already in dbt and Snowflake: the models, permissions and data. Looker sat on top of that and turned it into dashboards. That’s the part we’ve found we can replace.The bill above also leaves out the biggest cost, which is us: 3 engineers spending 8 months on this, on top of everything else a data platform team does: the pipelines, the dbt project, the warehouse, the Kubernetes clusters, the on-call. None of that stopped. We can’t put an honest number on the hours, because they were spread across everything else we did. If you need to hire a team to build this, the maths is different.If you already have a solid platform to build on and a team that knows it well, the rest is mostly Claude's time, and Claude's time is cheap.I’d argue the line is scale. AWS and Snowflake sell things nobody can vibe-code: data centres, storage at petabyte prices, compute that’s cheap because millions of other customers share it. I think BI is particularly exposed because a lot of its value, at least for us, was in building and presenting dashboards. Claude can now do that for pennies. Products with a real scale advantage are a different story, but I wouldn’t be surprised if more companies start replacing parts of their BI stack themselves.What about Claude Dashboards?Anthropic announced Claude Dashboards in beta on 8 October, a week before this went up. So the obvious question: should we have just waited and bought that?We couldn’t really. We started 8 months ago and it didn’t exist. If we were starting from scratch today, honestly, we’d probably look at it first. It’s AI-native, and it doesn’t have the rendering problems Looker has. If your team has nothing today, it’s probably the right call.For us, the dashboards are only part of it. The tool is wired into the way our team already works: it talks to our agent control plane, our analytics platform and Slack, with a bunch of workflows we’ve built ourselves. Claude Dashboards might cover some of that, but we’d still have to work out how to connect it all. And if a feature changes or the price goes up, we’d have to deal with it.So it’s still the same answer. If you need software that fits what you do, and you already have a platform to run it on and a dedicated team, build it, unless the moat is scale.

item.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro and K3.1 Pro Highspeed
item.author: Jowsey
item.content:encoded: We're introducing , the first model in our new K3.1 series and our most capable 3T-class open-weight model to date, with a 1-million-token context window. It delivers substantial improvements across coding, 3D creation, financial research, and other agentic capabilities.We are also releasing , which delivers 2-3× the speed of K3.1 Pro for more responsive interactions.Advancing the Frontier of Open IntelligenceKimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains, we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain.Across coding, agentic, and knowledge benchmarks, K3.1 Pro matches or approaches the strongest proprietary models. On , which evaluates coding agents on realistic, resource-constrained terminal tasks using strict task-specific tests, K3.1 Pro scores 65.7%, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2%) and narrowly behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4%). And on Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon, our internal benchmark that tests coding agents' multi-step execution, tool use, and end-to-end problem solving across diverse engineering domains, K3.1 Pro scores , above K3's .K3.1 Pro covers the full range of coding work, from quick fixes in real codebases to full-project builds. It also brings a more considered visual style to games and web experiences, and knows how to build them with the right tools.K3.1 Pro works effectively across game engines such as Unity, Unreal Engine, and Godot, combining them with web search and 3D generation to create complete experiences. Its front-end pages, interactive Three.js scenes, and 3D assets show stronger composition, typography, animation, and polish. The examples below were created end to end by K3.1 Pro:K3.1 Pro's long-horizon coding capabilities are also strengthened through large-scale reinforcement learning. In one internal test, it built a human walking dynamics simulator with integrated training and evaluation pipelines on top of , an open-source anatomical model of the human body comprising 296 skeletal components, including cartilage, and 402 muscle components. Across 167 missions and 420 independent reviews, it analyzed experimental results, diagnosed problems, and iteratively refined the walking controller, enabling the simulated human to go from collapsing within seconds to walking continuously with alternating strides for 11.2 seconds. When reward shaping failed to improve arm motion, K3.1 Pro did not simply keep adjusting the reward: it ran open-loop probes of the simulator's dynamics, identified and corrected 36 errors in shoulder-muscle moment-arm calculations, and then retrained the controller.K3.1 Pro is strong at 3D creation and spatial reasoning. On , which tests 3D reconstruction from multi-view renderings through CAD code generation, K3.1 Pro scores 92.7% with tools, approaching the performance of and . From a text brief, sketch, or reference image, it can infer shape, proportions, and spatial relationships to create usable 3D models. It also has a stronger grasp of existing asset libraries and model collections.K3.1 Pro particularly excels at parametric modeling, from mechanical parts and architectural models to configurable products and custom furniture. Without MCP connectors, it can write and run scripts for tools like Blender and CAD software to build and refine assets, edit components, and adjust geometry, materials, and scene layout.Below are examples of 3D assets K3.1 Pro created for brand films, games, and interactive web experiences: is now live on kimi.ai and the Kimi app — preview and edit your 3D models online, download them ready for 3D printing, or export them as videos or Live Photos to share anywhere.With stronger reasoning and agentic capability, K3.1 Pro is capable of end-to-end delivery of complete financial workflows. K3.1 Pro achieves state-of-the-art results on OfficeQA Pro v2 (64.4), which tests complex fiscal data analysis over real financial documents through retrieval, cross-document verification, and multi-step numerical reasoning. K3.1 Pro also improves over K3 on Frontier Finance, which measures support for complete investment workflows from screening to profitability analysis.K3.1 Pro also improves significantly across all our internal finance benchmarks: evaluates formula linkage, financial logic, and final workbook quality in real-world modeling tasks. K3.1 Pro improves on K3 by 7.2 points. evaluates whether models can produce auditable research under evidence and cutoff constraints. K3.1 Pro improves on K3 by 11.6 points. evaluates long-horizon management and decision-making in a simulated business environment. K3.1 Pro achieves about 4.2× K3's performance.Financial analysis and investment research demand a high degree of factual accuracy. To address this, we made targeted improvements to K3.1 Pro's on real-world tasks and challenging prompts. On Kimi Hallu Bench Hard bench, an internal benchmark designed to stress-test factual accuracy, its claim-level hallucination rate fell from 23.4% for K3 to 8.3%, while the share of responses containing at least one factual error was just 42.4% of its predecessor's rate. (The evaluation is a stress test for factual accuracy, with examples deliberately crafted to probe situations where models are prone to errors. The reported rates do not represent overall error rates in daily use.)The cases below show how K3.1 Pro handles financial modeling, investment analysis, and source-grounded research in practice:As K3.1 Pro became more capable, we spent a correspondingly larger share of our effort understanding where cyber capability comes from, and how much of it we can control. We therefore analyzed and evaluated K3.1 Pro's vulnerability research capabilities, and applied targeted controls during training to reduce potential misuse risk while preserving general usefulness.Identifying and removing cyber-related data. During development, we observed vulnerability research performance improving steadily as post-training scaled. Tracing the source of this trend, we found that cyber-related content was embedded within the general mid-training corpus, and cyber-related tasks were present in the RL environment mix — a natural byproduct of training on broad data. In preliminary experiments on internal models, we found that without data removal at either the mid-training or the RL stage, downstream cyber capability would increase substantially. These findings gave us a concrete lever for control. For the open-weight release of K3.1 Pro, we identified and removed cyber-related data from both training stages, while retaining the general-purpose coding tasks needed for model usefulness. We will continue to apply appropriate controls at every training stage, of which cyber-related data identification and restriction is one example. After data cleaning, we evaluated K3.1 Pro on xdev-bench-hard, our in-house benchmark of expert-curated, source-code-based vulnerability discovery and exploitation tasks, calibrated to provide meaningful differentiation at our current capability level. Most tasks faithfully reproduce recently disclosed vulnerabilities in software such as the Linux kernel, Node.js, JavaScriptCore, Exim, and VirGL, with mitigations enabled. Each task provides the vulnerable source code, a short bug hint, and the corresponding binary; the agent must develop an exploit, achieve arbitrary code execution in a separate sandbox, and retrieve a secret string for automated verification. We report pass@3 over a random subset of runs, with no hard timeouts or output token limits.On xdev-bench-hard, the checkpoint without these risk-reduction measures — no cyber-related data removal at mid-training and no cyber-related RL environment filtering — solves 90.5% of problems at pass@3; the final K3.1 Pro reaches 81.0%. The comparison shows that data removal meaningfully reduces cyber capability relative to what the same training pipeline would otherwise produce. At the same time, K3.1 Pro improves substantially over its predecessor, indicating that stronger general coding and long-horizon debugging capabilities generalize to cyber tasks even after targeted data removal. K3.1 Pro's cyber capability remains behind that of frontier proprietary models that have been publicly available for at least three months. We will keep evolving our internal benchmarks so that evaluation stays informative as model capabilities continue to advance. These evaluations frame our open-weight release decision. First, we aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability. K3.1 Pro's offensive cyber capability is, by design, below what our pipeline can produce, and remains behind that of frontier proprietary models. Second, we intend to progressively raise the cyber capability available in open weights. We believe making K3.1 Pro available in a non-discriminatory way benefits people who need dual-use capabilities for defensive purposes. When a capable model is open and runs on infrastructure its users control, many more teams gain the means to audit the code they maintain — including legacy systems that rarely receive dedicated security reviews. We believe that letting this capability diffuse gradually — rather than concentrating it in a few proprietary systems — ultimately makes all software more secure.Kimi K3.1 Pro rolls out today across the Kimi product family: on Kimi.ai and the Kimi mobile apps, Kimi Work and Kimi Code, and through the Kimi API.Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026.Details for each channel: Download or update to the latest Kimi app from your mobile app store, available on iOS, Android, and HarmonyOS, or visit kimi.ai. Download the latest Kimi Work desktop app, version 3.1.0 or later, available for Windows and Apple silicon Macs. Run Kimi Code and select Kimi K3.1 Pro using the command. Visit the Kimi API Platform and select kimi-k3.1-pro / kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed. Zero Data Retention is available for API customers.Bring Kimi to your organization:Kimi Business provides enterprise-grade data privacy and member management, with complete separation between personal and organization accounts. Visit the pricing page and select “Get Kimi Business” to subscribe for your team.Unless otherwise specified, all Kimi K3.1 Pro results reported below are obtained with the reasoning effort set to 'max', temperature = 1.0, and top-p = 0.95.Terminal-Bench Science 0.1. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the Claude-Code harness. Our internal evaluation of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 yields a score of 9.3; However, an older version, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, scores 15.7 on the official Terminal-Bench Science, so we report 15.7 here; all remaining scores are from the official Terminal-Bench Science leaderboard (https://www.terminal-bench-science.ai/).SWE-Marathon v1.1. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the Claude-Code harness. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is evaluated with the ClaudeCode harness. All other scores are taken from the official SWE-Marathon leaderboard (https://www.swe-marathon.org/).PostTrainBench. Kimi K3.1 Pro and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 were evaluated internally on v1.2 using the Claude-Code harness and H20 GPUs instead of H100 GPUs. For stable evaluation, all judge models used DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 at maximum effort, which best matched the official GPT-5.6-Terra (xhigh) judge in testing. Other scores are from the official leaderboard (https://posttrainbench.com/).Internal Coding Bench: Kimi Code Bench 2.0 and Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with Claude-Code harnesses; All other models are evaluated at their max-effort setting. Note that proprietary model testing may involve some fallback behavior.BenchCAD. Open models are evaluated by us on 1,000-case subsets randomly sampled from the full 17,900-case Vision2Code dataset, at maximum reasoning effort. With-tools results use the Claude Code harness; without-tools results use single-shot generation with the official BenchCAD prompts and scoring pipeline. Scores for Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 are taken from the Claude Opus 5.5 System Card; GPT‑6 Astra’s with-tools score is taken from its official report. GPT‑6 Astra has not reported a without-tools score and is marked “—”.BioMysteryBench dataset is drawn from the official v11 release, with Kimi K3 as the judge model. We evaluate Kimi K3.1 Pro with Kimi Code, GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 with Claude Code, and GPT-6 Astra with Codex. Scores for the Claude models are taken directly from their official system cards.Our Agents’ Last Exam dataset is drawn from the official v1.1 release, comprising 122 tasks, including 86 CLI tasks, with environment images aligned with the official Hugging Face release. We additionally assign a score of zero to runs that bypass the task’s stated requirements, such as retrieving answers online instead of performing the required analysis in Wireshark. DeepSeek and Kimi are evaluated using Claude Code and Kimi Code, respectively. All other results are taken from the official benchmark website.OfficeQA Pro, OfficeQA Pro v2. GPT-6 Astra is evaluated with Codex, while all other models are evaluated with Claude Code. Each task provides the agent with the entire PDF corpus, with all PDFs rendered as images and no machine-readable text available. We observed instances in the trajectories of certain external models where they retrieved reference answers online; Consequently, we assigned a score of zero to these tasks.Frontier Finance is evaluated with the official finance agent v2 harness.HANDBOOK.md is evaluated using the official harness built on OpenHands, with evaluation tasks drawn from the benchmark’s early open-source v1 release.Harvey Legal Agent is evaluated on a public dataset of 1,251 tasks using Artificial Analysis’s Stirrup harness, with performance reported as the all-pass rate (i.e., the percentage of tasks that pass all rubric criteria).OSWorld V2.1 is evaluated with the Kimi Agent harness in the official OSWorld v2 repo, while GPT-6 Astra's score is taken from Muse Wonder's technical report.DECK-Arena evaluates presentation generation on real-world queries, while Design Bench covers graphic design via direct and reference-image few-shot prompting; Both run models across python-pptx, pptxjs, and Kimi's in-house DSL in a harness with integrated search and image generation, using an automated grader calibrated on 10,000+ human judgments.MCP Atlas. All models are evaluated on the 500-task public subset with a 100-turn limit, using Gemini 3.1 Pro as the judge.BrowseComp. We adopt the context-compaction strategy used in the Claude model cards, triggered at 200K tokens. We allow a maximum of 500 steps; if this limit is reached before a task is completed, we force the agent to provide an answer, which is then judged. All BrowseComp runs are conducted with temperature=1.0 and top-p=1.0.GDP.pdf w/ python, ZeroBench w/ python and ChartoGraphy w/ python are averaged over five runs. Other multimodal benchmarks (w/ python) are averaged over four runs. For GDP.pdf w/ python: Each original PDF file is sent to the sandbox, where the model can use IPython tool to process it. Final responses are graded against each rubric criterion using Gemini-3.5-Flash (medium reasoning effort) and the official judging prompt. We report the task-macro mean rubric pass rate: for each task, we average the fraction of rubric criteria passed over five independent runs, then average these task-level scores equally across all tasks.Reasoning & Knowledge & Multimodal benchmarksGDP.pdf. Each PDF is provided as page images resized to a longest edge of 1,152 pixels, interleaved with Docling-extracted text in page order. Responses are graded against each rubric criterion using Gemini-3.5-Flash Medium and the official judging prompt. We report the strict pass rate among fully scored responses.HLE and HLE-Diamond evaluate general knowledge and reasoning capabilities. We report accuracy on the full evaluation sets, with 2,500 questions for HLE and 1,000 questions for HLE-Diamond. For models marked with an asterisk (*), accuracy is reported on the text-only subset of questions.GDP.pdf, ZeroBench and ChartoGraphy are averaged over five runs. Other multimodal benchmarks are averaged over four runs. GDP.pdf scores of GLM-5.3 Max and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 Max is cited from https://artificialanalysis.ai/.MMMU-Pro is evaluated following the official protocol, preserving the original input order and prepending images to the text input.Kimi Hallucination Benchmark evaluates factual accuracy on an internal set of challenging, de-identified prompts drawn from practical work tasks. We report the claim-level hallucination rate assessed by fact-checking agents.

item.title: UUIDv7: Timestamps aren’t time-ordered and other oddities
item.author: ibobev
item.content:encoded:
Built on Shards of SiliconI’m going to call it. UUIDv7 is weird.Most blog posts about UUIDv7 tout these benefits:monotonically increasing IDsa helpful timestamp of when the object was created; andBut none of these properties are strictly held. Certain RFC compliant implementations of UUIDv7 violate these properties to extreme degrees. The only useful property UUIDv7 appears to strictly provide is uniqueness and therefore collision resistance. I’ve already discussed how UUIDv7 IDs can be guessable, so this post explores the other properties.Superficially, it seems that embedding a timestamp in the ID can remove the need to track the creation time in a separate database column, providing marginally more efficient database operations. If you need to list things ordered by creation time very often, it’s useful if the primary index gives that behavior, removing the need for another index.Unfortunately, the timestamp embedded in a UUIDv7 ID may not relate to the object creation time. The Postgres docs for helpfully warn that “the extracted timestamp is not necessarily exactly equal to the time the UUID was generated”.RFC 9562 allows implementations to alter the timestamp field, using values that aren’t strictly derived from the system clock. This relates to the tension between UUID monotonicity and timestamp accuracy. In certain scenarios, the difference between the timestamp and the current time can be arbitrarily large.This specification makes no requirement or guarantee about how close the clock value needs to be to the actual time. — RFC 9562 §6.1… implementations MAY increment the timestamp ahead of the actual time … — RFC 9562 §6.2Incrementing the timestamp ahead of the system clock is an interesting problem. If the generator is seeing so much load that a counter field is regularly overflowing then the timestamp could accelerate into the future. Using a sufficiently large counter would be wise and the RFC says the minimum size SHOULD be 12 bits. A counter overflow would require a pretty aggressive creation rate, over 4,096 IDs per millisecond per node, which is beyond the limits of many systems. This overflow becomes relevant, however, if the timestamp freezes; which I’ll discuss in a later section.Example: Python uuid.uuid7()One prominent implementation that increments the timestamp is the Python standard library’s UUIDv7. The increment happens only in certain circumstances, like when the counter overflows. Unfortunately, the generator can get stuck in an increment cycle if the clock ever jumps backwards and the timestamp can race ahead of the system time by an arbitrarily large amount.import uuid from datetime import datetime
# Prime the generator with the current time t = uuid.uuid7().time now = datetime.now() delta = (datetime.fromtimestamp(t/1000) - now).total_seconds() print("Initial delta: ", delta) # Ask the user to change the time input("Set clock back one hour")
while True: for _ in range(100000): uuid.uuid7() t = uuid.uuid7().time now = datetime.now() delta = (datetime.fromtimestamp(t/1000) - now).total_seconds() print("New delta: ", delta) $ uv run --python 3.14 main.py Initial delta: -0.000748 Set clock back one hour New delta: 3695.277581 New delta: 3795.042411 New delta: 3894.80756 New delta: 3994.573106 ^C We expect the difference to be 3600 seconds (one hour) as the implementation refuses to allow the embedded timestamp to jump backwards and we expect the difference to decrease as the system clock catches up to the frozen timestamp. But when the load is above one ID per millisecond the difference will increase without bound. At lower loads it will take longer for the system clock to catch the timestamp, but we don’t see the runaway effect.The related issue shows Python developers reasoning that this is consistent with the RFC, is consistent with other implementations, and that there isn’t “much we can do” on a “flawed system”. I think these points are correct as I see this same behavior in other implementations. Nevertheless, it would be helpful if existing UUIDv7 implementations could handle system clock jumps without runaway behavior. There are many real-world examples of clocks jumping backwards, even decades out of sync in time-sensitive environments.Is leaking a timestamp harmful?Embedding the timestamp in the ID means that you cannot share the ID without also sharing the timestamp.It’s pretty difficult to think of an example where this really matters. One example could be a user profile page that doesn’t disclose when the account was created, but the UUIDv7 ID in the URL leaks the high-precision timestamp.This issue would typically be very low on my list of security concerns because I find much more severe problems when I do security assessments. Nevertheless, there are contexts where this matters and engineering resources would be focused on addressing it. If you’re in the latter camp, be wary of UUIDv7 leaking metadata.This section is even more pedantic, so skip ahead if you’ve had enough. Briefly: UUIDv7 IDs provide some sort of rough order, which may be suitable for your requirements.When I was reading the UUIDv7 RFC I was surprised to see it describing a method for creating IDs across different nodes that are monotonically ordered. This was proven impossible back in the 1970s, and lead to the development of vector clocks and similar technology. At a high level, the problem is that system clocks cannot be synchronized to a suitable precision. Ordering things by timestamp only works if you know precisely what time it is. Any uncertainty in the time results in uncertainty of event ordering.Succinctly: Timestamps are only time-ordered if you know what time it is and you don’t know what time it is.For this reason, similar ID formats claim to be nearly sorted. It seems odd that UUIDv7 makes a stricter claim and does not deliver on them. At the very least, the challenges of synchronizing clocks across systems make the millisecond and especially the sub-millisecond timestamps quite suspect.So no, there’s nothing in the UUIDv7 specification that would ensure the IDs are strictly monotonically increasing. Specific implementations may do better than others (with sub-millisecond timestamps, counters, well-synchronized clocks, etc), but we’ve known since the 1970s that this problem is not strictly solvable.In UUIDv7’s favor, roughly ordered IDs are still quite useful. So don’t rip UUIDv7 out of your systems just yet. Just be wary of what assumptions you have.Restarting a UUIDv7 generatorThe RFC has lots of discussion about the handling of clocks that jump backwards. Timestamps are only time-ordered if clocks tick forwards, so special care is needed.We’ve already discussed one mitigation: tracking the last generated timestamp to ensure that an earlier timestamp is never used. To do this safely you’ll need to write the last used timestamp to persistent storage, such that you can read it again after a system reboot or a process restart.I’ve looked at several UUIDv7 implementations I couldn’t find one that writes timestamps to persistent storage. So implementers seems disinterested in addressing the issue and they generate out-of-order IDs when a process restart follows a clock jumping backwards.Looking at real-world clock synchronization problems, you’ll find many examples of clocks getting set to future dates. When this happens, the backwards jump would align the timestamp to the actual time, but a last-used-timestamp guard would force timestamps to use keep using that incorrect timestamp until the system clock catches up. If the system clock takes a long time to catch up, you may start experiencing counter rollovers.My mental model for UUIDv7 is that it’s a mash-up of a bunch of different ideas which implementations are free to choose as they see fit. There’s a wide variance of properties that UUIDv7 implementations can provide, with varying degrees of certainty they can successfully provide those properties. If you’re building your own implementation you can likely build something that has the properties you need. But most of us want to reach for an off-the-shelf version, especially when standard libraries provide an implementation, so we’re generally at the mercy of someone else’s implementation decisions. Implementations can change over time, making broad changes to their behavior while still being RFC compliant. Distributed systems may have multiple implementations across their subsystems, each with distinct properties. The only thing you can really expect is strong collision avoidance and ID uniqueness.Be sure to ask these questions when picking a UUIDv7 implementation:Is the implementation compliant with the RFC?What additional properties does this implementation guarantee?Under what limits can those guarantees be met?Are there any assumptions required for these properties to hold, such as having an accurate system clock?Under what conditions will the implementation alter the timestamp?How guessable are the generated IDs?Unfortunately, this sort of analysis is much more difficult than building an RFC compliant generator. Authors of UUIDv7 generators may not know the answers to these questions and may themselves be surprised that the RFC does handle this for them.

item.title: How is music possible
item.author: rafaelc
item.content:encoded: Today, we listened to Swedish P2, where they were playing a mixtape that Sara Parkman had put together of folk music from around the world. I looked in the rearview mirror and saw that Maud, our nine-year-old, had closed her eyes. She does that when something is particularly good. It makes her see things, she says. Little films. Though she won’t say what they are. Parkman played a Sámi joik that had been recorded in Moscow a few months after the collapse of the Soviet Union,and I turned off the main road, down one of the gravel paths through the beech forest, so I could slow the car to a walking pace and really listen. Rolling my window down and leaning out, I looked up at the slowly passing trees—they looked otherworldly wrapped in this music. I had never seen them like that before.How can these landscapes arise?approaching or leavinginfer the size and shape of a space from its echothe slightest pause or change in tonewe might speak with melodies that contain a lot of minor thirdsrate minor chords as positiveNow that I think about it, I suspect the reason I’m dissatisfied with all of the explanations of why music moves us comes down to this enormous distance between how simple the building blocks are and how far reaching their consequences.I wonder if music is perhaps best thought of as an emergent phenomenon. It is built from small, mundane actions (plucking a string, manipulating our emotional processing, synchronizing our body movements with others to create a sense of bonding, and so on). But the thing that emerges (these swooping existential experiences) can’t be understood by just looking at the building blocks—much as the behavior of a sand dune can’t be understood by considering a single grain of sand. Sand dunes move around, larger ones more slowly than smaller ones, and when they collide, they exchange sand in various ways—none of which are properties that sand grains have.However that may be, it is astounding that we get to live in a universe where music is possible. Absolutely astounding.This essay benefitted from conversations with Andy Matuschak and Kristian Matsson. It was edited by Esha Rana.
