item.title: Pentagon grants DHS permission to test heat ray weapon for use at border
item.author: bushwart
item.content:encoded:
The Pentagon has given the Department of Homeland Security permission to test a military-grade heat ray and develop tactics to potentially use it in operations at the southern US border, according to a memo signed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last month and obtained by CNN.
The heat ray, officially known as the Active Denial System, is a nonlethal weapon that shoots an invisible beam of electromagnetic waves that can reach a little more than half a mile away, according to the US military.
The energy beam causes a burning sensation when it comes into contact with the human skin — which Pentagon officials have previously compared to feeling a blast of heat when opening a hot oven. Military officials have said the resulting “tingling effect” lasts between 10 and 15 minutes but also generates “an instinctive and irresistible urge to run from the effect.”
Deploying the heat ray at the US border would be an unprecedented step, even for the Trump administration, which has made border security and clamping down on immigration a top priority. The DHS request did not specify where or how the weapon would be tested and how it might eventually be used, but over the years, there have been internal discussions about potentially using it for crowd dispersal along the US-Mexico border, according to current and former Customs and Border Protection officials.
US officials had also considered deploying the system during moments of domestic unrest, including at the end of President Donald Trump’s first term when protests erupted over the murder of George Floyd, according to a former US official familiar with those discussions.
The memo authorizes the “temporary loan” of one ADS system for seven months, starting in September, and states that it “shall not be operated by DoW (Department of War) personnel,” appearing to absolve the Pentagon of any responsibility for how the directed-energy system may ultimately be deployed.
It also states that DHS is solely responsible for “system employment, use and development of tactics, techniques and procedures.” At the end of the seven-month loan period, DHS can submit an additional request for further use of the Pentagon system in border operations based on need, a defense official told CNN.
“CBP is continually evaluating new technologies, especially those that enhance operational effectiveness and strengthen mission capabilities,” a Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said in a statement to CNN.
The Pentagon referred CNN to DHS when asked for comment.
The US military briefly deployed the system to Afghanistan nearly two decades ago but ultimately declined to use it during active combat operations. The US military also considered using the system for crowd control purposes at US facilities abroad where terrorist detainees were being held at the time but ultimately declined to employ it for that purpose as well, according to a source familiar with those previous internal considerations.
Customs and Border Protection officials have previously entertained the idea of using the system in areas where there’s a high concentration of illegal crossings. Border officials have occasionally discussed potentially using the system as a crowd dispersal tool, but it has never been deployed.
Officials ran into hurdles over legalities, use of force, effectiveness, and potential issues over sovereignty, particularly if the system was deployed on people in Mexico who had not yet crossed into the US. Chief among those concerns, however, was whether people could be harmed, either directly or indirectly, by the weapon.
“Even if they’re chasing people back to the river, you don’t want them to go in and drown,” a former CBP official told CNN. “For the cost, for the training and for the policies you’re going to create, is the juice worth the squeeze?”
El Centro sector, which covers around 70 miles along the US-Mexico border, evaluated the system several years ago, when Rodney Scott, who now serves as CBP commissioner, helmed that sector, according to a CBP official.
At the time, officials were discussing whether the system might help agents with an influx of illegal crossings along the nearby river by discouraging people from trying to cross in that area or pushing them to get out of the water.
One of the considerations at the time was whether the system might result in more rescues if people were incapacitated by the technology, the official said, though it’s unclear why it wasn’t deployed.
In 2018, prior to midterms, CBP officials also weighed using it against migrants, but then-Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen shot it down.
“The issue was treating immigrants and citizens like enemy combatants,” a former DHS official familiar with previous discussions about using the weapon against migrants told CNN. “Thematically, inhumane treatments typically get rejected.”
Some Border Patrol agents have more recently cast doubt over whether they need the tool at all amid low border crossings and an increase in personnel, according to another former CBP official.

item.title: Gemma-4-26B-A4B with 39-69% less thinking at same accuracy
item.author: armcat
item.content:encoded: This is the fifth model in the ThinkingCap series. We reduced how much Google's gemma-4-26B-A4B-it thinks, without compromising the quality of its answers.Up to 69.1% reduction in thinking tokens, on average 38.9% measured across twelve benchmarks, for The first ThinkingCap on a Google model, and the smallest accuracy cost of any ThinkingCap so farLooping drops from 3.6% of the original model's responses to 0.8% of oursSame sampling settings (thinking on, temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95), same serving stack (vLLM), drop-in replacement want even better efficiency? The PRO version of this model uses up to 87.6% fewer thinking tokens, 62% on average. Faster answers and lower inference costs at scale. Contact us at .gemma-4-26B-A4B is Google's sparse mixture of experts — 26B parameters with about 4B active per token. It is the third model family we have applied this work to, after Qwen and NVIDIA. On this one we put extra effort into keeping the accuracy intact: thinking comes down 38.9% on average at a cost of only 0.15pp of accuracy, which is smaller than the run-to-run spread on most of the suite.Video comparison of the original model and the ThinkingCap model, prompted with the same input.Both models run on the same hardware and use the same inference settings.We start with gemma-4-26B-A4B-it. The goal is to spend fewer tokens getting to the answer, and change nothing else: preserve the knowledge, reasoning ability, answer quality, instruction following and safety behaviour.Accuracy per task family, gemma-4-26B-A4B-it against the ThinkingCap modelAccuracy barely moves in any family, and in two it moves up. Instruction following and agentic gains 0.65pp and maths gains 0.39pp; code is flat at 0.02pp; knowledge and reasoning costs 0.51pp and long-context and multimodal 0.92pp. Averaged over all twelve benchmarks the change is .Mean thinking tokens per task family, gemma-4-26B-A4B-it against the ThinkingCap modelThe thinking is where the change is, and every family gets shorter. Long-context and multimodal reduces the most, 54.4%, then knowledge and reasoning at 44.4%, maths at 36.1% and code at 27.6%; instruction following and agentic reduces the least at 17.2%. Averaged over the twelve benchmarks it is .Long-context & multimodalInstruction following & agenticEvery row is the original BF16 against the ThinkingCap model, run on the same harness with the same settings on the same questions. Accuracy is the mean over seeds, ± the 95% confidence interval from the spread between them. Every cell in the last row is an average across the twelve benchmarks, each counting once — so there is the mean of the twelve reductions, not the ratio of the two token figures beside it, which is 38.5%. The same distinction applies to the family bars above, which plot each family's mean tokens. On τ²-bench the thinking tokens are per task, summed across the rollout's turns, rather than per response. Column definitions are in Evaluation methodology.Every one of the twelve gets shorter. The deepest cuts are LongBench v2 (−69.1%), AA-LCR (−59.3%) and MMLU-Pro (−49.1%); the shallowest IFBench (−13.7%) and τ²-bench (−20.8%). The two shallow rows are the two whose work is least about thinking at length: following a list of format constraints, and applying a fixed customer-service policy through the right tool calls.On accuracy, most of the results are within noise: on eight of the twelve the gap is smaller than the run-to-run spread, and five of the twelve come out of the original model. The four that move further than their intervals allow are IFBench (+1.83pp, in our favour), GPQA-Diamond (−0.96pp), MMMLU (−0.66pp) and AA-LCR (−4.00pp). AA-LCR is the one real cost in the suite.Looping improves across the suite. The original model loops on of its responses, against for ours — and on the three benchmarks where it loops most, AIME 2026, HMMT Nov 25 and HMMT Feb 26, the rate falls from 5.5%, 8.6% and 17.0% to 0.9%, 1.2% and 4.5%.Accuracy against the thinking-token budget, both modelsRead left to right, this is the question a deployment actually asks: for a given token budget per question, how much accuracy do you get? ThinkingCap's curve sits above the original model's through the whole middle of the range — the same accuracy for a smaller budget — and the two converge once the budget is wide enough that neither model is constrained by it.Reasoning models are noisy to evaluate. At the recommended temperature of 1.0 both the content and the length of a response move run to run, so a single seed tells you very little. Everything below is multiple seeds per benchmark, with accuracy reported as the mean and a 95% confidence interval across seeds.Both sides are the same run. The original model and ours were evaluated by the same harness, with identical sampling and serving settings. The original model was measured by us, not quoted from published figures. The configuration: — our internal evaluation suite, running both models on vLLM. — generation capped at 65,536 tokens per response on every benchmark, and per turn on τ²-bench. — thinking on; temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 64. Ours inherits Google's recommended preset unchanged, so no part of the comparison is a decoding change. — the mean across seeds with a 95% t-interval, which says how far the answer moves when only the sampling seed changes. — 64 on AIME 2026, HMMT Nov 2025 and HMMT Feb 2026; 32 on GPQA-Diamond and LiveCodeBench; 16 on RealWorldQA, IFBench and τ²-bench; 8 on AA-LCR and LongBench v2; 4 on MMLU-Pro and MMMLU, whose question counts are large enough that question sampling is not the limiting noise. — AIME 2026 (30 problems), HMMT Nov 2025 (30), HMMT Feb 2026 (33), LiveCodeBench (175), GPQA-Diamond (198), MMLU-Pro (12,032), MMMLU (9,996), AA-LCR (100), LongBench v2 (370), RealWorldQA (765), IFBench (300) and τ²-bench (278 tasks across airline, retail and telecom). — exact match on the extracted answer, except LiveCodeBench, where the generated code is run against the problem's tests; IFBench, scored by its programmatic verifiers; and τ²-bench and AA-LCR, which are judged. τ²-bench also runs against a simulated user and is reported as the unweighted mean over its three domains. / — as above; is the difference between them, in percentage points. — the headline: the change in thinking tokens, totalled across the benchmark and divided by its question count, so a long question weighs more than a short one. are the tokens before the reasoning closes, averaged over every question and seed of the benchmark, written . — the share of responses whose thinking never closed, which score zero. — the share caught by a compression-based loop detector, which flags a response whose text compresses far beyond what ordinary prose does.Have any questions, or a workload you want this run against?Send us a mail at want even better efficiency? The PRO version of this model uses up to 87.6% fewer thinking tokens, 62% on average. Faster answers and lower inference costs at scale. Contact us at .

item.title: Investor-owned utilities charge 23% more for electricity than public providers
item.author: hubraumhugo
item.content:encoded: In 2025, homes paid 17.8¢ a kilowatt-hour at utilities, 14.5¢ at utilities and 14.1¢ at . Since 2020, investor-owned prices rose 34% and public ones 19%, against 24% inflation.Average home price by utility ownerChange since 2020 against inflation, or cents per kilowatt-hour since 2015.Every year since 2015: home revenue, kWh sold, homes, price and bill by utility owner, for the US and each state, as a gzipped CSV.Download CSV (gzip)Share of homes by their utility's average price per kilowatt-hour, in 2-cent bands.67% of homes paid 12 to 20 cents, and 11% paid 30 cents or more.61% paid under 14 cents. The bump at the high end is LADWP and Long Island Power Authority, 13% of public homes.52% paid under 14 cents.Price gap after accounting for locationAverage home price per kilowatt-hour in 2025. Hydro states get the most power from dams: WA, VT, ID, OR, MT, AK and SD.Public and co-ops, same stateOutage minutes a year by utility ownerMinutes without power for the average home, not counting major storms.Public power is common in cities and near federal dams, where power is cheap, and public utilities pay no income tax and borrow tax-free. That explains some of the gap, not why it grew.Most of the gap opened from 2020 to 2023, during the energy price spike: 25% at investor-owned utilities, 11% at public utilities and co-ops. Before and since, both rose at about the same pace.After inflation, investor-owned prices rose7.9%. Public and co-op prices fell4.3%.Co-op homes have the highest bills, $159 a month in 2025, because they use the most power.Homes that buy power from a retail supplier aren't in the investor-owned figures. Counting them, prices on investor-owned lines rose 36%.Price is what homes paid divided by the kilowatt-hours they used, from EIA's yearly survey of utilities. Federal utilities and the smallest ones are left out.The data shows what homes paid, not why. Investor-owned utilities earn a return for shareholders on what they build. Public utilities and co-ops have no shareholders. See the rate cases for increases utilities are asking for now.

item.title: Your Phone Is About to Stop Being Yours: 70 Days Until Lockdown
item.author: NackerHughes
item.content:encoded:
"This is a huge advantage over ios, you can't take this away 😢 ""The ability to download apps directly from developers is one of the main differentials of Android from IOS. Limiting this will severely impact the market share of Android by removing basically any reason anyone would want to use Android over IOS. ""The whole point of Android was it was an os that gave you the freedom to use your phone the way you wanted unlike apple this ruins it's whole purpose ""F droid is my primary way of installing apps. Blocking sideloading will fundamentally change how I use my phone, and make it impossible for me to use my phone in the way that I have for years. ""As an android user I love the way I want to use my phone and which app to install. Apps that are being developed my developers that are not on the play store tends to be even better than those on the play store. The freedom which developers have to develop and distribution of apps has changed on how we use the android devices, giving us more option and great experience with the device. ""This would severely limit any reason I have to use a google certified android phone. Without the ability to easily support open source developers and tinker with my own projects -- the android phone would cease to be my "daily driver". These are our computers, and we should be able to install what we want on them. It's disrespectful to take that right away. Please reconsider removing your hardware's greatest and most consumer friendly strength in the mobile market. ""Android was built on FOSS foundations and this anti-consumer move goes against the guiding tenants of the OS and Google's mission. No-one who uses Android wants to see Google pervert it into a second-rate apple. This move is a violation of consumer faith and a bad long-term business decision. Revert it in it's entirety before you loose the core attraction of your product. ""As a amateur developper involved in game development and fanmade communities, this decision would mean the death of a lot of project. This is unnaceptable! ""If you, as an Android user are happy using Android but dont understand what this is about, go out and buy an iPhone. Then you'll understand. ""Using Android has always meant having the freedom to customize your experience to your hearts content, this would be the end of an era. This would also be the end of many small app developers that can't or won't conform to the what one might say 'invasive' requirements to publish an app. You can say goodbye to FOSS and side loading which is a huge part of Android customization. ""Imagine not being able to install programs on your computer that don't go though Microsoft or Apple first. That is where this will go next if this type of practice is made normal/succeeded. ""Android has always stood for user choice. The freedom to install apps from outside an official store is a core part of what made the platform different and appealing in the first place. Removing options like sideloading moves Android away from its original philosophy.
I develop apps for personal use, and I have no interest in becoming an “approved developer” just to run my own software. Not everyone has the time or desire to navigate additional gatekeeping just to maintain control over their own devices.
Limiting these freedoms sets a concerning precedent. It shifts the platform toward tighter control, reduced openness, and potential monopolization. Android began as an open operating system — moving away from that foundation risks turning it into a closed ecosystem that mirrors the very model it once differentiated itself from.
Restricting user choice under the banner of “protection” doesn’t benefit everyone. Many users value autonomy, flexibility, and control over their own hardware. Removing those options feels less like protection and more like limitation. ""I went back to Android over Apple because of APK freedom. There is no reason to buy an Android phone if this change is implemented. Android users love DIY: researching, exploring new manufacturers, using independent APK repositories. Google is trying to destroy the one thing that makes Android appealing. We all might as well buy iPhones if this is the direction they are choosing. Or dump our money into PinePhone dev. ""Android was created as an open platform. That openness made custom ROMs, alternative app stores, and independent FOSS projects possible. Limiting third-party APK installation reduces user choice and hurts independent developers. Security matters, but it should not remove legitimate options. Keeping Android open protects innovation and freedom of choice. ""I stayed away from smart phones in the early days because they were locked down. It was only after I saw that Android was an open platform that I was willing to even try one. If Google locks down Android, then I will either switch to a basic feature phone, with no data (suits me fine, mobile data is ridiculously expensive), or I will hack together a Linux phone. What's the point in having Android if it just turns in to a.aecond-rate iOS? ""Having the ability to own your phone and use it as you wish is the ONLY reason I have used Android over Iphone for years ""Android is open source, period.
On top of that, I'm buying the device. I own my phone, and that means I should be allowed to do whatever the hell they want with it! If I want to click on links from sketchy sites and download things that are not directly from the Google Play Store, I should be able to. Google claims this is to protect their users, but it's nothing more than censorship and crushing competition from a private, anonymous, and often better competitors making free and open source apps on platforms like F-Droid or Obtanium.
It's like saying that you aren't allowed to hang a picture you bought from your friend in your own house that your bought, unless your friend pays Google $25 and gives them their ID, but you can hang as many pictures in your house as you like if you buy them directly from Google. Doesn't that sound absurd? ""People originally went to Android way back in 2008 because of the open source nature of Android. It's what still attracts so many people to use Android. It's what keeps people on Android. Google owes so much to the open source community, from app developers to OS developers like the CyanogenMod/LineageOS teams, the CalyxOS team, and the DivestOS team among others all the way to the people who have used XDA's forums since the days of the HTC Dream. I realize Google wants to go into the 3rd stage of "Embrace, Enhance, Extinguish" but that will drive more people to Linux phones. ""This change has pushed me into rooting and using a custom ROM making my phone more "unsafe" to the eyes of Google and banking apps, Monopolizing the app market isn't an act of consumer protection under the guise of "security" it's just an attempt at maximizing profits and It being a stepping stone in censoship besides think of all the internal use apk's that companies use on their devices be It for management, interaction with company equipment, etc had to now get verified by a 3rd party like Google when the ones using that app is only company employees ""This is one of the starting points/gates to mass surveillance. If we don't act now it will be too late when there's already multiple structures put in place enabling the next following steps intheir hold on control. ""this change would remove the main reason i even purchase these phones, stop it google ""The reason people have Android is not only because it's cheap ,but because of the freedom The OS has... taking away this freedom ,is like taking away someone's heart ""This is a disturbing move by Google. Side loading needs to remain an option for Android users to choose as an alternative when looking for apps made by developers that are not in the PlayStore. Side loading is also invaluable when wanting to utilise previous versions of apps on an Android device. ""Hopefully this movement is successful for the custom developmental purposes and devotion from the developers themselves. ""Google, pls keep the sideloading and freedom of anyone installing or developing apps and others choosing to use them open.
It is a breach of trust by making the ecosystem closed. People will hate google, no doubt I have started feeling so too with your move / proposed move. ""I use android because it is an open platform. If this goes through, developers will stop making apps so I might as well move to apple. ""I have Android phones for just one reason: The freedom they provided so far. Some of my main apps are side-loaded. This move of Google is a huge disappointment. It’s a terrible abuse of monopoly power. ""Dawg how am i supposed to live without sideloaded apks ""I'm not even a dev and I don't agree with this ""are we really trying to iOs android? why are we trying to be the competition? if this occurs, android will LOSE so many users ""If android isn't open source then it's straight up just a worse iOS
literally the only reason we use it is the fact that it's open source 💀 ""Limiting the installation of APK files (sideloading) is bad because it turns Android, known for its openness, into a "walled garden" similar to Apple's.
This restriction strips users of their freedom, treating them as if they cannot make decisions about their own devices.
Furthermore, it stifles competition and innovation. Alternative app stores, like F-Droid (focused on open-source), and developers testing their apps are directly harmed. This forces everyone to depend exclusively on the Google Play Store, giving Google total control over the market and what you can or cannot install, often under the guise of "security."
In the end, it's a trade-off of Android's fundamental freedom for centralized corporate control. ""free is the most important part of Android,no freedom no Android. ""1 federal lawsuit wasn't enough? Why after all that's happened, being convicted for monopoly must Google feel the need to throw ""I use Android phones rather than iphones because it allows for more user end control, including the ability to use/install open-source apk.
If the choice is made to restrict this functionality, my next phone will not be an android. ""Don't make daddy Torvalds mad what you did with his kernel ""Many game developers who don't want to go to the trouble of posting in an app store (because they don't want to be exploited by the algorithm or are just programming students wanting to share Your creation with friends) would have difficulties with the new apk restriction, in addition to old games that no longer exist in any store are made available in Apk form,Some older phones also cannot install applications from the play store etc. so applications are often installed through apk, especially Work apps ""Only reason I've always used android is because it's pretty open to apps I make for myself. If that is taken away, there's no reason not to go to Apple. ""Freedom to think and develop without cynicism. ""Keep android open source, resist surveillance and ID verification. Consider switching to Grapheneos ""As a newer developer I was shocked when I heard the app I had been working on was not approved because all the hoops to jump through. Then they wanted a monthly payment. I was so deterred that I discontinued development on a project meant to help mental health. I became the one who needed it. I was depressed and discouraged. To this day I haven't touched the code base and I was team Google. I think I'm more disappointed in my blind faith than anything else. Hope we can turn this around. ""Android was always desired by those who want an open platform. It should remain that way... for a laundry list of reasons. ""If Google "Walled gardens" Android, I will never buy a phone with their OS ever again. That's literally the only reason people buy Android, is because it is open not locked down like Apple. F.A.F.O. how much money you'll really lose Google. ""We can stand together to save Android and keep downloading what we love on our Android devices! ""As a regular user and consumer, I am frightened by this direction. Android has historically differentiated itself by being an open platform that users can customize to their liking - this is THE main reason I continue to purchase Android phones. I am a developer as a hobby, and will occasionally create my own apps to support my unique projects and requirements. I have no interest in becoming an authorized developer - that wouldn't make sense for me. In addition, I benefit STRONGLY from the community of existing open-source apps. I am an avid F-Droid user, and find the apps there to be of equal or better quality than those in the Play Store.
If Android is to become as locked-down as iOS, then my next phone purchase will be from Apple to benefit from their increased privacy protections. The main differentiator drawing me.to Android will be gone. ""Let me sideload my Android apps. ""A company like Google should not be allowed should not be allowed to do something like this. As a regular user I find what they are trying to do deeply concerning. When I choose to buy an Android phone, it's with the expectation of having control over how I use it, not to face restrictions or censorship, this is not even going over the massive privacy risks and data theft, this is an open source operating system and freedom should be key, I do not like how all of these companies and governments are trying to push age verification for everything, and I would hope for the decency of being given privacy ""android needs to be free and google has to stop controlling what users can do with their phones and devices. they are NOT our parents. we can do what the heck we want!!! ""This is my device, that i paid my hard earned money for. No one should be able to tell me what i can and can't install on something that I own. ""The freedom that Android offered was its defining feature. Without that freedom, it is no different than iOS. So when I go to buy my next phone, at least Apple hasn't pulled the rug out from under me, just saying... ""Android already provides security tools — Play Protect, install warnings, and permissions. These are the right solutions. A blanket lockdown is not security; it is control! ""FOSS IS WHAT BUILT ANDROID. THIS WILL HURT FOSS. ""I'll be concise. This is not the right direction to go. This really is a monopoly and openness is the right choice. You're causing more harm than good and people's freedom of choice needs to be addressed.
Thank you. ""I’m not even a developer, but this whole Google lockdown thing ticks me off. The reason I went with Android was freedom — being able to choose where I get my apps, try stuff from outside the Play Store, and actually use my phone how I want. Now Google’s trying to turn it into another Apple-style cage.
If they force everything through the Play Store, it’s not just developers that get screwed. We do too. Prices will go up because Google takes its cut, and half the cool niche or indie apps will disappear. I shouldn’t have to beg permission to install something from GitHub or F-Droid. It’s my phone, I paid for it — not some rental Google gets to control.
This isn’t about safety or quality, it’s straight-up greed. Android was always the “open” option, and Google’s throwing that away. ""The whole reason I love android is due to openness and freedom, Google taking this away makes me mad because that's a staple point for Android gone. As a regular user, I use the F-Droid store, as well as finding apps directly on GitHub. ""This solution simply doesn't make sense. It's not our fault, or the fault of all developers, that people don't know what to do to verify or install an application that isn't malicious. In my opinion, this should come enabled normally on new smartphones, but with a developer option to disable it. You don't have to complicate everything and force us to use an adb command just to install an unverified application. That simply doesn't exist. I provided the solution. ""I object to being forced to use Google "approved" bloatware and non-open source software on my devices. ""I bought this device. Keep your ransomware/malware away from MY device, Google. ""I choose to use android for the freedom. If
thry implement this in such a way that
hinders that, I will no longer have a reason to
pick android over iPhone. Guess I will see how this plays out. ""Hey Google, remember what you said? "Be together, not the same." ""I have been using Android since the HTC G1, and I've never been so disappointed with the whole thing as I am now. I recognise that Google is doing it's best to keep malware and malicious software out of its app store, but for people who are capable of installing F-Droid, NeoStore or one of the other alternative stores, this is a disaster. Many applications I use are only available here, and with this plan from Google, I'll be unable to access tools, applications and services I use on a daily basis. ""As a consumer, I bought and use Android platform devices because I care about my privacy and I care about accessing third-party applications that are not strictly on Google's Play Store. I utilize F-Droid and various other third-party app stores, and this would be a major impediment to me. I did not agree to Google pulling the rug from beneath me well after I bought several thousand dollar Android phones and devices. ""There is always the "security" claim, they got so many security tools already, built in the official app distribution, if the user want to experiment on the device they own they must have the freedom to do so, this is how tech should work, freedom is how tech progress ""It's a limiting choice for users and software engineers and it will depreciate Google's platform. ""then why get an android at this point? ""Please, allow for users to make exceptions or some other control, keep Android flexible. ""You pay all this money, over a $1000 dollars for a topshelf phones but yet it still isn't yours to do with as you please. This is just another example of corporations taking away your freedoms to choose. ""Hello, I have been using Android my whole life and I had always disliked IOS due to its highly locked down operating system and hearing that android (Google) wants to lock down android from 3rd party creators really hurts because not everyone can afford to publish an app onto the Google play store. also due to the fact android is the biggest OS worldwide many devices such as "Meta Quest" use android and they're store for applications would get shut down and cause many problems if they (Google) goes through with this plan. Especially as somebody who is soon to make and upload applications for Android this can be very limiting. Keep Android Open. Don't turn it into IOS. ""When we buy a phone, we’re buying the right to use it as we see fit. For years, the core promise of Android was that it was an "open" platform, a space where users had the freedom to choose their software and developers had the freedom to innovate without a middleman. The move to mandate central registration for APK files and developer verification fundamentally breaks that promise. I believe in a future where technology serves the person who bought it. Let's call on Google to honor the original vision of Android as an open computing platform. Let’s keep Android open for the creators, for the consumers, and for the sake of a free and diverse digital future. ""Google sucks if it changes android and will burn! ""Google is a monopoly at this point, break it up. ""As someone who believes in freedom and not being controlled by the big tech companies, we need Google to reverse this decision, otherwise, I'll just switch to a Linux phone. ""The entire reason I have stuck with Android phones until now was my ability to INSTALL apps outside of the play store—key word install, not sideload. Even using that term is brainwashed lingo. A phone is just as much of a computer as a PC is, and I should be allowed to download whatever I want on a device a pay for. Especially when, in some cases, a laptop can be cheaper than a phone these days. This has always been a meaningful feature to me.
Then there is the fact of censorship & creating a hostile environment for smaller dev teams. Having to pay a fee to Google, having to disclose IDs (this is also counterproductive to privacy focused apps). Any application that Google deems unfit, they can rip from the store. The 3rd party stores that Google will "let us" download from are no different from the Play Store. All those developers will still be subject to what Google is doing.
If Android is going to become reskinned IOS, I would rather move to Apple. It's better optimized with many apps that absolutely DO NOT function near as well on Android or get updates way later than Apple. It's a smoother, cleaner product. Though, truly, I want to go to Motorola as they are planning to work with GrapheneOS which is privacy & security focused (which Google isn't! And this move is not making Android more secure!)
These practices are anti-consumer AND anti-competition. Monopolistic, dirty practices. It's shameful that Google is still trying to act like they are an "open" system in the slightest while they actively shut out our ability to—again, INSTALL applications on our phone, which is essentially just a computer in our hands. Imagine if Windows did this, or even a Macbook. The free world is about having free choice, and this isn't that. I will absolutely be moving away from Android if this changes take effect. In the meantime, I'll take my in-app purchases to the actual websites behind them, use F-Droid & various places to download APKs to update in place of the Play Store.
This is abhorent.
TL;DR: Google is awful, hates consumer and developer freedoms, & yearns for censorship and growing it's monopolistic empire. I will be moving to any other phone if this happens. ""As a long-time Android user and small-scale app developer, I'm deeply concerned about the recent moves to restrict app sideloading. Choice has always been the core strength of Android—it's what set it apart as an open operating system. Forcing users to become "approved developers" just to build and install personal apps is impractical and unnecessary; I simply don't have the time or interest in jumping through those hoops.
This shift feels like the start of broader censorship and monopolization, transforming Android into little more than a reskinned version of iOS. We chose Android for its freedom, not for anti-consumer restrictions that claim to "protect" us but really just limit our options. Existing tools like Knox and Play Integrity are already intrusive enough—now even downloading from trusted alternatives like F-Droid or other third-party stores might face scrutiny? This erodes the open spirit that defined Android from the beginning.
Users deserve the right to create, modify, and install apps without sacrificing anonymity or control. It's our responsibility to educate ourselves on risks, not for big tech like Google (or GAFAM) to dictate terms. Android's appeal has always been its flexibility: I've sideloaded niche apps from lone developers for unique tasks, like custom music players and compass tools from F-Droid. I've even installed modded versions of stock apps, such as a camera tweak that added Google Pixel's Photosphere to my device—something impossible without sideloading.
There's no need for Android to head in this restrictive direction; it risks becoming a "mock iOS," stripping away the very reasons people like me chose it. Let's restore customization, user freedom, and innovation to the heart of Android. Please, reconsider this path—it's not protection; it's control. ""I always chose to use android because of its freedom to do whatever I want woth my smartphone. Now they want to become Apple. What is wrong with them? We can't let this happen. ""We were promised FOSS, keep it that way ""Android does not need to be the same as iphones are: locked and proprietary. ""I regularly use FOSS apps and apps I've been bringing with me in APK form from phone to phone, and the promise of being able to develop and run my own code has been part of what's kept me using Android all these years. For Google to then yank the rug out from under us is a betrayal of the highest order, and for what? Shareholders? To feed the addiction held by seemingly every person in a seat of power to know exactly what a given Android owner ate for breakfast on any given date? What a fall from grace from a company that once touted the mottos "Don't be evil" and "Do the right thing." ""I don't develop any apps, I do believe in freedom. Freedom to put whatever kind of gas I want in my vehicle(sorry EV's!). Freedom to make make some cash on the side whenever I decide to clean out my storage and have a garage sale. Freedom to choose what apps I can install on a device, running android os which I have rightly paid for. There are other options available Google if helping to keep people safe from running buggy apps on their devices is what you really care about. No need to try and be the app gatekeepers for the future. I pray someone snaps back to reality there before your company proceeds to far down this dark path. ""Compared to iOS, Android always felt less restrictive and easier to work with, both as a user and developer. Now, Google would like to take that competitive niche and throw it in the dumpster. This benefits no users or developers. It is blatantly greedy, controlling, and nonsensical. It adds more red tape for developers, higher potential for censorship at the whim of Google, and it will turn Android into another iOS. Android users chose not to go with iOS when they bought their devices, for several reasons. For me personally, I liked that Android allowed certain kinds of apps that Apple did not allow on iOS. If Android didn't have that advantage, I would've picked iOS. It's a bad move for Google's business, it's a bad move for developers, and it's a bad move for consumers. Terrible idea all around. ""I, as an Android user for 17 years, believe in, and chose Android for, device openness and the freedom of choice. To choose my device, the services I use, from where I download my applications, and to choose FOSS apps that don't require developer registration or sacrificing personal privacy by accepting trackers and/or unnecessary permissions being tied to my app usage. Choice and freedom is what built Android and differentiated it from other platforms, like iOS, Windows Mobile, and other early smartphone operating systems. The trend of destroying user choice through the inability to unlock bootloader and easily root devices, the effective and increasing destruction of the custom ROM community and options, and now the elimination of third party app stores that offer incredible FOSS apps with greater focus on user privacy is one more step Google and Android are taking towards an undesirable ecosystem for many of us who still choose Android for its few remaining, and quickly disappearing, advantages. The argument that Google is requiring developer registration and restricting the ability of alternative app stores, like F-Droid, to continue to thrive as legitimate and worthwhile options is anti-consumer and isn't to protect users. Rather, it's to give users and consumers less control over their devices and data and, in my opinion, that is unacceptable. ""As I'm planning on purchasing a new device soon, this announcement is making me reconsider choosing android at all. If it is moving towards controlling user freedoms, Android becomes less compelling, as that has been the major draw for me. ""We live in a declining society where it is becoming ever more apparent that those in power wish to hoard & guide technologies to enrich themselves more. Enough! Proprietary systems are no different than a safe, one you may use only in the manner that those with enough wealth & influence to have the safe's combination are willing to allow its usage. Such systems are a net negative to wider societal growth & stability. Meant to lock out new talent & stifle overall creativity which could massively improve the system overall. Just another example of a tech company's massive overreach. It should 100% be stopped. ""Without the ability to make my own choices on it I have no reason to use android. I am already tired of and furious about censorship if this goes through I will never use android again. ""Just because old fogeys keep sending their life's savings to "princes" in Africa or "tech support assistants" in southeast Asia, does not mean that Google deny us all the right to use our devices however we want. It's the governments' responsibility to spread awareness against scams and to shut down the scammers for good. This implementation is just yet another way for a megacorp to harvest user data, because apparently there's never enough data. ""Android has one major thing over apple, and that is the ability to download and use whatever software you want on your device alongside the variety of said software. As someone who enjoys finding projects made by other users, or full apps that can alter your experience for the better, we can't just let Google change that. ""It's Android's openness that has allowed its development and evolution to this day. To close it would break the promise of an open system and deprive users of great freedom! ""This is the main appeal of android to me. Having the freedom with my own device that I paid for instead of being limited. ""Android is built on the Linux kernel and owes much of its foundation to the GNU/Linux ecosystem. The spirit of that ecosystem is openness, transparency, and user freedom. Limiting APK installation beyond reasonable security safeguards risks turning Android into a controlled ecosystem rather than an open platform.
Security improvements are important, but they should not come at the cost of developer independence, open-source distribution, and user freedom to install software responsibly.
Instead of restricting APK usage, a better approach would be improving user education, providing clearer and more transparent warnings, and offering optional security layers that protect users without limiting their freedom. ""The ability of sideloading software is the biggest advantage android has over orther systems. I sideload a lot of apps and losing that ability means i have no reason to stay with android. Yes, apps from outside the play store do have more malware, but i can just not download them if i am afraid of getting hacked, this is not protecting anyone and is just removing freedom for users. Also, the ID verification google wants from the developers is a massive privacy and safety risk. ""As someone who enjoys playing modded versions of games, or even fan-games such as FNaF World: Refreshed, I feel as though limiting such use of apks is turning a blind eye. And forcing many people to reveal their real information, info that's sensitive in my opinion isn't safe. I used to feel safer and confine to android, but now I'm not really sure anymore if this is what you consider "safe". ""There are games, apps, that are FREE, because the authors want it that way, no charge. WHY SHOULD GOOGLE WIN MONEY WITH THEM??? ""At the very least let there be one platform that can stay open, don't close it down like everything else. Let us have this. ""Google has painted developer verification as 'security' but the Play Store already hosts malware and Play Protect scans for it already. This is simply another attempt at Google to try and monopolise (see Chrome or the RCS protocol) and no one should be wanting this to happen. This affects anyone who develops outside of the Play Store (including F-Droid or GitHub repos), privacy or anonymous apps, it suffocates our OSS devs, and introduces another way for Google to oversee everything or another vector for data to be leaked. Android has always been about freedom and user control and Google should not have a say in how users use their devices. I have been an Android user since Ice Cream Sandwhich and there are multiple reasons as to why I have never owned an iPhone. I would not be able to have the phone I do today or be able to use it to its full extent without the contributions of FOSS/OSS devs and their community. Shame on you, Google. If this goes through, I'll take my chances with Linux. "

item.title: Shitter – A Nitter Fork
item.author: eustoria
item.content:encoded:
A free and open source alternative Twitter front-end focused on privacy and performance. Inspired by the Invidious project.All requests go through the backend, client never talks to TwitterPrevents Twitter from tracking your IP or JavaScript fingerprintUses Twitter's unofficial API (no developer account required)Lightweight (thanks to @nim_lang, 60KB vs 784KB from twitter.com)Mobile support (responsive design)This repository does not accept Pull Requests, but contributions are welcome in the form of , which can be submitted on an issue and are much more convenient to merge and work with.It's impossible to use Twitter without JavaScript enabled, and as of 2024 you need to sign up. For privacy-minded folks, preventing JavaScript analytics and IP-based tracking is important, but apart from using a VPN and uBlock/uMatrix, it's impossible. Despite being behind a VPN and using heavy-duty adblockers, you can get accurately tracked with your browser's fingerprint, no JavaScript required. This all became particularly important after Twitter removed the ability for users to control whether their data gets sent to advertisers.Using an instance of Nitter (hosted on a VPS for example), you can browse Twitter without JavaScript while retaining your privacy. In addition to respecting your privacy, Nitter is on average around 15 times lighter than Twitter, and in most cases serves pages faster (eg. timelines load 2-4x faster).NOTE: The published image is multi-arch — runs natively on //.To run Nitter with Docker, you'll need to install and run Redis separately before you can run the container. See below for how to also run Redis using Docker.First create your config file. The Docker commands mount it into the container, so it has to exist on the host beforehand. If you've cloned the repo:cp nitter.example.conf nitter.conf If you're using the prebuilt image without a local clone, download
and save it as instead.To build and run Nitter in Docker:docker build -t nitter:latest . docker run -v /nitter.conf:/src/nitter.conf -d --network host nitter:latest A prebuilt Docker image is provided as well:docker run -v /nitter.conf:/src/nitter.conf -d --network host mv12star/shitter:latest Using docker-compose to run both Nitter and Redis as different containers: Change from to in , then run:Note the Docker commands mount (and for docker-compose) from the directory you run them in. If a mounted file doesn't exist, Docker silently creates a directory in its place and the container fails with not a directory: Are you trying to mount a directory onto a file. Remove that directory and create the file as shown above.To run Nitter via systemd you can use this service file:Then enable and run the service: systemctl enable --now nitter.serviceNitter currently prints some errors to stdout, and there is no real logging implemented. If you're running Nitter with systemd, you can check stdout like this: journalctl -u nitter.service (add to see just the last 15 lines). If you're running the Docker image, you can do this: docker logs --follow *nitter container id*To compile Nitter you need a Nim installation, see nim-lang.org for details. It is possible to install it system-wide or in the user directory you create below.To compile the scss files, you need to install . On Ubuntu and Debian, you can use .Redis is required for caching and in the future for account info. As of 2024 Redis is no longer open source, so using the fork Valkey is recommended. It should be available on most distros as or (Ubuntu/Debian), or /. Running it with the default config is fine, Nitter's default config is set to use the default port and localhost.Here's how to create a user, clone the repo, and build the project along with the scss and md files. $ git clone https://codeberg.org/shitter/shitter $ nitter $ nimble -l build -d:danger --mm:refc $ nimble -l scss $ nimble -l md $ cp nitter.example.conf nitter.conf Set your hostname, port, HMAC key, https (must be correct for cookies), and Redis info in . To run Redis, either run redis-server --daemonize yes, or systemctl enable --now redis (or redis-server depending on the distro). Run Nitter by executing or using the systemd service below. You should run Nitter behind a reverse proxy such as Nginx or Apache for security and performance reasons.

item.title: Is this the new cyber normal?
item.author: drewsberry
item.content:encoded: The last week has seen a flurry of severe and critical software vulnerabilities affecting thousands of major sites and sending people into a panic. What’s going on here, and what can we do about it?If we want to understand what’s going on in the world of software security at the moment, we need to understand what’s going on with all these bugs. I’m not a cybersecurity expert, so I’m going to link to external explanations instead of going into the gory technical details myself as these people are always going to do a better job at that.Two different security teams, one from California security company Calif (as part of OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” program) and another from Israeli-U.S. cloud security company Wiz (they’re part of Google Cloud, apparently), both found these two Remote Code Execution (RCE) bugs in PHP. They were both using frontier AI models (a.k.a. LLMs, specifically GPT-5.6 Sol/Gemini 4 Argon) to find these vulnerabilities and build the exploits.Interestingly, one of the bugs (CVE-2026-109618) was found by a security audit the PHP Foundation did in 2024 (funded by the Sovereign Tech Agency which is coincidentally one of the most interesting things happening in the open source space at the moment) but they basically ignored it because they had bigger concerns and couldn’t agree on a fix. The reasoning behind it was that no-one could really figure out how to create an actual exploit based on the theoretical issue.One thing LLMs are very good at is taking a theoretical security vulnerability, even if that vulnerability is a vague description of what the issue could be, and building it into a full exploit. This has become a major issue in recent months as any notice of a security patch will immediately result in people pointing their LLMs at the codebase, whereupon the agents can very quickly read through diffs until they find something that looks like a security patch, then go backwards to the vulnerability it covers, and follow this all the way to an exploit.This happens so fast, in fact, that at this point I think it is a reasonable that the moment you announce a security patch should be taken as a last possible date that the full exploit is being publicly or privately distributed.Someone called petecooper posted on Hacker Newsabout the CVEs, apparently unaware that there even was an embargo. This (and other apparent leaks) prompted this hurried statement from the PHP Group and bringing the patch forward from Thursday 22nd to Wednesday 21st. However, the patch still wasn’t going to be available till the next day. This unintentional leak included CVSS scores of 10.0 (i.e. , although weirdly the actual scores were 9.2 instead).Pretty much immediately, this news spread like wildfire and people started panicking. Even though this was found by “responsible security researchers” at , by the time the security patch actually got released, it was already being exploited in the wild. The PHP Foundation blamed Calif and a company called Chainguard by saying that Calif leaked a video of the exploit in action (with weird background music and a dancing anime girl) while Chainguard published fixes 6 hours before the embargo was due to lift, both allowing attackers to beat the systems administrators to the punch. The timeline is confusing, but it seems like multiple interconnected things have gone wrong here, all within the space of about 17 hours.There’s been lots of discussion about whether AI really is the game changer that completely revolutionises computer security or not. The big AI companies (and they are big) obviously want you to think that it is. Some people argue that PHP2Shell is overblown because LLMs tend to be paranoid about vulnerabilities and come up with “exploits” that make bad assumptions (like that the server will run PHP code you upload yourself via some existing file inclusion vulnerability) or cheat in some way. As LiveOverflow points out, LLMs make it very easy to create exploit slop that proves nothing and doesn’t work, but that doesn’t mean that the vulnerability isn’t real and easy to exploit using AI. You can have 10,000 bad slop exploits that don’t work but if there’s one that does, that’s all that matters. Maybe we just need to get used to wading through slop to find the important stuff now.Others point out that lots of governments (UK, EU, Japan, USA) got overexcited and released urgent announcements saying everyone had to unplug their computers immediately, so people panicked. I think the reason everyone panicked is that everyone kind of knows that PHP is intensely insecure and they use it anyway, so they’re kind of primed for bad news and to overreact. Also, it actually is really quite bad, so maybe panicking is kind of the correct reaction?The big takeaway for me from this is that – because of LLMs – the time from “hey I heard there’s a bad RCE in this project” to “there are sophisticated, automated, and concerted attacks using an exploit targeting this vulnerability” has gone from weeks/months to hours/minutes. The fact that there’s loads of non-working exploit slop just shows how genuine expertise is still required to make these things – if you don’t know what you’re looking at, you can’t tell whether the AI has cheated or made bad assumptions.On the exact same day (20th October 2026), Mozilla announced that they were blocking 8 intermediate certificates signed by Indian certificate authority eMudhra. This happened after a pseudonymous security researcher known only as “Wayne” reported to several big tech firms (such as Mozilla, Apple, Google, Microsoft, etc.) that the certificate authority were using laughably poor quality private keys for their intermediate certificates. Where a secure key might be a 100 digit number, eMudhra were using keys like “115”, “56”, and “4”. They must’ve been following RFC 1149.5:There are no indications that this was found or exploited using AI or LLMs, although researcher Scott Helme notes that given a single prompt, Claude was able to recover the private keys of the intermediate certs.At the time of writing (23rd Oct), eMudhra has announced that it will be retiring from the certificate authority space. In unrelated news, a farmer has announced that he has shut his stable door, following reports of an escaped horse.The next day, cloud provider Railway announced that they found evidence that hackers had accessed and even decrypted environment variables from their platform, which often hold secrets such as database credentials, API keys, etc. In their statement, they said that they believed that this was part of a concerted effort aimed at compromising companies that provide AI inference.What would the end goal be here? At the time of writing (23rd Oct), we have very little information to go on. Is this “unauthorized third party” (official announcements of “some randos got into our computers” always find a way to make it seem like a terms of service agreement, maybe that way they think people won’t pay attention to it) trying to spy on people using AI inference to see what they’re doing, even stealing new models or research? Or maybe they’re trying to build a network of compromised inference providers for their own nefarious generative AI purposes (like finding more PHP bugs).On 12th October 2026, GitLab warned of a max severity bug in GitLab CI/CD’s regular expression parsing that could enable attackers to execute arbitrary code (another RCE) using a specially crafted regex. This is a CVSS score of 10.0 which is the maximum possible, meaning “this is pretty much as bad as they come”. This was followed on 21st October 2026 by yet another regex integer overflow RCE, another 10.0.This follows hot on the heels of yet another 10.0 CVSS CVE from last month (CVE-2026-85706), that time related to path traversal. All three of these bugs were reported through GitLab’s HackerOne bug bounty program. When it became clear that LLMs could research vulnerabilities and write exploits, there was a lot of talk about shutting down bug bounty programs because they didn’t make sense anymore. I’m sure GitLab are glad they didn’t do that now.Although GitLab is used very widely across academia, government, and private companies, this doesn’t seem to have got as much attention. CVEs in GitLab are obviously very serious, especially for private companies, as a lot of their vitally important intellectual property is stored in there, and having that leak could be disastrous. Often, companies put their GitLab instance behind a VPN/firewall so that they aren’t publicly accessible, which greatly reduces the risk associated with this. It’s also not entirely clear whether these CVEs require specific conditions like publicly accessible projects, user self-registration, etc. It does seem like CVE-2026-110264 requires at least one public project, but I can’t find any information on the conditions around the earlier CVE.There’s no indication that these were discovered using AI or LLMs. They may have been, but there’s no reason at this point to think they were.On 21st October, a bug in musl’s libc related to regex (libc has regex? Apparently…) was announced that leads to denial of service at least, if not code execution. As far as I can tell, this is entirely coincidental in timing and not related to the GitLab bugs, which both also seem to be integer overflows when parsing untrusted regular expressions, one reported on the exact same day. Who knew a regex engine was such a security issue – is regex the new font rendering? The GitLab bugs were both found by a Swede called Johan Carlsson (joaxcar) while the musl bug was reported by Julien Voisin, a French self-proclaimed “open sourcerer”.Ah, hello my old friend LiteLLM. Proving that, when you’re made of metal and 200 feet tall, lightning can in fact strike twice. It’s not a good sign that when someone asks whether you’ve heard of the big 2026 LiteLLM compromise, you have to ask “which one?” In a piece of good fortune, the whole PHP2Shell and all the others have cannibalised much of the attention, meaning this isn’t getting quite the same traction as last time in March, despite being similarly bad.This time, it’s a malicious version on the Python Package Index (PyPI) and Docker images. For those who don’t remember, LiteLLM had a very similar thing happen back in March, where a malicious package was uploaded to the litellm package on PyPI that used the files to autoload malicious code (yeah, it was bad).This compromise again took advantage of files and this time also the file for autoloading malicious payloads, running in the preload step as soon as the Python interpreter starts up. According to the analysis from Wiz, the payload has “strong indications of LLM-aided development” – things like overly verbose variable names, overly defensive error handling, brittle edge cases, and all the comments saying “this is where it really bites”, “it’s worth sitting with that”, “lean into that”, and “that stays yours” repeatedly.According to LiteLLM, the incident occurred because the attacker had access to credentials for GitHub CLI which allowed them to run CI jobs. LiteLLM note that Claude Code will apparently sometimes embed a user’s GitHub CLI OAuth token into response bodies which could cause them to appear in LiteLLM logs.On October 19th 2026, an enterprise software company called “PingCAP” that develops a database called “TiDB” revealed “unauthorised access to PingCAP” with “no evidence that data stored in TiDB was impacted”. At the same time, a cyber extortion group called “FulcrumSec” (a.k.a. the “Threatspians”) said they had exfiltrated 10.6 TB of data from PingCAP and publicly released a torrent with 200 GB of data, as a “stage one release” (you’ve gotta get people invested in the sequel).They also posted full details of what they took and some of the excellent security practices of PingCAP, including putting client AWS secret access keys inside Jira tickets and attaching massive unredacted logs to Jira tickets including OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, xAI API keys. Yikes. If you’re willing to visit the cyber extortion group’s website, they do a pretty interesting write-up of it. Gone are the days of shoddy broken English back when the Russians had to write these things up without LLMs to do it for them and remind them of definite and indefinite articles.The good news for PingCAP is that not finding evidence of data extraction is actually incredibly easy. In fact, I’m doing it for thousands of companies right now, for free. I’m sure there’s a business proposal in there somewhere. All you have to do is not look (see also: U+1F648). To be fair, I think their argument is that no data was compromised. 10.6 TB seems like a lot of data if that’s the case. There’s clearly still tons of customer data.Linux vulnerabilities accidentally posted in wrong group chatLinux kernel development all happens through mailing lists. Naturally, some of those are about security sensitive things, so these are private. Over the night of 21st-22nd October 2026, the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), a software vulnerability initiative owned by Trend Micro, reported a bunch of high severity (upwards of 9.0 CVSS) CVEs to the public mailing list, instead of the private one. Naturally, the assumption is that anyone with an LLM and a heart full of dreams will then be able to take those reports and turn them into active exploits within a matter of minutes. This isn’t quite as bad as that time Pete Hegseth accidentally texted details of upcoming military strikes in Yemen to The Atlantic, but it’s still interesting how seriously people take this now.I think it’s fair to say these last few days have been abnormally active in terms of all of these cyber incidents and security disclosures. There are many commenters on the Hacker News discussions for these incidents that say that this is nothing and it’s only going to get worse. Honestly, I’ve not decided yet. To be honest, if you’d asked me 4 years ago how far LLMs would go, I’d never have guessed they’d get as good as they are right now. Even so, people do tend to get overexcited by these announcements and suggest that we are going to live in a world where no software is secure and everyone is vulnerable.It’s worth noting that while a lot of the online discussion around this focusses on AI and LLMs, only some of these disclosures were researched or created with LLMs. We don’t know about some of them like the PingCAP one, but there’s clear evidence that many criminal and state-sponsored groups are using AI to do more hacking and faster. Why wouldn’t they? It seems to be pretty good at it. Many of these vulnerabilities were good old fashioned software vulnerabilities found and written using human meat fingers, but the online conversation focusses on the exciting, scary new thing. Why wouldn’t it?You can see why organisations like NHS England decided to take all of their open source code private (even though that was a silly decision). When these LLMs are so good that anyone can point their agent at some open source code and find tons of vulnerabilities, then write full exploits for them, that is concerning for many. So what’s the solution here?Your code isn’t online anymore, so people can’t point their LLMs at it and do things like analyse every commit for security fixes, find tons of previously unknown critical bugs, etc.The open source community and the future of computing are slightly worse off for every open source repository taken offline.You can’t close source every codebase in the world – some things like programming languages (which are often the source of critical bugs) rely on open source to function. Making Python a closed source project would be catastrophic to the world of computing.It’s only closed source until someone leaks it. And they probably will eventually. And when they do, you won’t have had the years of public scrutiny on the codebase that keeps it clean and secure in the first place.Sometimes you use a programming language where this doesn’t really matter, like Python and Java where you can recover source code from bytecode.LLMs can even reverse engineer compiled binaries pretty effectively.If the code used to be online, that old version still is. You have to assume that someone will have it somewhere. Shellshock was in GNU Bash from 1989 until 2014 before it was fixed, and that’s one of the most widely used programs on the planet.The AI-embracer approach: if you can’t beat ‘em, join ‘em. In other words, they can’t use LLMs to find vulnerabilities if we’ve already run our better LLMs on our code faster and with more money and better models.Makes a few very wealthy tech CEOs very happy.Makes a few very wealthy tech CEOs very happy.Will find tons of bugs. (Someone is gonna have to fix those.)Even though AI makes it easier, it still requires expertise and deep technical knowledge to do this stuff properly (for now).The optimist approach: universally better, standardised approaches to reporting, handling, and mitigating security vulnerabilities followed by all companies having top-notch security postures, well-understood risks, well-documented processes, and so on.Why didn’t anyone else think of this?Gee, we are so clever. Have we just solved this?We do not live in this world. We will never live in this world.Did I mention this is actually quite hard? And possibly impossible?There are some easy wins we could get from this moving forwards, like “never announce details of a critical vulnerability before the patch is ready to install”, but in this case unintentional leaks meant everyone knew about the vulnerabilities even before the official announcement. Maybe even that’s asking too much. In this case, it was a series of mistakes from multiple people and companies that led to or accelerated the exploit being in active use hours before the patch was available, hence everyone taking their servers offline. AWS have since said they saw someone trying out this vulnerability from 17th October, before any of these leaks happened.Even something like minimum release age which gained popularity after shalk/debug, Shai-Hulud, & March LiteLLM incidents, as it means big updates that fix widely exploited vulnerabilities don’t get patched for a few days, giving attackers ample time to hack you to pieces. At the very least, we could maybe do with some better client management to avoid everyone panicking and taking all their servers offline.Maybe we just need to accept that if you expose something to the wider internet, it will get hacked, and plan accordingly. Maybe it’s our expectations that are at fault.There’s definitely a story about AI and security here. It’s changing the world of software, and it’s not yet clear whether that’s for the better or the worse. Money has a way of warping truth like matter warps spacetime, and there’s enough money in AI to cause whatever the truth equivalent of a medium-sized black hole is. There’s an incredible amount of money being spent on AI and it all wants you to think that it’s going to change everything about your life, including software and security. That doesn’t mean it’s not true, of course.Some people say automated analysis tools led to loads of new bugs being found back in the ’10s, and now the same thing is happening again. It feels categorically different to me, but perhaps there will be an initial period of escalating bug reports before it all settles down and goes back to how it was. I suspect not. Some people say this is only happening because humans wrote all the dodgy code in the first place – once AI is writing all of the code to start with, there’ll be no vulnerabilities because LLMs are better at writing secure code than humans. I am not convinced by this argument.While I’m not making many predictions about the future (because I don’t want to look like an idiot in 12 months’ time when I’m inevitably proven wrong), I will say that the software industry is going to change, and open source is going to change, and it is our collective responsibility as members of the software community to make sure that this change is for the benefit of all of us, not special interests and private corporations.This is a developing story – I’ll note any updates in here. I wrote this in somewhat of a hurry, so I may also make some incremental improvements to the wording and evidencing behind some bits.

item.title: Job loss and cortisone mania
item.author: speckx
item.content:encoded: On the morning of 18th August, I got invited at short notice into a 1:1 meeting by my manager, which was . I think I knew what was coming, and I was right: The company is restructuring, and I’m being let go (among a lot of other people). I had time until lunch to say my goodbyes to my colleagues as I would be logged out of my account after that. Because I was still in my six-month probation period, I was put on paid leave for two more weeks; after that I’d be out of a job for the first time since I started working roughly 10 years ago.I’ve seen it happen to other people and entire departments, but it had never happened to me — I guess I’m a real tech worker now!Shortly after, I got sick. I believe it was a Covid infection; I didn’t have any respiratory symptoms, but low energy, joint pain and general feelings of stiffness. Every move was a show of strength. I developed a cough that is now — 2 months later — still subsiding but present.I’m not sure if it was Covid, but being sick triggered the autoimmune condition I have. I mostly got out of bed, watched shorts, videos and movies, and then I went to bed again. I had to take some trips into the city by bike, and hours later it would hit me like a brick wall, leaving me even more exhausted on the next day. I lost my appetite and some weight, which is not good since I rarely moved and I’m fairly lean to begin with.This state dragged on for three weeks until I went to see a specialist and got all the blood work and tests done, so that my medication could get adjusted. Being sick for a couple of days is something I can bear, but not being able to perform even the smallest tasks for such a long time was a disheartening experience.I was put on cortisone treatment, which relieved my symptoms immediately. Cortisone essentially lowers your body’s immune response — which is great when your body tries to defend itself against itself, like mine did. On the other hand, cortisone is not meant for long-term or permanent treatment, and it has a lot of potential side effects.After one or two days, I was back to my normal self, energised, vital, with no signs of inflammation. I now fully realised that I was out of a job, and had the chance to fill my time meaningfully. Job searching doesn’t take up your 16 waking hours.In some phases of my life, I can take a giant step back, and look at it like from a bird’s eye view. I’m approaching 30, but how will I live when I’m 40, 50, 60, 70 years of age? Will I be healthy? Will I still pursue my hobbies? Will I have children, or grandchildren even? Who will be close to me? I can’t force my fate, but I can make conscious decisions every day to aid this transition. I felt mindful, present in the moment, and free. Lucid.So I researched a sleep routine. Cleaned the entire apartment. Discarded useless stuff. Created lists and overviews. Organised. Shopping lists. Meal plans. Jotted down recipes. Fixed broken things. Impulse-bought some personal items for my living room.I addressed tiny things that stuck out to me more than once, like a mark on the wall that I painted over, or re-seasoning my cast-iron pan since it was in a bad state. Every time I looked at these, I felt remorse or the need to do them, but never followed through.I did all of this, and it felt incredible. Focusing on something, and realising it (as in putting it into reality). Self-efficacy. While I can’t vouch for the movie, it surely felt like this scene from Limitless.I didn’t realise right away, but I was feeling strong signs of restlessness. My heart felt like it was racing, even though I wasn’t doing anything exhausting. I couldn’t sit still for an extended time. My mind was jumping from thought to thought. I felt like a wound-up toy, manic. I used this frenzy to tackle all the chores and tasks and projects and minuscule things, and yet I still kind of liked it. 110% productivity.Other side effects I noticed: My face swelled up a bit, making it look more full (which looks good on me tho). My knee joints feel weird. My sleep is basically broken: I go to bed at 23:00–00:00 every day, and try to wake up at 8:00. The routine is there, but falling asleep actually takes some time, and I usually wake up at 5:00 or 6:00, completely awake. Not necessarily fully rested, but not sleepy anymore.Right now, I feel healthy and great. As I’m tapering off the cortisone, the side effects will cease, but all the work I put into improving my daily life will still be there.Maybe this post can inspire you to take a step back from your own life, and assess your priorities. I can rarely get into this mindset, but when I do, it makes me feel serene, in control. Every day life can get to you in so many ways.
