item.title: MPs moving to restrict gambling ads in Canada
item.author: Teever
item.content:encoded: This story is part of a CBC News series examining the public health impacts of online gambling.For T.S., a 22-year-old Ontario man recovering from a gambling problem, widespread advertising for online casinos and betting during sports broadcasts is "frustrating.""Imagine you're an alcoholic and there was a beer ad during every show you watched," he told CBC News. His gambling started three years ago as a fun Friday night activity with friends, but escalated. One night last year he found himself locked inside a bathroom, losing it all — having bet away $14,000.T.S., who CBC has agreed not to name, says he quickly sought treatment and hasn't gambled since. But during his spree, all those ads fuelled him to gamble more."It certainly … would trigger me to go back and place another bet."Politicians in Ottawa are moving to curb the widespread advertising currently seen across sports broadcasts, social media and online video games. WATCH | Sports gambling ads are everywhere. There's a push to change that:The federal standing committee on Canadian heritage meets next week to vote on , a law that proposes to rein in the ads across the country, amid new findings of increased addiction and gambling-related suicides in Ontario.CBC partnered with the University of Bristol to assess the 2026 NHL playoffs to count the numbers of logos and gambling messages. Across seven televised games featuring Canadian teams, viewers faced 3,000 gambling messages. Ninety-five per cent of those instances included no information about harm reduction or age restrictions.Raffaello Rossi, the lead researcher and a senior lecturer in marketing at the University of Bristol, says by reviewing every second of the game, his team found ads or logos appearing two to three times every minute.Ads appeared on stadium rinks, jerseys, helmets and during commercial breaks.WATCH | Researcher Rafaello Rossi on his findings:"Advertising via logos around the stadium, on the jerseys, on the helmets is much more efficient, because you've got a lot of knock-on effects," he said. "For example, if a news broadcast shows the highlights of a match, you will see these logos all across the sporting event. If somebody shares something on their social media, you will see those logos."He says viewers are additionally seeing the emergence of ads for prediction markets. The new analysis also confirms little has changed since with Rossi's team in 2024 revealed viewers were bombarded with thousands of ads and product placements in five NHL games (up to three per minute). Rossi says that's because Canada is behind other countries in passing legislation to curb gambling advertising."Multiple countries since then have introduced quite strict regulations and restrictions on gambling marketing in sports. So, for example, in Belgium and Italy and Spain, there's almost entire bans on sponsorship during sports."Proposed Canadian ad standardsIf Bill S-211 is approved at committee next week, the legislation — which has already passed the Senate — would be presented for a third and final reading in the House of Commons."It is a national framework around sports betting advertising," says the bill's sponsor, Bardish Chagger, the MP for Waterloo.She says limits on advertising are a way to address emerging harms, including growing rates of gambling addiction and suicide deaths, like those witnessed in Ontario after the province allowed private online casinos and sports betting in 2022.MP Bardish Chagger is sponsoring a bill launched by Sen. Marty Deacon to restrict gambling ads. The standing committee on Canadian heritage is set to vote on the bill in late October.(Dave Seglins/CBC)"People are being impacted in a very harmful way. They are losing their livelihoods, they're losing their homes, they're losing their savings, they're losing their lives," Chagger told CBC News.Sen. Marty Deacon first spearheaded the bill in the Senate and says it is time Canada tackles some of the negative public impacts of online gambling."These ads are ubiquitous across the country, especially in national broadcasts that are sponsored by betting companies, with logos plastered across broadcast desks, arenas and fields; this encourages Canadians in every province to gamble, even in those provinces who have held back," she wrote in an email to CBC News."We know where this is going, but we're allowing it to happen anyway."Sen. Marty Deacon first spearheaded the bill in the Senate, where it has passed.(Twitter)Current Canadian regulations are supposed to restrict gambling advertising targeting minors, at-risk people and gamblers who have asked to be excluded from the sites. But the code doesn't go as far as some European countries, which have outright banned televised promotions on sportswear and during events. Belgium, the Netherlands, the U.K., France and Germany have imposed time-of-day bans on gambling advertisements, restricting them to after 9 p.m. In France, companies have to get approval for their promotional strategies from the regulatory authority and submit an annual action plan to curb addiction. While Canada's Bill S-211 isn’t prescriptive, it asks the federal government to acknowledge the harms of online gambling and hold consultations to craft stricter regulations. Toronto Maple Leafs celebrate a goal flanked by advertising for Jackpot City online casino.(Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)Chagger says she hopes her bill will eventually lead to a ban on gambling promotions on sportswear and during live sporting events, outlaw ads during certain hours and prohibit celebrities and athletes from collaborating with gambling companies. Ontario and Alberta oppose the federal bill. In a letter to the federal government, Minister of Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction Dale Nally said the bill creates a two-tier regulatory system and threatens future provincial revenues.Ontario's Attorney General Doug Downey wrote to the federal government earlier this year, saying that the province should be left to regulate ads."Ontario has already established comprehensive and modern regulatory framework for online gaming and sports betting, which came into force in 2022. Advertising standards and protections were a central component of this work," he wrote. "The entire world is grappling with this in some way," said Matthew Young, a leading gambling researcher at Greo Evidence Insights."The real challenge right now is that we have a regulatory regime that is built upon physical borders, but a product that doesn't respect physical borders."Addictions researcher Matthew Young is calling for limits on gambling ads and better monitoring of harms.(Ousama Abdel Rahman/CBC)"The argument that it's provincial and territorial jurisdiction was all fine and well until ads from Ontario blanketed the nation and then suddenly New Brunswick had to deal with ads from Ontario."The Canadian Gaming Association (CGA), a national trade group representing 80 companies that run casinos and online sports betting, has opposing the plan to regulate gambling ads across the country.Instead, the CGA wants the government to spend money on assessing the "underlying health challenges" of gambling addiction, and let provinces decide advertising standards for themselves.""Unlike alcohol and cannabis, online gambling platforms, both regulated and unregulated, are readily accessible with just a few clicks. In this environment, advertising plays an important role in directing consumers toward regulated operators that are subject to stringent oversight, consumer protection requirements and responsible gambling standards," the CGA submission states. Recovering gambler T.S. says advertising for online casino games should be banned or require warnings, similar to rules for other addictive substances, like tobacco and alcohol."I think similar to cigarettes, you could put labelling on the apps themselves, as well as the ads: 'Here's what happened to Terry when he spent half his life savings on blackjack one night.'"Are you, or someone you know, suffering from gambling? Support is available.ConnexOntario 1-866-531-2600 or Text CONNEX to 247247

item.title: What’s getting pwned right now
item.author: mrkd
item.content:encoded: Linux kernel: unpatched ZDI bug reports with repro details leaked to public LKML (ksmbd RCE, CVSS 9.0)On Oct 21, Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative sent several unpatched Linux kernel vulnerability reports to security@kernel.org but Cc'd the public linux-kernel and subsystem lists, so full technical details (code paths, KASAN traces) are now public before fixes ship. The worst are two ksmbd (in-kernel SMB server) remote code execution bugs that ZDI scores CVSS 9.0: an SMB Direct integer underflow (needs an RDMA device and a writable share) and a protocol-dispatch race (needs a guest share). Also leaked: an skb_zerocopy local privilege escalation (ZDI-CAN-33367, CVSS 7.8), a vmwgfx out-of-bounds write LPE, and an nvmet info leak. ZDI-CAN-33367 now has a working public exploit: CloudLinux confirmed it gives any local user root on AlmaLinux 8, 9 and 10, Debian 12 and 13, and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04 where unprivileged user namespaces are allowed, and setting user.max_user_namespaces to 0 closes that path. No CVEs yet and no fixed mainline or stable release; the skb_zerocopy fix is posted for review but not merged, KernelCare has a livepatch only for CloudLinux/AlmaLinux 10, the ksmbd race fix sits in the ksmbd maintainer tree, and an SMB Direct fix is in a branch aimed at Linux 7.5. No exploitation in the wild reported. Only machines running ksmbd are exposed to the RCEs.updated Oct 24, 2026, 02:18 UTC

item.title: Show HN: OnKey – I'm a bad singer, so I built an app to show where I'm off-key
item.author: dsmurrell
item.content:encoded: I was pretty terrible at singing, now I’d say I’m bad but not terrible. This is because I’ve been using a singing app (won’t name it here) that scores me on my pitch and timing throughout the song so that I can improve.Lately however, the app I’ve been using has flooded their song list with songs that aren’t originals. I didn’t like this at all as for me, it’s easier to try to improve when you’re singing along to the original.So, I asked an agent (Claude Code) if it could write some code to listen to Spotify and also listen to me and see if it could detect both pitches and score me. It impressed me by writing some Python and showing me my pitch in the terminal!It couldn’t go all the way though and detect the singer’s pitch in real time.So I found the next best setup and built OnKey, a Mac app that needs to listen to the song once (it doesn’t save it) and then when it’s learnt the song (takes a couple of minutes), you can sing along to the pitch track that it’s learnt. OnKey is free to use and open source under the MIT license.It can listen to Spotify, Apple Music, and YouTube playing in your browser with the right permissions.During the build I found that someone had done something similar in Nightingale, but this requires a library of songs exported to disk and who has this in 2026 (maybe some of you ;) - but we need to help the normies too).The app sends out to find the song info (short Shazam fingerprint, and looks up song details), lyrics (from LRCLIB), and checks for updates.The app never sends the music (it doesn’t save this to disk) and your voice. Everything you’d expect to stay private does.It’s still weak in a few places:- when the song’s backing is noisy it’s hard to pick the pitch track out- sometimes it gets a note an octave off- it’s limited to Apple Silicon Macs, M1 or later, and only macOS 14.2 up because extra drivers aren’t required past this point- the scoring is built for beginners like me so it’s fairly easy on youWould love for people to try it out and let me know what works and what doesn’t for them!

item.title: Crystal 1.22
item.author: ksec
item.content:encoded: We are announcing a new Crystal release 1.22.0 with several new features and bug fixes.This release includes 251 changes since 1.21.1 by 33 contributors. We thank all the contributors for all the effort put into improving the language! ❤️Below we list the most remarkable changes in the language, compiler, and stdlib. For more details, visit the full changelog.Crystal processes exit immediately when writing to STDOUT or STDERR fails with . This closely resembles the default behaviour of the signal. Previously, the failing write would raise , which typically prints an error message and exits. This error message is now removed (#17335).You can opt out of this behaviour with STDOUT.exit_on_broken_pipe = false.Constants can have type declarations (#16951). They work exactly as you would expect the combination of constants and type declarations to be.The targets and moved from Tier 2 to Tier 1. The only missing piece was that we were lacking official builds, but we have that since 1.19. had been deprecated sine before 1.0 and now we finally removed it (#17367)New macros enable more text operations at compile time: (#17176), (#17169) and supports (#17170)New constants and provide access to the compile time flags (#17392).We completely revamped DWARF parsing to enhance performance and reduce memory usage. The DWARF parser now scans sections on demand (#17283) and builds an efficient index table once (#17410, #17455), which results in blazingly fast look ups. Decoded backtrace lines are cached in an LRU cache (#17285).Also added aupport for DWARF 5 features and (#17445).We merged numerous improvements and bug fixes for HTTP. and moved from to (#17196)Add (#17326)Serialize in HTTP body with header (#17388)Reject unrecognized HTTP header (#17140), invalid (#17262), and invalid HTTP trailer (#17337) Fix the return values of and (#17257, #17273)Fix HTTP.parse_headers_and_body to not raise with (#17272)Close on during request (#17318)Fix Content-Encoding: deflate (#17261)Fix parsing empty header name (#17254)Fix HTTP::Request#form_params? to ignore invalid content-type (#17256)All targets support a native event loop based directly on the system selector and use it by default.We enabled on Solaris (#17370) and on all remaining BSD targets (#17421, #17420). is still available as a fallback, but now it’s strictly opt-in and becoming technically obsolete. We expect to deprecate in a following release.We finally enabled support for Kernel TLS in the OpenSSL bindings by default (#17059)This was reverted in 1.22.1 and will stay disabled. (#17307), as well as , , now receive a argument(#17391)Add (#17428)Add Time::Span#to_nanoseconds etc. (#17190)Fixed backtraces when linking with on musl-libc (#17316)Uppercase instance and class variables (#17160)HTTP::Request#local_address and (#17260) and (#17494)Support for LLVM 23.1 and 24.0 (#17432)Updated distribution-scripts (#17178) brings upgrades of package dependencies, docker base images etc.This is the first release featuring builds for .Crystal established a forward compatibility policy in RFC 30: Building Crystal 1.22 requires a stage-0 compiler at 1.14 or higher.We have been able to do all of this thanks to the continued support of 84codes and all other sponsors. To maintain and increase the development pace, donations, and sponsorships are essential. OpenCollective is available for that.Reach out to crystal@manas.tech if you’d like to become a direct sponsor or find other ways to support Crystal. We thank you in advance!Contribute

item.title: Amazon identifies Oct 17 PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure
item.author: cubefox
item.content:encoded: Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating to Oct. 17, 2026, in MadPot telemetry, four days before public disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network. While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure.The PHP embargo window was set to be lifted on 2026-10-21 1400 UTC. On the day of the release, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified multiple proof of concept exploits for the vulnerability, with the earliest around 2026-10-21 0200 UTC. Subsequently, from 2026-10-21 0200 UTC to 2026-10-21 0800 UTC, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified additional exploitation attempts of PHP2Shell targeting MadPot from additional anonymized infrastructure. The actual payloads and choices in anonymization infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors. Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems.The actual release of the embargo window was 2026-10-21 1400 UTC. Once the embargo was lifted and the patch was released, additional proof-of-concept exploits appeared within hours, and we saw them used against our sensors almost immediately. PHP2Shell is now seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild.Two lessons from this event apply well beyond this one vulnerability:An embargo protects defenders only until someone else finds the same bug. Coordinated disclosure is still the right model. But defenders should not assume the public disclosure date is the earliest date of exploitation. With PHP2Shell, compromise may predate the advisory.The time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons. In the past, most exploitation we observed came after a public proof of concept was released. A small number of capable actors built exploits, and everyone else waited for them. That dependency is weakening. AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. As a result, more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed.For security leaders, this changes several working assumptions:For critical vulnerabilities in internet-facing systems, measure patch and mitigation timelines in hours. A 7-day or 30-day SLA assumes a delay that no longer exists.Start investigations from the earliest known exploitation, not from the disclosure date. For PHP2Shell, investigate from at least starting on October 17.Invest in detections that don’t rely on a signature for a specific CVE. The first exploitation will often come before those signatures exist.How AWS helps protect customersAWS deploys multiple layers of protection to help safeguard customers. Our internal threat intelligence system automatically detected and restricted malicious scanning attempts targeting this vulnerability. We analyze over 200 billion events per minute and integrate threat intelligence from our MadPot honeypot network to identify and block known exploitation attempts in real time. Our honeypot system provides us with early detection of exploitation attempts, enabling rapid response and threat analysis.Immediate recommended actionsUpgrade immediately to the fixed PHP versions. Upgrading is the only complete remediation for both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. There are no configuration-only workarounds that fully address both issues.Consider blocking multi-part file uploads in PHP deployments that cannot be patched immediately, but determine how this would affect your application prior to deploying.Look for POST requests with the PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS string in form uploads.Review web server logs for suspicious activity.Check for unexpected process execution or file modification on web application servers.Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)The identified IP addresses include shared anonymization infrastructure and are not exclusive to this threat activity. Organizations should investigate any observations involving these addresses as opposed to blocking.

item.title: The Quake Fan who built the map editor everybody uses
item.author: klaussilveira
item.content:encoded: Back in 2010, a Mac user named Kristian Duske wanted to make Quake maps again. Small problem though: nobody had built an editor Duske actually liked. ToeTag by Warren Marshall was out there, but the workflow just did not click. So Duske, who already had some 3D programming under the belt, did the only sensible thing: wrote a new one from scratch. Fifteen years and a couple of full rewrites later, that editor is TrenchBroom. If you have played a custom Quake map in the last ten years, there's a good chance it was born inside of it. Mappers swear by its 3D first workflow. Indie teams used it to build modern retro shooters like Wrath and GRAVEN. Godot projects have been using it with Qodot and other extensions. And the Quake scene, which by all means should now be gathering dust next to the Voodoo2 in your parents garage, is having one of the best runs in its history, with TrenchBroom sitting right in the middle of the party. The punchline? Duske never made another map. Not one. Not in TrenchBroom, not in anything else. We caught up with Duske by email, somewhere between a full time programming job at a music company, a family, and a worrying number of hours in Control Resonant. We talked about the spark that started it all, the code that should have stayed simple, the move from wxWidgets to Qt, the CSG algorithm that refused to be tamed, and the fine art of maintaining a project of this scale. Grab your rocket launcher. Here we go.What was the spark that made you create TrenchBroom? Was it a small itch, or had you planned it for a while? I started TrenchBroom in 2010 because I wanted to make maps again, but I was (still am) a Mac user and couldn’t find a level editor that I liked. There was ToeTag by Warren Marshall, but I wasn’t super happy with the workflow. Plus, I had already experience with 3D programming and wanted to improve my skills. So I started TrenchBroom as a macOS (then called Mac OS X) app, written in Objective C and C only. This version was released in 2012. People were interested in the 3D only approach, but since most Quake modders and mappers used Windows at the time, they couldn’t use it. I decided I would start over, but this time using C++, which I also wanted to learn, and with portability in mind. TrenchBroom 1.0 came out a year later, initially for Windows and macOS: TrenchBroom 1.0 release. The Linux builds came out a bit later. Since then, there has been one major rewrite (TrenchBroom 2.0 in 2018) and in 2020 we switched the UI frameworks from wxWidgets to Qt. Ironically, I never made a single map again, using TrenchBroom or otherwise...It's been 15 years since April 2, 2011, the first commit on GitHub. What would the Kristian of 2011 be most surprised by in TrenchBroom today? That it’s so successful and that I’m still working on it. I wasn’t expecting that at all when I started it. And maybe the 2D views, because I originally didn’t want to add those at all.Any design decision from the early days you would take back? Lots! TrenchBroom has a lot of over engineered code that I’m still cleaning up to this day. I wish I had kept things simpler back then and used much less object orientation. I have spent enormous efforts in undoing past mistakes.How has your relationship with the project been all those years? Any moments you stepped away or nearly quit? What made you come back? There have been fluctuations, which you can see on my github profile if you go through the years, but overall it has been relatively constant. I never quit the project, so I never had to come back either. Lately I have been more motivated to work on it because AI support allows me to take on tasks that I couldn’t take on alone before. For example, I was able to reorganize the project into smaller libraries and improve the build system using AI, which I had been wanting to do for a long time, but doing that manually in the evenings would have taken too long. These quality of life improvements make working with the code much easier, so now I can focus on the more interesting features and contributions.The Quake mapping scene has had a real renaissance in recent years. How much of an impact do you think your technical decisions in TrenchBroom had? That’s a tough one to answer, but I think a few factors may have contributed here: The 3D centric workflow allows for more direct control and quicker iteration. I also believe that using 3D views predominantly instead of 2D views influences how mappers think about their designs.Linked groups make it much more pleasant to establish and evolve a design language. Some designs in recent maps have clearly been influenced by this feature (look for symmetry).TrenchBroom supports large maps relatively well, so mappers can create such maps and work comfortably with them.We use the textual map format instead of a custom format for storage, so maps can be edited in other tools. This makes it easier to use other tools for tasks that TB doesn’t support so well. I hope that the sum of my technical decisions (and UX decisions) have enabled mappers to reach flow state easily. Flow state is fun and rewarding, so people spend more time using TB to make maps.What was the hardest feature you had to implement in TrenchBroom? The hardest feature I never got right was a nicer CSG subtraction algorithm. I wanted it to produce the same output that a mapper would produce, with no unnecessary added vertices and nice symmetry features etc., but it’s a very hard problem to solve. The problem is NP complete, which is a comp sci term that means “proven to be untractable for large inputs”. I tried this for months with many approaches, but they all failed, so I gave up and did the simple approach that we have now in TB. The hardest feature that did make it into TB was linked groups. Linked groups affected almost everything else, and it took quite a while until the feature became stable and performant, in particular with the supported protected entity properties. But I think the effort paid off handsomely because if used well, linked groups can transform the entire mapping workflow and make it much more efficient and fun!Was the switch to Qt worth it? Do you think it's still relevant? Yep, that was worth it. It was almost fully driven by Eric Wasylishen, who was my co-maintainer at the time. wxWidgets forced us to make many platform specific work arounds, and Qt abstracts most of these away, so the code is much nicer to work with. Making code nice to work with is quite important for a hobby project like this. I really don’t want to spend my free time working on ugly and hard to maintain software, so I invest a lot of time into making the code nice to work with for me. Opinions vary of course, so what I find hard to work with might seem terrible to others...What was it like supporting several Quake-derived engines? What kind of brush quirks did you have to battle with? Daikatana has the most quirks of them all, and TB still doesn’t support them all 100%. Other than that, it wasn’t too hard, although we are still lacking full support of a bunch of engines. For example, Quake 3 support is still not finished, but I’m working on it.What about the different texture projection formats? The original Quake format only has axis aligned texture projection, which distorts the textures on slanted surfaces, making texture lock impossible. That’s why we need the Valve 220 map format. I don’t think anybody is still using the original Quake format anymore. Linked groups also wouldn’t work very well without exact texture lock. There’s a third option that TrenchBroom doesn’t support yet: Brush primitives from Q3Radiant. Brush primitives don’t offer anything else than Valve 220 maps that I’m aware of, so it’s not exactly a high priority for me to add support for them.How did you get into gaming? And what made you cross the line between playing games and wanting to learn more about them? I started playing games on our home computer back in the 80ies. I played point and click adventures and the early flight simulators like Secret Weapons of the Luftwaffe, or X-Wing by Lucasarts. One day my brother got ahold of Wolfenstein 3D and from then on I was hooked on FPS games. I played Doom, mail ordered a Doom level editor and fell in love with mapping. Then came Quake and Quake 2 and online deathmatch. I downloaded and played lots of custom deathmatch maps for Quake and Quake 2 and released a few myself using WorldCraft and the original QERadiant. I became a part of that scene and made some life long friends. It felt like a natural transition from being a player to making my own content. I was quite young, maybe around 20, the internet was still new and the possibilities were endless. I also started my first Quake related programming projects back then, starting with a converter tool that allowed me to use QERadiant, a Quake 2 editor, for Quake 1 maps. Later I ported the FitzQuake engine to SDL so that I could play Quake on my Mac. But I originally started programming even earlier when I was around 16 or so. Back then I was very much into electronic music and bought a couple of synthesizers and samplers to make Techno, but since I spent all my money on hardware, I couldn’t afford the software. Being naive, I decided to write my own sequencer and MIDI utilities. I had taken some basic programming class in school and learned everything else from books and offline manuals. Later I studied computer science and now I work as a programmer for a music company, so I somehow ended up where I started, only with slightly more understanding of what I’m doing. These days I mostly play games on my Playstation 5. I love The Last of Us, Death Stranding and Control. Currently I’m playing Control Resonant, which is why TrenchBroom progress has taken a bit of a nose dive. I still play Quake, but I don’t play every released map like I used to in the past.How do you maintain the vision? How do you keep motivated? I don’t have a super clear vision, just a few guiding principles. These have become very ingrained into my thinking over the years so it’s essentially second nature and what appears as a vision maybe just arises from these decisions. I try to keep TB’s UX and workflow simple. Sacrifice some control for ease of use. Don’t introduce too many options or preferences. Don’t overwhelm users. Don’t surprise them. Of course I don’t always succeed. The TB user base has grown a lot in recent years, and I’m not a part of the other communities that use TB as much as I am a part of the Quake community, so I don’t understand their needs and requirements as well. For me, TrenchBroom is still a Quake level editor first and foremost, so that informs my decisions and priorities when working on features, but sometimes these decisions and priorities are at odds with the requirements and wishes of other communities. But TrenchBroom is open source, so people can fork it and with AI tools, they can adapt it to their workflows. What motivates me is seeing what the Quake community creates with TrenchBroom, and how TrenchBroom enables people to be creative. That really makes me happy. You don’t need much to make Quake levels. You don’t need a super beefy computer or additional hardware. Almost any laptop will do. The tools are available for every major platform. So Quake mapping is sort of democratic and inclusive by design, although not all communities haven’t always been so welcoming to everybody. TrenchBroom has also been used by indie developer teams to make retro shooters such as Wrath, and that makes me proud, too.Is it hard to say no to contributors? In the beginning, it was more difficult to say no because there was much less interest, let alone contributions. To me it makes a big difference whether a feature request would benefit a lot of people, or whether it just benefits a vocal minority, in which case I’ll usually deny it nowadays. I try to be graceful but I know I don’t always succeed. I answer issue reports and pull requests during work breaks or in the evenings before dinner, and sometimes my answers will be brief. Some things have been discussed to death years ago, and when such a topic comes up again, I’lll just say “I don’t want to discuss this again”. That doesn’t seem very graceful on the receiving end, but I’m just one guy with a family and full time job. I simply don’t have the time to write a lot of prose, or I wouldn’t get any feature work done at all.

item.title: Tell HN: I unknowingly broke the PHP RCE embargo. I am sorry

item.content:encoded: I posted here about the then-upcoming PHP RCEs related to CVE-2026-109618 & CVE-2026-109619. I appreciate this has had considerable knock-on effects with the schedule for co-ordinated disclosure, and created additional workload.I am truly sorry. I have learned my lesson.

item.title: Faster than earcut: triangulating 3.7M map polygons in 489 ms
item.author: molind
item.content:encoded: We have published the polygon triangulator of our map engine as a small library, earstrip, under the ISC license, the same one earcut uses. It is one C++ header, and a WebAssembly build on npm that takes the same arguments as earcut. In C++ it is 14% faster than earcut.hpp, in the browser 1.4 to 2.1 times as fast as earcut.js, and the comparison is near the end. This post is about how we got there.A GPU fills triangles and nothing else. A map, on the other hand, is mostly polygons: buildings, parks, parking lots, the strip of grass between two tram tracks. Here are a few blocks of Śródmieście in Warsaw the way our renderer reads them from a map file, :Before any of this gets a fill, every outline has to be cut into . Hover over a polygon, or tap it, to see what it turns into. These blocks hold 331 polygons with 5,151 vertices, and they become 4,514 triangles.Zoom level 13 of our offline map of the Masovian Voivodeship, the region around Warsaw, has 3,740,425 polygons. On one core of an M4 Pro, the constrained Delaunay triangulator in our engine needs 2.93 seconds to cut all of them. This October I replaced it with ear clipping. To write this post I rebuilt the ear clipper one idea at a time, one commit per idea, and timed every commit on those same 3.7 million polygons, so each section below ends with a number.A triangulation of a set of points is Delaunay when no point lies inside the circle through the three corners of any triangle. Two triangles that share an edge are enough to see how the rule works. Drag the point D:While D stays outside the dashed circle through A, B and C, the shared edge is AC. and the edge flips to BD; and it flips back. Each flip is a local repair, and a triangulation where no edge wants to flip is Delaunay. Of all the ways to triangulate the same points, it has the largest smallest angle. The arc marks the smallest angle of the two triangles, and the line under the figure shows what the other diagonal would give: wherever you put D, the edge the circle rule picks wins."Constrained" means that the polygon's own edges must stay edges of the triangulation, even where the circle rule would flip them away. Our triangulator inserts the vertices one at a time. For each new point it walks across the triangles built so far until it finds the one the point falls into, splits it, and flips edges around the new point until the circle rule holds again. It also forces the polygon's edges in, and at the end it keeps only the triangles that lie inside the polygon and outside its holes.Well-shaped triangles matter when you interpolate something across them or run a simulation on them. A flat fill doesn't care: a GPU fills a needle-thin triangle as correctly as a fat one. And most of the work is spent on polygons that hardly need any. Almost half of the Masovian polygons, 1.8 million, have four vertices or fewer. A triangle needs no cutting at all and a convex quad is two triangles, yet the Delaunay code spends 302 ms on them, building each triangulation from scratch.An ear of a polygon is a corner you can cut off with one straight cut. Take three consecutive vertices a, b and c. If the corner at b is convex and no other part of the polygon reaches into the triangle abc, that triangle is an ear. Cut it off, and what remains is a polygon with one vertex fewer. In 1975 Gary Meisters proved that every simple polygon with more than three vertices has at least two ears that don't overlap. So there is always another ear to cut, and a polygon with n vertices falls apart into n − 2 triangles.Here is one of the buildings from the blocks above. Move the slider to cut its ears one at a time, or :The triangle is the next ear to go. The algorithm needs one test, "is this corner an ear?", and the simplest version of it checks the corner and then every other vertex of the boundary. is the 2×2 determinant found in every geometry codebase; it is positive when c lies to the left of the line from a to b, so for a boundary that runs counter-clockwise a positive means a convex corner:A point on an edge of the triangle counts as inside: if the ear touched the rest of the boundary, cutting it off would leave a polygon that touches itself. The one exception is a point at exactly the position of a, b or c, which happens where an outline meets itself at a single vertex. Holes make that common.Ear clipping works on one closed boundary, and 11,345 of the Masovian polygons have holes, such as courtyards and clearings in forests. The way to deal with them is to cut each hole open and stitch it to the outer ring with a bridge, an edge from a vertex of the hole to a vertex of the boundary, walked once in each direction. The boundary then runs around the outside, crosses the bridge, goes around the hole the other way and comes back. There is no area between the two copies of the bridge, so the polygon is the same, but now it is one ring.The bridge must not cross anything. David Eberly's write-up of ear clipping has a neat way to find one. Take the rightmost vertex of the hole, m, and cast a ray to the right. The first edge the ray hits, at I, has an end P further to the right. If no boundary vertex lies inside the triangle m, I, P, the bridge m–P is safe. You can drag the hole around: the triangle is empty and the bridge goes to P. the sits inside the triangle, and the bridge goes to the dent instead: of the dents in the triangle, Eberly takes the one closest in angle to the ray. Holes are bridged rightmost first, so a hole further left can bridge to one that is already part of the boundary.Map data adds two cases of its own. Our coordinates are integers on a tile grid, so a ray along a grid line runs all the time; the crossing test passes over such a vertex, and my first version got exactly this case wrong. And mappers often draw a courtyard that at one point. Such a hole needs no bridge: the two rings are joined at the shared vertex.The naive clipper (−1,812 ms)​With holes bridged, the first complete version walks around the boundary, tests corners with the above, cuts every ear it finds and writes each triangle as three indices. On the Masovian polygons it takes 1.12 seconds, 2.6 times faster than Delaunay. The chart splits each time by polygon size; hover over a part of a bar to see its number, or click a row: is shorter than in every size class but the last. The 1,123 largest polygons, with 257 vertices or more, take 199 ms to clip and 90 ms with Delaunay. Each ear test there walks hundreds of vertices, and a polygon needs hundreds of tests, so the cost grows with the square of its size. The rest of this post is about making the ear test cheaper and needed less often.Test only the dents (−237 ms)​Look at which vertices can actually stop a convex corner from being an ear. Say some vertices lie inside its triangle, and take the one closest to the corner itself. Its two edges can't cross the sides of the triangle, so both run back, away from the corner, and the polygon wraps around that vertex from the corner's side. That makes it a reflex vertex, a . So if anything is inside the triangle, a dent is inside it too, and the test only has to look at the dents.The engine keeps a list of them. A dent leaves the list when cutting its neighbour makes it convex, and a convex corner never turns into a dent, so the list only shrinks. The test becomes:The 28.1 million ear tests now look at 185 million points instead of 353 million, and the total drops to . That is less than you might expect, because building outlines have a lot of dents. The building with the arch above has 15 of them among its 27 vertices. And the smallest polygons get slower, from 34 to 54 ms: for a triangle or a quad, sorting the corners into dents and the rest costs more than the walk it saves.Skip tests on convex polygons (−2 ms)​A polygon without dents is convex, and every corner of a convex polygon is an ear, so it can be cut without a single test. Checking for that needs care. "Every corner turns left" is not enough:The turns left at all five corners, because it goes around its centre twice. The engine adds one more condition. Walking around a convex ring, the edges go right along the bottom and left along the top, so their x direction changes exactly twice, at the leftmost and the rightmost point. The passes; the star changes direction four times, at the corners, and goes to the ordinary ear tests. Both counts come out of the same loop that marks the dents, so the check costs almost nothing. Triangles and quads get their own shortcut before that loop.The shortcut removes 4.4 million of the 28.1 million ear tests, but those were the cheapest ones: a ring without dents has nothing to scan. On its own it barely moves the total, , though the polygons with four vertices or fewer win back part of what the dents cost them, from 54 to 48 ms. It matters more in the next step, where a convex ring becomes a single strip.So far every triangle costs three indices. A GPU can also draw a triangle strip, where each new index adds a triangle made of it and the two before. A convex ring makes one strip if you zig-zag across it:The ear clipper can write strips too. Cutting an ear makes the corners of its two neighbours sharper, so they are good candidates for the next ear, and cutting one of them extends the strip by a single index. The engine tries them first and keeps alternating between the two ends while the ears last. In its code the neighbours of the cut vertex are a and b:When the next corner is not an ear, the strip ends and the walk goes on from where it stopped. The 21.5 million triangles now take 35.8 million indices instead of 64.5 million. The ear tests don't get fewer: the naive walk already went on at the next corner after a cut, and now every strip also ends on a test that fails, 25.0 million instead of 23.7 million. Still, the total falls to , and the largest polygons drop from 146 to 103 ms.Sort the dents into buckets (−65 ms)​A forest or a lake can have thousands of vertices and hundreds of dents, and each ear test still reads every one of them. When a polygon has more than 32 dents, the engine sorts them into buckets along the longer side of their bounding box, about two dents per bucket. An ear test looks only at the buckets that its triangle spans. As dents turn convex and leave, the index is rebuilt once half of it is gone.Points scanned fall from 181 million to 101 million, almost all of it on the large polygons: the polygons with 257 vertices or more go from 103 to 57 ms. Total: .Count without branches (−178 ms)​The loop in the dent test exits at the first dent inside the triangle. Most of the time there is none: the test reads all the dents and says yes. An early exit then buys nothing, and the three comparisons per point are branches the CPU has to predict. The engine first runs a pass that only counts dents inside the triangle, with no branches at all:The smallest of the three determinants is non-negative exactly when the point is inside the closed triangle. Only when the count is not zero does the exact loop from before run, to rule out dents that sit on a corner. The bucket version does the same with a bounding-box test, 64 points at a time into a bit mask. The total falls to , and the middle sizes gain the most: polygons with 33 to 256 vertices go from 327 to 216 ms.Test only the marked dents (−30 ms)​When the count is not zero, the exact loop reads all the dents again, although the first pass has already seen which ones were inside. The bucket version keeps that in its bit mask. The short list, up to 32 dents, can do the same: the first pass sets one bit per hit instead of counting, and the exact test looks only at those dents:Points read fall from 128 million to 120 million. This is the last step, and it is the code of earstrip as published: , 6.0 times less than Delaunay on the same polygons.Meisters' theorem is about simple polygons. Map data is rounded to a tile grid, and rounding can break a simple polygon. Here is the outline of Warszawa Śródmieście, a railway station less than a kilometre from the blocks above, rounded to grids of different size. The orange rings mark vertices that land on the same point as their neighbour: per tile side, the grid our map files use, a grid step is 18 cm. Even there 31 of the 154 vertices merge with a neighbour, because mappers often place points a few centimetres apart, and the outline survives. nearly half of the vertices merge, and the clipper still cuts it. the rounded outline touches itself in a way that leaves no ear at all, and at 10 bits it happens to work again.When the clipper walks all the way around the boundary without finding an ear, it drops the corners that have no area and walks once more. If that fails too, it gives up, and the engine triangulates that polygon with the Delaunay code, which still exists for this. In the Masovian data 76 polygons end up there. They come from a map built before the last change on the other end: our map generator now rounds every polygon to the final grid with GEOS's snap rounding and checks that ear clipping can cut it. In a fresh build of the Masovian map that repaired 273 polygons, and ear clipping can cut every polygon in the file.Delaunay has one more job. Every hole needs its own bridge, and finding one scans the whole boundary, so a polygon with thousands of holes pays for thousands of scans. Our world map has a polygon with 11,675 holes: ear clipping takes 606 ms on it, Delaunay 17 ms. The engine now sends every polygon with 128 holes or more to Delaunay. In the Masovian data that is two polygons.The library keeps both of these fallbacks inside. earstrip covers a polygon with a constrained Delaunay triangulation of its ring edges when the ears run out, when the triangles they leave cover the wrong area, and when it has more than 128 rings; in C++ and in JavaScript say which way a polygon went. On the 56,472 polygons of our world map tiles, with up to 11,675 holes in one, earstrip takes 459 ms and earcut.hpp 2,892 ms. On the zoom 13 polygons that the ears can't cut exactly, earcut's triangles differ from an even-odd fill of the rings on 31% of the pixels on average, earstrip's on 0.15%.Before the new clipper went into the app, I compared it with earcut, the ear clipper behind MapLibre and Mapbox GL, in its C++ version earcut.hpp 3.2.4. Natively the two are close, and that could have been the end of it. But we are working on a web renderer that runs the same C++ engine compiled to WebAssembly, so I went further and compared the browser side too: both clippers compiled to WebAssembly, and earcut.js 3.2.4, the JavaScript original that web maps run today. For that I took the clipper out of the engine into earstrip. On all 5.8 million polygons of our test sets it writes exactly the engine's strips, and its repository has these polygons and the code behind every number in this section. Its native benchmark is the one behind the chart above, and the native row below is the last step run against earcut.hpp. Every WebAssembly build gives exactly the same triangles as its native version on all 4.4 million polygons of zoom levels 13 and 9. Milliseconds for the 3.74 million polygons of zoom 13, best of 7, one thread, V8 in Node and JavaScriptCore in Bun:WebAssembly, loop inside the module, V8 / JSCWebAssembly, one call from JS per polygon, V8 / JSCnpm package, one call per polygon, V8 / JSCnpm package, direct calls, all polygons in one call, V8 / JSCNatively earcut.hpp is 14% slower than earstrip. Compiled to WebAssembly and run in V8, earstrip loses 23% and earcut.hpp loses 67%, almost all of it in its main loop that searches for ears. It isn't the allocator: builds with mimalloc and emmalloc give the same time. I haven't dug further. In V8, earcut.hpp in WebAssembly ends up only 19% faster than plain earcut.js, and 10% once each polygon is a separate call from JavaScript.The package rows are what a web page gets, and the earcut column there is earcut.js. The call that replaces earcut takes the coordinates as JavaScript numbers and returns a new array of triangle indices every time: 1.4 times as fast as earcut.js in V8 and 1.6 times in JavaScriptCore. About half of what it loses against the loop inside the module goes into copying the coordinates in and turning the strips into a list, the rest into calling into WebAssembly once per polygon. The direct calls skip all of that: the polygons go straight into the module's memory and come back as one index buffer of strips for WebGL 2 or WebGPU, 1.7 and 2.1 times as fast as earcut.js.Some of the ideas above are in earcut too. It also relies on the fact that only a dent can block an ear, but it checks that last, for every vertex that passes the bounding box and triangle tests, instead of keeping a list of dents. Above 80 vertices it links them in z-order and scans only the stretch of that curve the triangle's bounding box covers, which does the job of the buckets. What it doesn't have are the shortcut for convex polygons, the strips and the count without branches: it writes three indices per triangle and stops at the first point inside.earstrip is on GitHub and npm, with the polygons from this post and the code to time it against earcut on your own machine.

item.title: Jailbreaking the Switch 2
item.author: ledoge
item.content:encoded: You can get a copy of the exploit from the ns2jb repository.ns2jb is a software-only, tethered jailbreak for the Switch 2. It allows running arbitrary native code as any ordinary sysmodule, and as the built-in sysmodule. This lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO. To my knowledge, it’s the first such exploit for the Switch 2.To demonstrate the capabilities of this jailbreak, Codex modded a Switch 2 exclusive, Mario Kart World. Thanks to my friends in Dabney House who helped me choose characters to add and playtest the game.The very first thing I did was set up a harness around the Switch 1 and 2 so Codex could, ideally, jailbreak the Switch 2 without me:Edit: Many people have been asking me if I actually used this prompt. No, it’s just a silly caption. I set a /goal for userland code execution, but that didn’t succeed. The jailbreak itself took substantial effort for ~2 weeks. The Mario Kart World, however, was entirely vibecoded in a day, and was just for fun.The JetKVMs allow Codex to send controller inputs to the Switches over USB and receive video output over HDMI. We also need a way to press the power button—when the Switch 2 crashes, it needs a button press to restart.That’s what the Bluetooth light switch flicker from Amazon is for. When the lever comes down, it presses the power button. Once the power button is fully pressed, the rest of the lever’s torque lifts the mechanism.WebKit is a popular target for console jailbreaks, so it’s unsurprising that Codex has picked it for initial code execution.Code execution through the browserIt claims to have “native control-flow hijack” by taking advantage of a WebKit n-day loaded via a custom Wi-Fi captive portal.We’d like to get code execution in microkernel services (or “sysmodules” on the Switch), so we can run homebrew, mod games, download saves, etc. Unfortunately, this approach of replacing one JavaScript function object with another doesn’t generalize beyond existing functions—we’d need a new way to make arbitrary IPC calls. That looks difficult.WebKit has execute-only memory, or XOM, so even with arbitrary memory RW, we don’t know where a gadget that could perform arbitrary IPC calls is.Even if we did, perhaps by parsing relocation data, it’s not clear how we’d construct a signed pointer for it because of PAC.And even if we could, with some signing gadget, it’s not clear how we’d call this pointer, since CFI type-checks most call sites.Codex has reset the goal to complete these steps. It’s a side bet; it may succeed, but let’s be real: the accessibility of WebKit and the Nintendo BBP reward have probably incentivized many before me to look here.While that runs, let’s explore other options.Code execution through smilehax2My idea was to target Switch 1 games, for two reasons:They’re built by developers. It’s less likely we’ll need to deal with PAC and CFI, especially because the Switch 1 does not support PAC.Since the Switch 1 root of trust is owned, we can decrypt the code and read it.Maybe we can still get the upsides of the browser attack surface—orchestrating from JavaScript, using existing n-days, etc—while avoiding the downsides of WebKit mitigations by finding a Switch 1 game that embeds a browser? Something analogous to Electron, but for games, so we could pull off an exploit like this Discord RCE. I can’t disclose this approach’s findings publicly at the moment, but luckily, there are other Switch 1 games.In particular, I’m interested in SmileBASIC. This is because it’s been pwned before, in smilehax, giving userspace code execution on the 3DS. It’s a giant C++ codebase; surely, if there was an exploitable memory corruption in the BASIC interpreter, there can be another.Codex found a useful 32-bit integer overflow in the interpreter. When removing items from an array, the interpreter checked position + count <= array.length, but the sum could wrap and become negative. To fill the gap created by removing elements, it’s supposed to shift the remaining elements left, like so:Say we have a string array of length 4, and we run REMOVE R,&H60000000,&H3FFFFFFF. wraps to . As a negative signed 32-bit integer, it’s less than . The multiplications by 8 also wrap, so we end up performing memmove(backing, backing - 8, 32), pulling the previous 8 bytes into the array. The command does report an error, but it doesn’t matter, since the copy has happened already.This is useful because the 8 bytes preceding any array in SmileBASIC contain a pointer to the array itself! After the , operations on will treat the array backing as if it were a string.Since a pointer occupies what would be the length field of , the string length is enormous, and we can perform reads and writes out of bounds. We read and write to memory by copying to and from substrings of .This was a Switch 1 game, so the SmileBASIC agent could work on the exploit on my Switch 1, while the WebKit agent worked on the Switch 2. After some time, it got ROP.Which sysmodule should we pursue? We don’t have their code, so it’s unclear which sysmodules have which privileges.I gave a few Codex instances the goal of getting sysmodule code execution. Most chose to focus on audio and ldn. I think that’s because audio and ldn have had bugs on the Switch 2. Codex also looked at the NV service, probably because GPU drivers are generally fruitful?It’s probably similar to the module in the Switch 1, since the filesystem API didn’t change very much.The first reason is the most attractive to me. Even if we can’t get a useful jailbreak from , we can at least decrypt some of the other sysmodules so Codex can find bugs in them. Other sysmodules like and look enticing because they have permission to map executable memory, but they don’t have large attack surfaces, especially from SmileBASIC. We’ll come back to them later.Buffer overflow with path normalizationPaths containing a parent-directory component with a backslash, like , call into a helper that allocates a temporary heap buffer of 0x301 bytes. Our path is copied in, but it can be larger than the buffer, causing a buffer overflow. lolWe’ll need a good victim allocation to overflow into. Codex found that the object allocates a cache entry for its files. If that entry has its dirty bit set, reads and writes to the file follow a pointer to cached data. We can hijack that for arbitrary read/write.From here, I scanned through memory to find SmileBASIC’s connection object and set the saved PID to 1. Now, my process has “FullPermission”, meaning I can perform privileged filesystem actions. I dumped internal storage and all ordinary sysmodule code, so Codex could perform offline analysis and I could understand where to go next.Homebrew and modding typically rely on executing our own native code. Looking at the dumps, the only ordinary sysmodule with permission to map executable code is . All these sysmodules have CFI, PAC, and XOM. The interface for the module seems pretty minimal too. It seemed more fruitful to pursue a logic bug than to look for memory corruption in directly.Let’s revisit that first point about serving decrypted code. This was useful for dumping the code for ordinary sysmodules. What’s the intended functionality of this interface? Loading programs?Games and ordinary sysmodules are distributed as Nintendo Content Archives, or NCAs, containing a filesystem image called ExeFS. This contains a file for the main executable, , and program metadata, .To load a program, the built-in sysmodule asks to open ExeFS, and replies with an IPC handle to the filesystem. also provides two pieces of cryptographic information about the NCA header: the header’s SHA-256 hash and the developer’s signature of that hash. The loader uses this information to perform two signature checks:Is Nintendo’s signature of ’s process permissions and the developer’s public key valid?Is the developer’s signature of the NCA header hash valid?Seems cryptographically sound to me, because, in theory:the NPDM signature fixes the process permissions and developer key;the key fixes the NCA header’s signature;the signature fixes the NCA header’s hash;the hash fixes the NCA header’s contents, including its filesystem hashes;those hashes fix the executable content.In practice, however, I’m doubtful of that last claim, because it’s the responsibility of the module to ensure the served filesystem matches the NCA header’s filesystem hash, and we have ARW in it.Arbitrary r/w to native code executionIndeed, with ARW, we can replace the ExeFS object behind the loader’s IPC handle with our own temporary filesystem. This filesystem still needs to serve a valid developer for the loader’s first check, but the executable itself can be arbitrary. The second check will pass because, by the time the loader opens the filesystem, has already submitted the valid NCA header hash and signature for the original filesystem.There are two writes we perform:The first puts a temporary filesystem object we’ve made into the domain-table entry for the loader’s ExeFS. This temporary filesystem contains the original and our replacement .The second puts the loader’s ExeFS object into the domain-table entry for our temporary filesystem. It’s just to keep refcounts consistent and prevent from crashing.These writes must happen after the loader requests the ExeFS filesystem but before processes the subsequent file requests. How do we ensure this?The process maintains a list of its IPC connections. When a connection has a new IPC message, processes it. Using our arbitrary read/write, we can replace the handle waits on for the loader’s IPC connection with an event handle we control from SmileBASIC. That lets us control when processes a loader message.With this, we can execute arbitrary code as any program we have a for!Getting built-in sysmodule native code executionWhat s do we have? Well, all of them. With ARW, we can use to the loader’s connection to copy the NPDM of any ordinary sysmodule or game.We’ll use this capability to launch our own code using ’s NPDM. As mentioned earlier, ’s NPDM gives it permission to invoke kernel SVCs like SetProcessMemoryPermission, , and . In this case, we’ll use to create a writeable view of ’s existing code. We can also dump ’s code by reading this view.These calls, however, require a handle to the process. To get a handle to , we’ll use our ARW to overwrite ’s 4-byte handle with and then call from SmileBASIC. The kernel interprets this value to mean “the current process’s handle”, so SmileBASIC gets ’s handle.We can then send this handle to our custom process, who patches ’s code.Arbitrary code execution with any ordinary sysmodule’s permissions seems really powerful. We can investigate hardware without first exploiting each device’s driver. I’m hopeful this will help the homebrew community make progress toward CFW.In the short term, there are a few next steps I think would be interesting:Porting the sysmodule exploit to WebKit. Now that we know what bug we want to exploit, being able to perform arbitrary IPC calls is not as valuable. We might be able to trigger ARW in by changing the data used by WebKit’s existing filesystem code.This jailbreak is tethered, and we don’t currently have a way to compromise built-in sysmodules other than . is a built-in sysmodule, so SM skips service ACL checks from , providing the same capabilities as smhax. I wonder if we can find bugs in other built-in modules?With native code execution in , we can orchestrate its crypto hardware directly. For example, it’s used for NCA4 decryption.The exploit has also been tested on the Switch 1, but I haven’t gotten around to packaging it yet. It wouldn’t provide the capabilities of a modchip, but it wouldn’t require any external hardware.For now, I’m excited to see all the upcoming Switch 2 homebrew, emulation, and modding.

item.title: WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal
item.author: alphax314
item.content:encoded: I fine-tuned a 360M-parameter language model to act as a terminal. There's no shell or filesystem behind it: every keypress goes in, and the model predicts how the screen changes. It can create files, run vim and tmux, play snake, and usually remembers what you wrote a few commands later. The biggest wins were teaching it to repair its own mistakes and decoding screen rows in parallel. Try it in your browser (208 MB) and type to see that it's not a real shell.The demo is designed for a desktop browser with WebGPU and a physical keyboard. Chrome or Edge is the best place to try it. It should work on a modern phone, but painfully slowly.When I first saw Genie 3 last year, I started imagining a future where applications aren't written in code but learned. Instead of a game engine rendering the scene, a model predicts the next most likely frame from the user's inputs.Naturally I wanted to train my own world model. But I don't have a massive GPU cluster or a pile of video data, so I scaled down my ambition: instead of a game world, a terminal.A terminal turned out to be a good fit. It's just a grid of characters rather than pixels, and I can generate as much perfectly labelled training data as I want by running real shells. A pretrained language model also already has a pretty good idea of what or should print.What I really wanted to know was whether it could maintain a consistent world, or just generate convincing terminal output.The final model is based on Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, fine-tuned on terminal sessions recorded from real programs running inside Docker. Jump to example videosStandard LLMs take a prompt and then append tokens to the end, one at a time. That doesn't map well to a terminal. A single keypress can do something on its own, like in vim, and output doesn't always go to the bottom: wipes the screen and sends the cursor back to the top. So instead of predicting a stream of text, I need to predict changes to the screen. I treat the terminal as a grid of characters, one per cell. The model doesn't see the grid directly, but a sequence of tokens describing its contents and the changes made to it.Every session starts with a snapshot: the screen size, its contents and where the cursor is.The size is part of the input, not fixed at 32×96. In the demo, you can set the rows and columns when creating a custom starting screen.This also lets me start partway through an application. Give it a bash prompt, vim buffer or a game of snake, and the model tries to continue from there. (It does better from bash.)After that, each keypress goes in as the raw bytes a real terminal would send. Letters are themselves, Enter is , Escape is and ← is and so on.The model answers with which rows to rewrite and where the cursor ends up:In words: on row 0, starting at column 17, write , then move the cursor to row 0, column 18. The last means the cursor is visible, since full-screen apps sometimes hide it. Nothing gets cleared first. New characters are simply drawn over the old ones.I didn't need new tokens for characters. Qwen already has tokens for all 256 byte values, which I reuse for characters, coordinates and other small numbers. So a coordinate like 17 takes one token, not two.Time is an input too. If nothing is pressed, the model gets a WAIT token with a duration instead of a key, which is how snake keeps moving on its own.When you reach the bottom of the terminal window and press enter, every line has to move up by one. I could just ask the model to output every row again in its new place, but that's around 3,000 tokens for a single keypress. So I added a operation instead:ROW_0 COPY 1 ROW_1 COPY 2 ROW_2 COPY 3 ... Each operation copies a row from the previous screen. In this example, the old row 1 becomes row 0, row 2 becomes row 1, and so on.A scroll now costs three tokens per row instead of roughly 96.The same trick covers clearing the screen, inserting and deleting lines in vim, and navigating man pages. You can also copy a row and then overwrite part of it.Altogether, the model uses a tiny vocabulary of 333 tokens: 256 byte tokens, 64 row tokens and a handful of special operations. Decoding is grammar-constrained, so every prediction is a valid screen update. That tiny vocabulary comes back later, when I squeeze the model into a browser.Generating the training dataI initially looked for existing datasets of terminal recordings, including asciinema, but couldn't find one with the precise keystroke-to-screen alignment I needed.Luckily it wasn't too hard to create my own.The basic idea was to generate believable terminal sessions by running real commands inside Docker containers, recording every keypress and the screen after each one. The synthetic recipe was:Randomize usernames, hostnames, prompt styles, terminal sizes.Randomize directories and files based on a fictional persona (developer, sysadmin, etc.).Pick 6–24 weighted activities (modify files, vim, python, tmux, etc.).Track state, so sessions mostly open files that exist.Type like a person: one keypress at a time, with tab completion etc. I set the typo rate to 1.2%, which is generous to me.35% of sessions start partway through, forcing the model to learn to work from any state.The terminal size was mostly 32×96, with some 24×80 and 40×120, so the model doesn't overfit to one size.I kept expanding the dataset as the model became more capable, and finally landed on 336k episodes, which corresponds to roughly 2B tokens. For comparison, the base model saw around 18T tokens during training.I used Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B as the starting point. I needed a small model to get close to realtime performance. Being a coding model, it had also already seen plenty of CLI usage. I started off by doing straightforward supervised fine-tuning: give a screen history and a keypress, predict the screen delta produced by the real terminal.Ordinary typing was learned quickly: a letter appears, backspace removes it, the cursor moves. In longer sessions, though, errors started to compound: a mistake in a filename propagated through the rest of the session.Learning from its own mistakesTo address this I took a page from DAgger, where a model learns from the states it visits rather than just the ideal demonstrations.For each training example:Pick a point in a recorded session, usually close to the command that produces the output.Let the model predict the next 1-4 events.Compare the resulting screen with the real recorded screen. If the difference is small enough, construct a correction that repairs the model's screen on the next keypress.Continue training on the corrected frame and a few subsequent real events. The delta takes the model's incorrect screen to the correct next screen. In essence, it learns to "repair" its own mistakes.There's one important restriction: the model must have enough information to infer the correction. Any words introduced by a correction must have appeared on an earlier real screen or in the user's typing, not just in the model's own predictions.For example, if the model misspells a filename that appeared earlier, I can teach it to fix that. But if it lists a filename it has never seen, I can't expect it to get it right. Training on those examples would actually reward hallucinations, which I really don't need more of. About a third of the sampled sessions produced useful correction examples. I repeated this in three rounds, each time collecting mistakes from the latest model. Self-correction was one of the more effective training changes. Along with some additional training data, it improved PresetBench (defined below) from 24/47 to 38/47 at int4.In total, training the model and its later refinements took roughly 75 GPU-hours on an RTX 4090.I use three tests. has 106 commands across 24 handwritten bash sessions, scored by exact output. has 47 scripted cases drawn from failures I hit in the demo. Neither test appears in the training data.The has 32 worlds. Each writes two random values to two files, then reads them back in separate sessions. A world passes only if both readbacks are exact, giving 64 readbacks overall. The names and values never appear in training.How much does fine-tuning help?Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, promptedThe biggest difference was memory: WorldTUI got 9/13 readbacks right, compared with 2/13 and 3/13 for the prompted models.It's still far from a reliable filesystem. It handles familiar commands fairly well, but combining them in new ways can quickly break things. For example, after , running often doesn't show the appended line.For a while I stayed away from autoregressive models altogether. A full redraw is around 3,000 tokens, and generating those one at a time seemed hopeless for something that's supposed to feel like a terminal.But they just performed so much better than the alternatives I tried, so I gave in. With one token at a time, typing felt fine at ~38 ms per key, but anything that redraws the whole screen (, , ) took up to 12 s on my RTX 4090, exactly as feared. Plenty of time to reconsider whether I needed the manual. And I wanted this to run on my Mac, in near real-time.What I'd missed was that most rows in a frame don't depend on each other, so there's no reason to generate them one after another. I run one batch element per row. Each gets the same previous history (including KV cache) but generates only its own update.That changes the decoding cost from the sum of all rows, up to 3,000 steps, to the length of the longest row, roughly 100 steps. The cursor then becomes its own step at the end that can see the whole set of row updates. This required a matching attention mask during training, but the speed improvement was worth it. Large-frame p95 latency dropped from 6.7 s to 0.87 s.Large-frame p95 latency (RTX 4090) ↓Rows that can't talk to each otherThis might sound too good to be true, and it was. The issue is that since rows are independent, they can't coordinate, which led to opening on row 3 instead of row 0, or several rows adding food for snake at once. The solution was speculative decoding.Normally speculative decoding uses a small model to draft tokens and a larger model to verify them. Thanks to causal attention, several tokens can be verified in a single forward pass.Here I use the same model for both: the parallel rows produce a draft, which the model then verifies sequentially.The verifier keeps tokens up to the first disagreement. From there it generates its own correction and re-proposes the remaining draft. In the browser on my M4 Mac, typing a single character takes about 60ms. A larger update like takes 2.5s sequentially, or 0.9s with parallel drafting and verification.I started with Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, which has roughly 494M parameters. I really wanted a web demo, so I needed to shrink it. The embedding table for its 151,936-token vocabulary is 136M parameters. I only need my 333 tokens, so I can drop almost all of it, which takes the model from 494M to about 360M parameters (990MB → 716MB).I then quantized it to int4, which brought it to 208 MB. The browser demo uses a custom JavaScript implementation of the Qwen decoder, with compute shaders written in WGSL and run through WebGPU. The shaders unpack the 4-bit weights during inference. Activations and the attention cache use 32-bit floats. All inference runs locally in the tab.Distilling it into fewer layers taught me something about which layers memory depends on. The teacher was an earlier checkpoint, which scored 78/106 on ShellBench. Removing just layer 7 without retraining barely changed next-token accuracy: 99.3% fell to 98.9%. But exact memory readbacks fell from 64/64 to 0/64. These tests fed in the true history, so the failure wasn't caused by errors compounding on the model's own output.My first distilled student kept every even-numbered layer, but used the final layer, 23, instead of 22. It still wrote plausible terminal output, but returned the right value in only 31/64 memory readbacks. It always printed one of the two values it had written, but picked the wrong one about half the time. That's chance, and it hadn't recovered after 480M training tokens.That student had dropped layers 1, 7, 15 and 22. A 16-layer student that kept those four passed all 32 memory test worlds, with 64/64 exact readbacks. It still passed all 32 worlds at 4-bit, at about 138MB. There was a cost elsewhere, though: it got 65 ShellBench commands right against the teacher's 78. So a student can look fine and have quietly lost its memory.In the end I gave up on distilling it.This was the part I was most interested in. Generating a convincing directory listing is easy. What I wanted was to create a file, edit it, wander off, and come back to find it unchanged.The first time I started tmux, opened a file in vim, changed it, saved it and then in a different tmux window read the updated contents with , I felt like Dr. Frankenstein: it's alive! It was very important to me that this should work beyond the bash prompt, so I trained on vim, python, man pages, snake and even tmux. In vim, it handles the mode switch on and lets me save, quit or go back into insert mode. Probably the most compute-intensive snake in the world.What really blew my mind was tmux: I can create multiple panes, do various things in each and jump between them. It's not perfect, but it's a small model. It even manages environment variables and variable expansion.Since the base model is a coding model, I was curious how it would handle the Python REPL. It makes a decent attempt: small additions are usually right, and list comprehensions return a list, though often with the wrong contents. It's also slightly forgiving of typos: launches Python, but doesn't.I didn't allow the Docker containers internet access, so tools like lynx are fairly boring. Python can handle very simple operations, but anything harder produces answers that remind me of GPT-3-era hallucinations. Sometimes, when I create nested directories, it gets lost and all of a sudden I'm in a different path. There's clearly a lot of room to improve consistency.In my testing, the demo ran about 20× slower in Firefox than in Chrome. It uses WebGPU in both. I haven't managed to establish the cause.As always with projects like this, I tried to solve it myself first and only then looked at how others had approached it.WorldTUI is closer to the original ChatGPT terminal trick, except that it's trained specifically on keypresses and screen updates, including full-screen applications like vim and tmux.I had a blast building this. Is it useful? Not really. But for a 360M-parameter model running in a browser tab, it's far better than I expected.What interests me most is that it manages to maintain a somewhat consistent world without implementing any of the rules underneath.It's obviously a pretty weak world model, and I'd love to see how far this approach could go with better consistency and a different way of generating screen updates, perhaps using diffusion instead of autoregressive decoding.One experiment I want to try next is training on thousands of randomly generated applications, each with its own controls and rules. The idea is to see whether the model can learn to predict the behaviour of an application it has never encountered before, given enough contextual clues.Try it here. It's a 208 MB download, runs entirely locally, and works best in Chrome. Try to break it, and let me know what you find.I'll post the weights soon and add the download link here.
