item.title: There isn't an easy exploit for this PHP vulnerability
item.author: zkldi
item.content:encoded: I know, I know. It's all you're hearing about. That, and the number .Don't get me wrong, there's clearly a bug here and it really does matter. But this is easy to exploit. It is certainly nowhere near as easy as Log4Shell/Heartbleed/RoRYaml etc. Putting this up here so people read it. You should patch your servers anyway. There a real vulnerability here, but exploiting it is significantly harder than people are making it out to be - it is certainly not as easy as e.g. log4shell.Justify yourself, you lunatic!I don't think this PHP vulnerability is that exploitable. I think that 5 years ago people would've understood this, but now people are being deluded by their LLMs telling them they have an exploit when they don't.If you take a look at github right now, there are thousands, literally thousands, of "PoC" exploits for this vulnerability. One thing you'll notice about all of them though, is that they against a vanilla PHP instance.Go ahead, stand up a php server you think is vulnerable in Docker and then . Don't get your LLM to do it. No. Run the script, yourself. The exploits don't work.Where's the exploit, Lebowski?I think that a lot of people had assumed that LLMs will be able to build an exploit chain instantly from reading the diff, and that even if this was harder to exploit than other exploits, LLMs would've levelled the playing field. Well. There's no working exploit. Now what?When I think about "we're very fucked" CVE10s on the Internet, I think of the following vulnerabilities:RoR YAML decoding (send a post body with bad yaml in it)Log4shell (set your user-agent to ${jdni:ldap:})Shellshock (copy env x='() { :;}; echo vulnerable' and edit to taste)Heartbleed (ask for Content-Length 10000000)The second these vulnerabilities made the news, there were botnets doing the rounds causing damage. And this was before LLMs! People have to write the botnets. With their hands!It's been 10 hours since this vulnerability has been posted, and half the software world is looking at it, and lord knows 100,000 people have got their "superintelligence" on the case. Nevertheless, there's no working exploit. The ones doing the rounds are fake, or only work in a lab, because...Script kiddies (and script adults, who have also switched their brains off) now all think that, well, they don't understand UAF chaining, but this Claude guy knows everything and can totally make an exploit.Hilariously, this results in the LLM giving their younger-brother an unplugged controller. It says exploit all across the screen... and has some smoking gun transcripts... but it's modified the server you're testing against to have a severe vulnerability. Cheating!!I just plucked these three because they were the ones with the most stars, but it goes on for miles and miles.One really amusing thing in common with most of these "PoC"s is that they lean on "LFI", or local-file-inclusion, to make the vulnerability. In non-php terms, their exploit chain requires the server to already have a severe code-level vulnerability.The strangest thing is that so many people have independently made this extraordinarily weird defect in judgement. That is because they haven't independently made this decision. Claude/Etc. has done all of the judgement for them, hence the bizarre distribution in logical errors.There's something important to be said here about how many people have Claude/GPT make design decisions for them, and how AI is the primary decision maker in the world right now. You've got this bizarre case of "Decision Schelling Points" where a method of solving a problem is extremely overrepresented, because it's what Claude does out of the box.It's especially bizarre in this case, where AI is inserting a vulnerability on the server... to prove that the server is vulnerable to your "exploit any PHP instance" attack!So why was everyone so scared?A PHP core team member said that this was cataclysmic ("exploits will start appearing 15 minutes after the patch drops")We all deep down know that PHP is insecureThe exploit video had an anime girl in itWe all know that LLMs are looming over the internet like a 100 ton chekov's anvil, and we know that code isn't secureAnd we've had things like this before, but not in the LLM era yet. Luckily for us, this doesn't seem to be that day. This is too difficult to exploit easily. It isn't a Log4J moment.EDIT: I have added my contact details to this post and fixed a broken link. I added the disclaimer at the top that you should still patch.

item.title: Security Disclosure
item.author: passenger
item.content:encoded: Earlier this morning, Railway detected anomalous activity involving systems that store customer environment variables. After further investigation, our investigation to date indicates that an unauthorized third party may have accessed encrypted environment variables and, for some of them, obtained the decrypted contents. Environment variables may contain secrets such as API keys or database and registry credentials.We believe this is part of a series of attacks recently targeting platform companies with the aim of compromising AI inference providers. We have notified these upstream providers to revoke all keys proactively, as we take these kinds of events extremely seriously.While our initial analysis suggests the impact may be limited to a subset of users, we are nevertheless recommending that all users take the actions described below as a precaution to protect your systems while we complete our review. As such, we strongly recommend that you immediately roll all environment variables, including any API keys, stored in Railway, as well as any private registry credentials, and review logs for those services for unusual activity.All deployments are paused while we investigate. Until builds are restored, you will not be able to roll out new versions. We apologize for this inconvenience. Follow this incident to be notified when builds resume.As we confirm which accounts were affected, we will contact those customers directly by email with additional details.We will provide new updates on this announcement, and on status.railway.com as we narrow the scope of impact.

item.title: PHP web runtimes (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619)
item.author: hayd
item.content:encoded: This is an ongoing issue. Information is subject to change. Please refer to this bulletin for the most updated patching information. 2026-143-AWS AWS Important (requires attention) 10/21/2026 14:30 PM PDT 10/23/2026 13:30 PM PDTTwo critical issues have been identified in PHP web runtimes (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) that can allow an unauthenticated actor to run code on affected systems. A remote caller can send crafted web requests to affected PHP workers and execute arbitrary code, read process-accessible data, or cause denial of service.AWS services are not impacted by these issues. Customers using the affected versions of PHP within the services listed below could be impacted and should review the guidance provided. Affected versions 8.5.0–8.5.11 · First fixed version: 8.5.12 Affected versions 8.4.0–8.4.26 · First fixed version: 8.4.27 Affected versions 8.3.0–8.3.35 · First fixed version: 8.3.36 Affected versions 8.2.0–8.2.34 · First fixed version: 8.2.35 No upstream fix released. End-of-life and have no planned fix. Migration to a supported branch is required.This issue is accessible remotely by an actor without authentication over the internet-to-customer-application boundary, which can result in code execution, unintended access to process-accessible data, or denial of service on the targeted PHP worker. The issue is bounded to the affected worker and its application-level permissions; no cross-customer propagation has been established to date.Current Mitigation Status: Amazon EMR on EC2 clusters launched with Ganglia included in the application set are affected, specifically EMR releases 4.2.0–5.29.0 and 5.30.0–6.15.0. Amazon EMR on EKS and Amazon EMR Serverless are not affected, on any release. On Amazon EMR on EC2, clusters running release 7.0.0 or later, and clusters launched without Ganglia installed, are also not affected. For affected releases, customers launching new clusters should omit Ganglia when it is not required. Where possible, customers should upgrade to EMR 7.x, which no longer includes Ganglia, and use the Amazon CloudWatch Agent for telemetry and monitoring. AWS has applied configuration-level controls and has completed the upgrade to PHP 8.3.36. No customer action is required. AWS has released updated PHP platform versions for all supported PHP versions (8.2 through 8.5) containing the upstream PHP fix. Customers with Managed Platform Updates enabled will receive the update automatically during their next maintenance window. Customers who have not enabled Managed Platform Updates should update their environment's platform version by following the documentation: PHP 8.5/8.4 and PHP 8.3/8.2. AWS Lambda does not provide a managed PHP runtime. Customers who have deployed PHP as a custom runtime or container image are responsible for updating the PHP version used in their functions. We recommend upgrading to a patched PHP release as soon as possible and redeploying your functions. For guidance on building and maintaining custom runtimes, see the AWS Lambda documentation. If you use the third-party Bref project to run PHP on Lambda, Bref has published a security release containing updated layers and Docker images with the patched PHP versions. Please follow the Bref security release for update instructions. Updated PHP packages are available for all regions. Customers running PHP on Amazon Linux should apply the updated packages as soon as they are available. Please follow CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 in the Amazon Linux Security Center for details. Updated Lightsail blueprints are now available in all regions. AWS cannot update running Lightsail instances in place. Customers running PHP workloads on Lightsail should create new instances from the updated blueprints and migrate their applications following the documentation. to a patched PHP release is the only complete fix: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35. The configuration changes below may reduce impact for customers who cannot update immediately, but none is a complete mitigation.End-of-life runtimes 5.4–8.1: Apply interim configuration controls for CVE-2026-109619 where effective, restart PHP workers, and begin migration to a supported, fixed PHP branch immediately. No fix is available for CVE-2026-109618 on end-of-life branches.Compensating controls if using AWS WAF:Patching is the only complete fix, and customers should upgrade PHP as their first priority. As patching a fleet takes time, we recommend reviewing this blog post, which shows how to use AWS Web Application Firewall (AWS WAF) to help reduce exposure during that window. Please note, this blog will be updated with AWS WAF guidance changes as this situation evolves. We are continuously updating the AWS WAF PHP Managed Rule Group to add protection for both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Customers using the default version will be automatically protected without any action on their part. Customers who have pinned a specific version should update to the latest version to receive this protection. For the latest version and details on the rules added, please refer to the AWS WAF Managed Rules changelog and subscribe to the AWS Managed Rules SNS topic.

item.title: Mistral Large 4
item.author: funnym0nk3y
item.content:encoded: Today, we’re launching a public preview of Mistral Large 4. Unofficially ML4, very officially: . ML4 pushes the frontier of open-weight performance. You can try the preview API today on Mistral Studio. Weights drop end of this month. ML4 is a 1 trillion-parameter natively multimodal model with 52 billion active parameters. It is our largest and most capable model to date, and it continues to improve rapidly as we refine it.The model demonstrates exceptional performance across coding, agentic workflows, and multimodal understanding. It already achieves performance competitive with the strongest open-source models globally, while significantly outperforming any open-weight model developed in the US or Europe. On critical enterprise workloads, including cybersecurity, finance and law, we find it to be state-of-the-art among open models. In some domains such as visual grounding, it goes further still, surpassing even frontier closed models.We will release the weights by the end of the month. Until then, we are red-teaming the model in real-world settings with cybersecurity leaders, vetted partners, and state authorities, who will access the same model with reduced moderation and expanded cyber capabilities.Forged in Europe. Built for AI sovereignty.ML4 was trained from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral’s own datacenters in Europe. The public preview is served on that same infrastructure. It is a significant milestone in our long-term investment across infrastructure, research, and product development: state-of-the-art performance in critical verticals, delivered through open weights, designed to give customers control over their AI.This is particularly important in cybersecurity, where provider-level refusals can block legitimate vulnerability research and incident response, and where losing access to a capability mid-incident can itself become a critical security risk. ML4 pairs top-tier cyber performance with open weights and self-deployment, giving organizations both the capability and the autonomy to run advanced security work under their own policies.The model will be available across multiple regions worldwide, including a European deployment that Mistral operates end-to-end, independently of other digital service providers and under European law. Fun fact: a significant share of ML4’s training data was multilingual, spanning more than 160 languages, including every official language of the European Union. We’ve been working closely with leading enterprises across the world in finance, engineering, manufacturing, logistics, pharmaceuticals, science, shipping, public sector, and other mission-critical industries to train ML4. In fact, the model uses the same training, customization, and RL environment we offer our customers through Mistral Forge.There is still more to come. As we work toward releasing the weights, we will share further details on the model architecture, additional benchmarks, and our post-training methodology.This model will also serve as the foundation for a new generation of specialized and optimized Mistral models. In the meantime, we invite you to try the preview API and share your feedback with us on social media.ML4 is one of the world's strongest AI models for cybersecurity. On the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, an independent evaluation of how well AI models find and fix security flaws in real software, it ranks among the top five models globally and leads open-weight models developed outside China by a wide margin. On one of the index's tests, which asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch it, ML4 scores 82%, the highest of any model. It also solves 93% of the challenges in Cybench, a set of 40 exercises drawn from security competitions, one of the highest scores reported for an open-weight model.That top score reflects a practical advantage. Several leading closed models, including Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, score near zero on the same test because they refuse to perform the task. Yet defending software often starts with proving that a flaw is real, exactly the kind of work safety filters in closed models can block. This matters even more as threat actors increasingly jailbreak those same models to support offensive cyber activity: defenders need systems that can match those capabilities without being constrained by the same refusals. ML4 can do that work, and its capabilities extend beyond what it was explicitly trained for: in internal testing, it proved useful for analysing malware, prioritising vulnerabilities, and writing detection rules. For organisations that need sovereign, auditable AI for security operations, it will be able to run on private cloud or on-premise.ML4 against the field : efficiently reasoning over diverse complex challengesMalware reverse-engineering: solving an out-of-distribution investigation taskML4 excels across software engineering, repository understanding, and complex terminal workflows, scoring 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.We also ran a blind human evaluation with Surge AI on coding quality: professional annotators rated model outputs on a 1–5 scale, with model identities hidden. ML4 Preview ranked second of five models (3.74), ahead of Kimi K3 (3.59), GLM-5.3 (3.60) and GLM-5.2 (3.40), and behind only Claude Opus 5 (4.22).ML4 runs general-purpose agents that gather information, use tools, and produce finished deliverables across complex workflows. On AutomationBench — 657 business workflows across apps like Gmail, Google Sheets, Slack, and Salesforce — it scores 59.9%, ahead of Kimi K3, MiMo-V2.6-Pro, and DeepSeek V4 Pro.It's just as strong on the professional deliverables that knowledge work actually produces: spreadsheets, slides, and PDFs. On AA-Briefcase, which evaluates long-horizon knowledge work, it reaches 1,393 Elo, ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro.ML4 is a step change in the ability of our models to understand images. It reasons powerfully across complex documents, charts, and natural images, and brings vision to the industries where perception is critical such as engineering, manufacturing, and earth observation.The model can further combine visual grounding with agentic capabilities: from inspecting gigapixel satellite imagery — helping disaster-response teams act when time counts — to analyzing engineering-drawings — zooming in, inspecting, and verifying until the answer is exact. In our demos above, ML4 grounds dense natural scenes, verifies mechanical parts in technical drawings, retrieves evidence from PDFs, and scans massive geospatial images for the hardest-to-find objects.On visual grounding particularly, we find ML4 to be one of the most capable models we tested, for instance surpassing GPT-6-Astra on Dense 200 (42% vs 41%).ML4 brings strong scientific capabilities, built by combining AI-driven methods with our researchers' expertise in mathematics, physics, and chemistry.It's highly proficient at agentic coding for scientific tasks such as data analysis, modeling, and simulating physical reality, which lets researchers focus on the questions rather than the plumbing. In benchmarks, ML4 is state of the art on SciCode-Verified among open-weight models. In practice, it can generate a full Hartree–Fock simulation in one shot — a complex, multi-step chemistry task built from a series of advanced routines.ML4's math is stronger too, in both formal reasoning and applied mathematics. In our human evaluations it reasons more precisely and with more structure than GLM-5.3, and it can sustain long, domain-specific applied-mathematics tasks, including work relevant to frontier theoretical physics.Together, these capabilities make ML4 a strong research assistant across the full technical workflow — from the first question to the final result.SciCode-Verified tests the capabilities of models to implement complex scientific workflows in code for domains such as physics, mathematics, material science and biology. Internal eval on STEM tasks (math and physics) of ML4 against GLM5.3ML4 is our most capable model for the real-world tasks which professionals handle every day. It can create, edit and fix complex spreadsheets and documents, showing exemplary performance on both legal and financial benchmarks.Notably, we evaluated ML4 through third party evaluators () on representative tasks for both legal and financial tasks, finding the model exceeds GPT-6-Astra in both cases. On HarveyAI’s Legal Agent benchmark, ML4 outperforms all open-source models.FinWorkBench tests model capabilities at creating/editing spreadsheets on real life Finance and Accounting use cases. Financial analysis demands precision and the ability to synthesize information from multiple sources, a process that remains time-consuming at many financial institutions today. In this demo, ML4 compared to other top OSS models take on the same multistep corporate finance challenge, searching through public company filings and financial reports, such as those available via EDGAR and equivalent European databases. An animated semantic map traces each model's journey toward a solution, highlighting every document retrieved along the way. Each track's position reflects the evidence gathered, the results of calculations, and the questions that remain unresolved. Viewers can follow how the investigations unfold and compare the distinct paths each model takes before arriving at its final answer.ML4 has saturated our benchmarks on robustness to indirect prompt injections, putting it at the frontier of OSS models (compared to GLM-5.2, GLM-5.3, Kimi-K2.6, Kimi-K3, DS-V4-Pro-0813). On Lakera’s public , ML4 resists 93.3% of attacks – we see no higher scores among competitors.ML4 also engages more responsibly with users than any of our previous models. We highlight our results on the , where ML4 again sits at our highest measured score among OSS models (1.691, with 2 being the maximum denoted as “”). Of particular relevance is the model’s propensity to refuse malicious requests regarding cybersecurity. Despite strong performance on Cyber benchmarks, the average refusal rate of the model on cyber prompts from , , and is higher than all OSS models.We ran an internal evaluation in which expert annotators across coding, computer-aided design (CAD), finance, mathematics and physics compared Mistral Large 4 with GLM-5.3. ML4 was preferred in CAD and STEM, while performing on par or close to GLM-5.3 in finance and coding.Reinforcement learning at scaleBase models are improving fast, and our post-training has to keep pace. A recipe tuned for yesterday's model leaves capability on the table with today's frontier, because ground truth samples that once pushed a model to its limits won’t anymore. We use Reinforcement Learning (RL) because it adapts as the model does: we train on the outcomes of the model's own attempts, and we can raise the difficulty and the breadth of the tasks as it gets stronger.Our RL library was designed to make new environments easy to add and train at scale. A shared, composable interface allows a single training run to combine tasks ranging from single-turn chat and complex scientific problem solving to safety alignment, factuality, and long-horizon tool use. These environments share scaffolds and resources such as code sandboxes, web search, and external APIs. The same composability extends to verification, with reward models, unit tests, LLM judges, and static checks combined as needed for each task.At runtime, an autoscaling fleet of actors generates tens of thousands of rollouts in parallel while model training proceeds asynchronously. The generation and training pipeline is optimized for long trajectories, supporting rollout budgets of millions of tokens across multiple compactions while keeping staleness low. Novel methods and optimizations across both stages minimize off-policy drift and enable stable RL over long horizons.At our current scale (3k GPUs), a single training run produces roughly 33 billion tokens per day, of which around 16 billion are trainable completion tokens after filtering and masking. We can see the run progress directly in the training rollouts: training rewards rise across several representative environments as the policy learns to solve increasingly complex tasks. Below are a few examples.The improvements are not specific to the environments we train on; they transfer to downstream evals, and the final model owes them to both post-training stages (supervised fine-tuning and RL), as shown in the charts.This is only the beginning. ML4 is the first milestone on the roadmap funded by our €3 billion Series D — the largest equity round ever raised by a European technology company. That capital is already being put to work: we are significantly scaling up our compute capacity in our own European datacenters, and much more is coming online in the months ahead.More compute means more training. The reinforcement learning run behind this preview is still in flight, and the model is showing no signs of saturation — there is substantial headroom ahead. As we scale up training on our expanded infrastructure, we expect large and rapid improvements in the weeks and months to come.We will release the weights by the end of the month, along with more details on the architecture, additional benchmarks, and our post-training methodology. And ML4 is only the foundation: it will serve as the base for a new generation of specialized and optimized Mistral models, built for the industries and workloads our customers care about most.The pace of progress from here will be fast. Stay tuned.

item.title: Claude Duet
item.author: kuberwastaken
item.content:encoded: Claude Duet uses your Claude account, including memory, skills, and connectors. The Claude app waits for you to open a chat, and you work on something alongside Claude. Claude Duet comes to you. It tells you what needs your attention each morning, takes tasks you hand it by message, and reaches out when one is done or needs your approval.

item.title: GitLab critical patch release
item.author: artooro
item.content:encoded: On October 21, 2026, we released versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, 18.11.13 for GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE).These versions contain important bug and security fixes, and we strongly recommend that all self-managed GitLab installations be upgraded to one of these versions immediately. GitLab.com is already running the patched version. GitLab Dedicated tenants running 19.3.5-internal0 and 19.4.2-internal0 or later already include these fixes and do not need to take action.GitLab releases fixes for vulnerabilities in patch releases. There are two types of patch releases: scheduled releases and ad-hoc critical patches for high-severity vulnerabilities. Scheduled releases are released twice a month on the second and fourth Wednesdays. For more information, please visit our releases handbook and security FAQ. You can see all of GitLab release blog posts here.For security fixes, the issues detailing each vulnerability are made public on our issue tracker 90 days after the release in which they were patched.We are committed to ensuring that all aspects of GitLab that are exposed to customers or that host customer data are held to the highest security standards. To maintain good security hygiene, it is highly recommended that all customers upgrade to the latest patch release for their supported version. You can read more best practices in securing your GitLab instance in our blog post.We that all installations running a version affected by the issues described below are upgraded to the latest version as soon as possible.When no specific deployment type (omnibus, source code, helm chart, etc.) of a product is mentioned, it means all types are affected.GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server due to integer overflow when compiling a specially crafted regular expression.In addition to our standard patch releases, we have backported this fix to GitLab CE/EE versions 18.11.13, 19.0.10, 19.1.9, and 19.2.9. GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 7.0 before 18.11.13, 19.0 before 19.0.10, 19.1 before 19.1.9, 19.2 before 19.2.9, 19.3 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3, and 19.5 before 19.5.1 10.0 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H)Thanks joaxcar for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty programGitLab security has released two threat detections to support customers with self-managed instances, listed below. GitLab-managed infrastructure, including GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated, remains patched.CVE-2026-15723 - Improper Authentication issue in OmniAuth-to-LDAP auto-linking email lookup impacts GitLab CE/EEGitLab has remediated an issue that, when OmniAuth SAML and LDAP auto-linking were both enabled, an authenticated user could have taken over an existing LDAP-backed account without any interaction from the targeted user, due to improper input sanitization in the LDAP email lookup path used during OmniAuth identity linking.Thanks stealthy for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty programCVE-2026-112212 - Cache Poisoning issue in OAuth/OIDC discovery endpoints impacts GitLab CE/EEGitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, an unauthenticated user could have poisoned a shared cache’s OAuth/OIDC discovery document to redirect certain flows to an externally controlled server, due to improper trust of user-supplied values when constructing endpoint URLs in cached discovery responses.This vulnerability has been discovered internally by GitLab team member Peter ArtsCVE-2026-12664 - Improper Access Control issue in GraphQL work item email address field impacts GitLab CE/EEGitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user with a read_api-scoped token to retrieve a project’s incoming email address and create work items, bypassing the token’s restrictions, due to insufficient scope enforcement on a GraphQL field.Thanks go7f0 for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty programGitLab has remediated an issue that, when the instance-wide SAML or LDAP membership lock was enabled, an authenticated user could have granted or accepted project and group membership outside the identity provider’s control, due to incomplete enforcement of the membership lock on requests created before the lock was enabled.Thanks 3nvz for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty programGitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, an unauthenticated user could have retrieved sensitive internal server credentials due to improper filtering of internal response headers.Thanks altair00 for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty programCVE-2026-13319 - Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key issue in group milestones API impacts GitLab CE/EEGitLab has remediated an issue that could have allowed an authenticated user to read milestone metadata, including titles, descriptions, and full project paths, from arbitrary private projects across the instance without any project membership, due to missing authorization checks on a user-supplied project filter parameter in the group milestones API.Thanks a0xnirudh for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty programGitLab has remediated an issue that under certain conditions could have allowed an authenticated user to access paid AI features without a valid subscription due to insufficient server-side validation in billing eligibility checks.This vulnerability has been discovered internally by GitLab team member Halil CobanGitLab has remediated an issue that, when a merge request in a public project referenced a confidential issue from a private project, an authenticated user with no project membership could have read the confidential issue’s title, due to a viewer-independent fragment cache key that incorrectly shared per-user-redacted rendered content across all users.Thanks 20kilograma for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty programCVE-2026-14288 - Improper Access Control issue in merge request approval policy enforcement impacts GitLab EEGitLab has remediated an issue that under certain conditions could have allowed an authenticated user to bypass a required merge request approval policy on a protected branch due to improper access control during approval rule synchronization.Thanks 3nvz for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty programCVE-2026-112326 - Improper Cleanup on Thrown Exception issue in security findings impacts GitLab EEGitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user with read-only permissions to permanently delete existing vulnerability records due to improper cleanup logic that failed to distinguish between pre-existing records from newly created ones during error handling.This vulnerability has been discovered internally by GitLab team member Gregory HavengaCVE-2026-103515 - Improper Access Control issue in group Duo admin-lock enforcement for Amazon Q settings impacts GitLab EEGitLab has remediated an issue that, when an instance administrator locked a group’s Duo availability, an authenticated user with group Owner permissions could have re-enabled AI-backed data egress to a third-party service for that group and its descendant projects, due to insufficient granularity of the admin-lock enforcement controls.Thanks 3nvz for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty programImportant notes on upgradingThis patch includes database migrations that may impact your upgrade process.Impact on your installation:: This patch will cause downtime during the upgrade as migrations must complete before GitLab can start.The following versions include regular migrations that run during the upgrade process:The following versions include post-deploy migrations that can run after the upgrade:To learn more about the impact of upgrades on your installation, see:Receive Patch Notifications

item.title: Meta ordered to pay $25B penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case
item.author: cbg0
item.content:encoded: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg attends the annual Allen and Co. Sun Valley Media and Technology Conference at the Sun Valley Resort in Sun Valley, Idaho, U.S., July 9, 2026. Brendan McDermid | Reuters was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago. The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services. Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion."The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing.The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full."For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement.He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences."Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal.""This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September.In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg-led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users, raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices. Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. "Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said. Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial. Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal.

item.title: EA is shutting down BioWare
item.author: aaronbrethorst
item.content:encoded: Through every major moment we’ve faced as a company, your commitment to creating awesome games and experiences for our players continues to be impressive. Together, we’ve built epic worlds and global communities that are part of the lives of hundreds of millions of people.Today, we’re the number one publisher in Western HD gaming. That’s an extraordinary position to lead from, and one we should be proud of. Yet our industry is changing quickly. Players have more choices than ever for their time and attention, competition is intensifying, and some of our biggest opportunities for growth are beyond the markets, platforms, and business models where EA has traditionally been the strongest.That’s why, over the past several months, we’ve taken a hard look at our business, how we operate, and what it will take to lead in this next era of interactive entertainment. We’ve challenged assumptions, confronted hard realities, imagined new possibilities, and made deliberate choices in order to deliver exceptional experiences for our players and to drive sustained growth.We believe our best creative work happens when we’re clear about what matters most for our players and give our teams the freedom to move quickly. So, we’re concentrating our teams, technology, and investment behind these three strategic priorities.These priorities will bring clarity and focus to your work every day, and so will the way we work. We’ve spent time listening to teams about what’s working, what’s getting in the way, and what you need to do your best work. The feedback was consistent: you want clearer priorities, faster decisions, and teams that work more closely together. We’ve already begun simplifying how we work so we can spend more time creating and innovating for our players.Across our portfolio, we’re making deliberate choices to align talent and investments where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth.In our business Battlefield 6 was a great success, and we learned a lot from the launch and the live service. We’re going to take those learnings, balance our resources, and leverage the technology to deliver a shooter portfolio that unlocks growth. In addition to our future Battlefield titles, we’ll be bringing together our Respawn and DICE studios to collaborate on a future project that will help us achieve that ambition. We can’t wait to share more when the time comes. We’re also continuing to invest heavily in Apex over the next few years by introducing brand new gameplay modes in multiplayer, and other new experiences, to expand the universe. is one of the most competitive and high-stakes genres in the industry, where every game needs our full weight behind it. We’re continuing to deliver on our two huge launches coming up with Marvel’s Iron Man and the next Star Wars Jedi game. Beyond that, we will concentrate our efforts on fewer simultaneous, large-scale projects, ensuring that every game we build in this space is fully set up for success.As we focus on these larger opportunities, we’ve had a small team at BioWare working on early-development for Mass Effect. We’ve made the decision not to move forward with this development, which means we’re closing the studio and our Edmonton workspace. BioWare is a legendary studio that helped define the role-playing genre, and we do not take this decision lightly. continues to operate from a position of strength. We are fully committed and investing in the global growth of our FC franchise and across the full EA SPORTS portfolio. We have two new projects in development you’ll hear about over the next few months, including a brand-new, social-first open-world experience for our American Football team that we call “Project Gridiron,” and we are also in pre-production to bring back a beloved, fan-favorite in Fight Night, leveraging capabilities from our simulation fighting team.In , we’re focusing on the long-term potential of The Sims and skate. We’re going to prioritize our efforts on “Project Evergreen” for The Sims to give the team more time to reach the full potential and vision for the game, and to help make this possible, we’re pausing development on “Project Lotus.” For skate., we’ve had a lot of success in bringing players into the game, and we need to create an experience that keeps them engaged over the long-term. To do that, we are making changes to the studio to have a more focused, smaller team to deliver on a very clear roadmap for our community that we believe will build a healthier and more sustainable business.The decisions we’re making in our priorities, how we work, and with our portfolio reflect our belief in EA’s future. Some open exciting new possibilities. Others are difficult, especially for the people and teams across the company who are directly affected. In those cases, we will support impacted employees in exploring other opportunities within EA, and we’re committed to treating impacted colleagues with care and respect.We’re sure there will be questions about what these changes mean for individual teams and for EA more broadly. You can speak directly with your leaders to hear more on that, and we’ll make sure to spend time discussing our direction and the work ahead at our next Global Town Hall in November.The past several months have strengthened our belief in what EA can become. We have extraordinary people, franchises that matter to millions of players, and opportunities to build experiences we’ve only begun to imagine.Our responsibility is to make the choices, provide the clarity, and create the conditions for our teams to do their best work. We also want to give every game we choose to build its best chance to succeed for our players and fans around the world.We look forward to building more great games and experiences together.

item.title: Show HN: Omnara – Open-source alternative to Claude Managed Agents
item.author: kmansm27
item.content:encoded: Hey all, Kartik from Omnara (https://omnara.com) here. We're building an open-source API for running durable agents. You create an agent with an API call, and Omnara runs the agent loop, gives the agent sandboxes to run commands in, and handles secrets, permissions, and RBAC. Each agent's state is stored in Postgres, so agents survive restarts and cost nothing while idle. You can message them and stream their events over the API.You may remember us from our early days, when we made a remote-control phone app for Claude Code and Codex. Since the harness ran on a laptop back then, we had to build a relay to reach it, it stopped when the laptop closed, and moving it to a cloud sandbox meant syncing code and agent state between machines. We didn't think remote-controlling a local agent was end-game for how people would run agents, so we built a new product where the agent runs in the cloud, any client can talk to it through an API, and it can still use your laptop as one of its machines.Anthropic and OpenAI are building hosted versions of this, like Claude Managed Agents and the OpenAI Agents API. Omnara is an open-source version you can run on your own servers and use your own models. It's basically a harness server like the opencode or codex servers, but durable, scalable, with the usual harness features like file and shell tools, subagents, compaction, permission prompts, MCP, skills, memory, yada yada yada.Here's some interesting architectural decisions we made while building this out:Most harnesses, like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Goose, etc, run the agent loop in one long-lived process that keeps its log in a JSONL or SQLite file. In Omnara, the log is an append-only event log in Postgres, with inputs, model outputs and tool calls stored as typed rows in their own tables. The loop runs on stateless workers in the control plane. A worker runs one iteration of the loop, either a model call or the tool calls it produced, then releases the agent and puts the next iteration on a queue in Postgres. Whichever worker is free picks it up, so each iteration of an agent's loop can run in a different process on a different machine. Each iteration's result commits in one transaction, so the model output, its tool calls, usage and the next wakeup are saved together or not at all. If a worker dies mid-iteration, nothing commits, its lease expires, and another worker retries it. Agents waiting on a user, a tool or a retry don't hold a worker, so one worker can multiplex thousands of agents.Also unlike other harnesses, the machines that the workers (our agent loop) run on aren't where the agent runs its commands. Instead, any macOS or Linux machine with an internet connection, like your laptop or any cloud sandbox, can run a small daemon (omnarad) that connects out to Omnara, so it doesn't need any open inbound ports. The agent then gets tools for that machine, like running a command or editing a file. An agent can have any number of machines connected to it. A fun thing I like to do is I have my laptop and a cloud sandbox connected to the same agent, so when my laptop is on, my agent codes there and I can interact with it, and I have it often push to Github. When I close my laptop, my agent sees the laptop went offline, pulls the latest changes to its cloud sandbox, and continues there.

item.title: Today's PHP security release, and how we're strengthening security
item.author: ejohnso49
item.content:encoded: Earlier today, the PHP project released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. These releases fix two critical vulnerabilities that, under the right conditions, allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on servers running PHP. If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now. The announcement on php.net contains and references technical details on the vulnerabilities, attack vectors, and instructions on how to update on which systems.This post isn't about how to update. It's about how these vulnerabilities were found and fixed, what has changed in how PHP security is handled over the past two years, and what we need from the organizations that depend on PHP to keep PHP's security work going.CVE-2026-109618 / GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w: (out-of-memory): If a request reached PHP's memory_limit at exactly the wrong moment, PHP could leave partially initialized internal data behind and later treat it as valid, corrupting memory. On Apache with mod_php, an unauthenticated request can trigger this before any application code runs, and full remote code execution was demonstrated with default settings. Remote code execution was also confirmed on PHP-FPM through application-level code paths.CVE-2026-109619 / GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp: RCE via stale global state: A fatal error at the wrong point could leave internal state pointing to memory that belonged to a previous request. A later request handled by the same worker could then use that freed memory. A use-after-free and worker crash were confirmed, and the reporter demonstrated remote code execution against a real-world application running on Apache with mod_php.Both issues sit in parts of PHP that nearly every request touches: memory management and error handling. Their central place in PHP is what made both vulnerabilities serious, and also so hard to fix without breaking compatibility, hurting performance, or forcing changes on the large ecosystem of third-party extensions.A first external audit and increased security focusIn 2024, PHP underwent its first external security audit in years. The PHP Foundation secured funding from the Sovereign Tech Agency to organize this audit through OSTIF, and it was carried out by Quarkslab. While fixing one of the issues Quarkslab reported, a PHP core developer contracted by the PHP Foundation found the first signs of the OOM problem behind CVE-2026-109618. In 2024, a potential exploit for the OOM problem was theorized, but no concrete vectors were found and other concrete issues with clear impact overshadowed these concerns.To fix the OOM problem, the PHP security team developed several competing approaches, but each came with its own trade-offs: backward compatibility breaks, new denial-of-service potential, or requiring changes to many third-party extensions which seemed impossible to coordinate. The PHP security team, operating on consensus, struggled to choose between these and feared the repercussions of shipping the wrong choice. Combined with the lack of a known path to remote code execution and the small team of core developers with the necessary deep knowledge of the engine occupied with many responsibilities, this decision process caused work on a fix to stall and restart repeatedly over months. We won't pretend otherwise: the delay was a structural failure, caused by both the security team's decision process and its lack of resources. The security team has since started changing its processes, and that work continues, so that decisions can be made by majority and compromises are encouraged.Building a sustainable professional security organizationOver the last months the way PHP security work is organized has changed considerably. In May 2026, the PHP Foundation created the Ecosystem Security Team, which works alongside the PHP security team on triage, coordination, and hardening. Volker Dusch's work as AI Security Engineer in Residence at the PHP Foundation has significantly improved communication and collaboration between the PHP security team and the Foundation. Alexandre Daubois joined the PHP Foundation in July to help the PHP security team triage, handle, and fix security reports and Daniel Scherzer joined in September to take on hardening work.Earlier this year, we worked with Alpha-Omega to scan PHP with Anthropic's Claude Mythos. But since the Mythos scan, we have added other tools, including OpenAI's Daybreak Red for validating reports and exploits, alongside sanitizer builds and reproduction environments that match our CI on every platform PHP supports.The PHP Foundation got the PHP project into the Patch the Planet program, as part of which security firm Calif began an audit of PHP on July 30th, 2026. On August 11th, researcher Ryan A at Calif reported an unconditional remote code execution with the same root cause as the OOM problem we had found in 2024. OpenAI independently reported the same root cause, followed by further attack vectors from OpenAI on September 18th and from Wiz on August 24th. More recently, Trail of Bits has also been auditing PHP. The reports from Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz made the full impact of the OOM problem clear, and from August 11th onward, fixing it became the top priority for all of the PHP Foundation's team working on security. Without the Foundation’s funding it would have been impossible to have multiple people work on this issue full time, eventually through weekends and around the clock to coordinate and communicate with other involved parties.The growth of AI-assisted research also means the PHP security team receives far more reports than before. As Alexandre Daubois described last week in How the PHP Security Team Handles Your Reports, the team has published 15 CVEs since July 1st and worked through more than 100 reports that turned out to be invalid, duplicates, or not reproducible. AI helps the team validate reports and group reports sharing the same root cause, but a person makes every call and works on every patch.Leak and disrupted disclosureThe coordinated disclosure of these vulnerabilities worked well until 2 days ahead of the targeted release date.On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC. It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC. Distributors were still packaging the fix, so releasing immediately would have left many users without an easy way to update. Moving the release forward by one day was the best compromise between acting quickly, giving people time to prepare, and making sure everyone had a simple update path when the vulnerabilities were disclosed.As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues, mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st.Mitigation advice we started providing to a few critical infrastructure providers around Oct 20th 23:00 UTC, may have leaked as well. The PHP security team closely monitored and inspected appearing PoCs after the leak but did not identify any functional exploits at the time of release/public disclosure.On October 21st at 07:41 UTC, more than six hours before the coordinated release, Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix. Like other distributors, Chainguard had received the patch in advance so its users could update the moment the vulnerabilities were disclosed. Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release. This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure.A cautiously optimistic outlookToday's release shows the progress we’re making in how PHP security is handled. Once the full impact of the OOM problem was understood in August, the security team, the foundation, and the release managers delivered a fix for this deeply rooted problem across all supported branches, and distributions and LTS vendors received the patch ahead of time so their users can update quickly.We are confident that a serious vulnerability with a fix stuck on hard trade-offs would now reach the PHP Foundation leadership much sooner, as we’re changing processes so leadership can help steer the situation to a timely resolution. We are now prioritizing measures to make sure vulnerabilities that need similarly complex fixes get resolved faster when they are reported in the future. The PHP Foundation and the PHP security team learned a lot in the last weeks and will work to turn their experiences into lasting repeatable processes.PHP runs a large share of the web, including government services, online stores, banks, media sites, and much of the software that businesses rely on every day. Yet security work on PHP itself still depends on a small group of foundation-funded developers and a little volunteer help.Tools now find bugs faster than ever, for defenders and attackers alike, and the number of reports will keep growing. What tools cannot do is decide on the right fix for a long-standing design decision in the engine, weigh the compatibility trade-offs, and review the patch. Making those decisions takes experienced engineers who know the entire PHP codebase, and today there are too few of them.A core part of the PHP Foundation's mission is to grow the number of engineers with deep knowledge of the PHP codebase and give the security team the resources it needs. We can only achieve this goal with funding from those who depend on PHP:Companies that build products and services on PHP: please sponsor the PHP Foundation at a level that reflects how much you rely on it.Hosting providers, cloud platforms, and distributions that deliver PHP to millions of users.Governments and public institutions whose services run on PHP. The German Sovereign Tech Agency's funding of the 2024 audit shows what public investment can achieve, and we need more of it, on a sustained basis.Sponsoring the PHP Foundation is the most direct way to ensure structural issues like the OOM vulnerability are addressed sustainably, before they turn into emergencies. Become a sponsor at thephp.foundation/sponsor, and if your organization would like to talk about a larger commitment, get in touch.Thank you to the PHP security team, volunteers and PHP Foundation contractors alike, the release managers, and the package maintainers at distributions and LTS vendors who made these releases possible. Thank you to Calif, especially Ryan A, Wiz, OpenAI Codex Security, especially Amy Burnett, OSTIF, and Quarkslab for their research and responsible disclosure; to Alpha-Omega, OpenAI, and Anthropic for giving the team access to their tools and funding some of the security work; to the Sovereign Tech Agency for funding the 2024 audit; and to all of our sponsors, whose support made this work possible.

It’s written the way Chaplin put it: life, viewed up close, is a tragedy, but viewed from far away, it’s a comedy.It details extreme ambition, social anxiety, prison life, homelessness, addictions, and making money.Currently being written...
